#5640. 1969 Chevy Camaro Z/28 For Sale With 3,000 Miles Shown Since Odo Reset Pairs 302 V8 And 4-Speed Stick

#5639. 7 Concerning And Strange Items From Real GM Service Bulletins

Have you been looking for some new reading material, something amusing, maybe strange, or even alarming? Have you thought about perusing automotive service bulletins? Probably not. But we're a bunch of incurable car nerds here at Jalopnik, so service announcements are exactly the kind of thing we might read over our morning bowl of Cheerios.

It turns out there's some entertaining — and sometimes surprisingly concerning — stuff in those bulletins. For example, did you know that a little nest of spiders could cause $300 worth of damage in some Chevy vehicles? That's not all. Some General Motors (GM) vehicles repeatedly prank-called OnStar for a while, and it turns out that the rugged full-size 2024 and 2025 Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra were no match for car washes. You might also be surprised to learn that safety features like airbags and automatic emergency brakes can turn on you, and that a leaky roof can cause your key fob to stop working — and then there are all of the strange noises and odors.

You might expect some new cars to have problems or bugs that need to be corrected under warranty — maybe a transmission that doesn't shift right, some early coolant leaks, or a leaky sunroof. One thing you don't expect from a new car is it making prank calls to OnStar. Yet, according to one GM service update for the 2007 GMC Sierra, certain 2001-2008 light-duty trucks, Hummers, and even Saabs were exhibiting a "condition to which the vehicle owner/operator would be unaware of resulting in repeated incomplete calls to the OnStar being made." So, maybe instead of prank calling, it's more accurate to say the vehicles were doing the automotive electronic equivalent of butt dialing. The solution was a recall where the dealer would replace the OnStar Module (VCIM).

GM had acknowledged similar problems in an earlier service bulletin for the 2006 GMC Canyon, applicable to 1996 through 2008 OnStar-equipped vehicles, but the company mostly blamed the problem on customers. One explanation involved the customer hitting the white button, followed by the system misinterpreting a random sound, or background noise such as a "cough," as an emergency. Really, a cough? What would it do in case of a loud sneeze? Deploy the airbags?

Listen, people, you've got to take care of your trucks. That means not doing recklessly negligent things like washing them. At one point, drivers of some 2024 and 2025 Sierra/Silverado 2500 HDs and 3500 HDs found their check engine lights were coming on. Dealership technicians would see that the trucks were kicking out a DTC P244B diagnostic code, or "Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too High Bank 1." The culprit? According to Bulletin No. PIP6020A (PDF), "Engineering has found that this code may set if the vehicle was recently washed."

But that's not the only way water has vexed GM vehicle owners. Some owners of 2021 Chevy Tahoes and GMC Yukons were hearing "gurgling noises" after heavy rains and, you guessed it, car washes. It turned out to be residual water in sunroof drain tubes. The fix was to turn on the HVAC blower in fresh air mode to blow out the remaining water.

At first, the Cybertruck was the only truck that would get messed up by car washes, as the simple act of taking a Cybertruck through a car wash could brick it and possibly void its warranty. GM followed suit, though the worst its trucks could muster was a measly check engine light.

Modern cars come with lots of safety features to help you avoid accidents. Unfortunately, those safety features can sometimes go rogue. The Cadillac XT4 comes equipped with automatic emergency braking, which will stop the car if it detects an obstacle before the driver sees it. We imagine it's probably prevented more than one distracted driver from rear-ending a stopped car. That's all well and good until the car starts coming to a halt for objects that aren't there. That's exactly what some 2024 XT4s were doing, as reported by Service Bulletin 24-NA-053 (PDF). Yikes.

We'd hate to have that happen to us when we're trying to merge onto the freeway while everyone else is going 80 mph. The bulletin said the cause "may" be limitations in the camera. The confidence conveyed there is very reassuring. Of course, that's not as scary as the time GM recalled several cars due to temporary loss of braking.

In a similar case, Program Bulletin 12084 (PDF) alerted dealers that the Sensing and Diagnostic Module on some 2013 Chevy Malibus could reset itself after a hard braking event, a process that lasted three seconds. If the driver were to execute an "aggressive" turning maneuver during those three seconds, the side airbags could deploy. Or, if there was an accident during those three seconds, the seatbelt pretensioner might not work. These scenarios seem oddly specific, causing us to think that maybe this actually happened more than once.

Everyone knows that one friend who is, shall we say, "hygiene-challenged" and would benefit from a good shower. Perhaps among carmakers, GM is that friend, considering how many service bulletins have to do with odd smells emanating from their vehicles. These odors range from annoying to downright alarming.

For example, one GM Bulletin addressed gear oil smell in vehicles with remote vents. On the dangerous side, one safety recall of the Buick Regal GS and Pontiac Grand Prix said that owners may notice a burning smell, indicating a fire under the hood. Drivers of several 2022-2024 GM models noticed a smoke smell coming from under their seats, and technicians were likely to find "melted burn marks around the height adjuster motor."

Meanwhile, one GM bulletin treated unwanted odors as a sales opportunity for its proprietary product, GM Vehicle Care Odor Eliminator. It pitched it to the dealerships to be used by their service center techs for detailing as well as prepping their used cars for sale. To be fair, some smells can make a car hard to sell. It suggested that the product be given as a gift with a new car sale, as in, "Here's a little something for those unpleasant odors that will inevitably plague your new car." According to GM, displaying it prominently for sale would "increase dealership traffic" since the product isn't sold in stores. Sure, we can see people beating down the door to get their bottle of GM Vehicle Care Odor Eliminator.

Who doesn't like to hear a low growl that comes out of a powerful internal combustion engine? It's disturbing, though, to hear a growl when you put the car in park, whether the engine is running or not, but drivers of certain 1980 Oldsmobile Ninety Eights were hearing a growl when they would park the car on an incline. The GM bulletin that addressed this directed that drivers be told to engage the parking brake before shifting into park, then make sure the car is really in park.

What is the opposite of a growl? Chirps and squeaks might make good candidates. Those are the noises that have been coming out of some 2019-2023 model full-size trucks and SUVs. If we buy a full-size pickup with a huge V8, chirps and squeaks are not the kind of noises we want to hear coming from the engine. According to Bulletin 26-NA-021, ticks, taps, and typewriter noises have been heard coming from 2019 – 2026 Trucks. That has to be disconcerting.

Meanwhile, Bulletin 14-06-04-004G said that GM vehicles equipped with a two-stage vane-type oil pump have been known to make "Rrrrp" or "Rasp" noises when the engine starts in freezing weather or if the engine has been sitting for a few hours. Even weirder, the same bulletin said that vehicles equipped with a 6.2-liter engine may let out a "moan" after a cold start, at idle, or during operation at low RPMs. What's really weird is that GM says that all of these noises are normal.

Key fobs stop working from time to time. When it happens to us, we order a new battery from Amazon and call it a day. However, it has never occurred to us to check the car's roof. GM Service Bulletin 23-NA-107 (PDF) addressed pinhole leaks that would sometimes occur in the 2024 Chevy Trax. Oddly enough, that could cause the key fob to stop working. Apparently, water would get into some of the electronics, which somehow impacted the connection with the key fob. We have to give kudos to the engineer or technician who put two and two together and figured this out.

Key fobs don't have to be malfunctioning to help with troubleshooting, though. Some owners of the 2023 Cadillac XT4 and 2024 and 2025 Buick Envision had complained that the lights would flash when the vehicle was parked and the battery would be drained until it died. GM said this was likely caused by a defect in the K171 Rear Closure Hands Free Module. How could the tech tell for sure that this was the cause? Easy. The bulletin said to tape the key fob to the rear wiper. If the rear gate opens when the lights flash, it must be the K171 Rear Closure Hands Free Module. Again, we marvel at the mind that was able to connect the dots in this way.

No one likes to see the check engine light come on, but it was showing up on the dashboards of certain Buick Encore, Chevy Trax, and Chevy Sonic models during the 2010s for a surprising reason. Those vehicles were kicking out P0446 or P0455 error codes, indicating a restriction in the EVAP canister. Inconvenient, sure, but not strange — except that the service bulletin instructed technicians to check the EVAP canister for spider nests. We don't know why spiders liked this part so much or how many times techs found spiders in these EVAP canisters before this bulletin was put out, but apparently it happened enough for GM to rule arachnids as the likely cause.

You'd think that the remedy would just be to evict the spiders from the EVAP canister. Nope. GM said that the entire EVAP canister would need to be replaced. That's a $300 part. Who knew that a nest of spiders could do so much damage?

You might not think it, but service bulletins can make for an entertaining read, and we've just skimmed the surface with the examples we've covered here. If you're bored, you can check out more GM bulletins on the company's official website, and let us know in the comments if you come across any gems you find interesting.

#5638. NAED Energy Holding Inc. Details the Rating of Its PV-1 Tandem Cell Line: 16,000 Wafers per Hour per Line, 4.6 GW from Six Lines

NAED Energy Holding Inc. (NAED) just published the rating of PV-1, its production line for T2X perovskite/silicon heterojunction tandem solar cells. Each PV-1 line is rated at 16,000 G12 half-cut wafers per hour: 400 wafers every 90-second index, a rate set by the line’s inline PVD tool (ITO-1). The line’s four PECVD modules are built for a faster 76-second index, about 18,950 wafers per hour.

At NAED’s planning basis—85% availability, 97.5% yield, and the T2X programme target of 30% cell efficiency—one PV-1 line produces about 116 million cells and 0.77 GW of tandem cells a year. NAED’s six-line site, at 96,000 wafers per hour, has a rated capacity of about 4.6 GW a year.

Throughput and capacity in this release are rated values, and cell efficiency is modelled. NAED will publish measured throughput, yield, and efficiency, with their test basis, as results are logged. For all technical information on PV-1 and the T2X cell, contact cto.fusion@naedcorp.com.

The 34.4% figure is NAED’s modelled T2X cell (Voc 1.969 V, Jsc 20.18 mA/cm², fill factor 0.867, 217.2 cm² half-cell). For context, the highest published efficiencies for perovskite/silicon tandem cells of this size are in the 32–33% range, including Maxwell’s certified 32.38% on a G12 half-cell reported in January 2026. NAED’s planning figures use the 30% programme target.

The comparisons below are rate-to-rate. A PV-1 figure describes a complete integrated line, while some benchmarks describe a single tool; supplier figures are the suppliers’ own published ratings.

A single PV-1 line runs at or above the rate of leading single deposition tools while carrying the full tandem process — wet clean, PECVD, PVD, top-cell deposition, printing and test — in one line. Six lines carry the output of about three large HJT lines or seven to eight commercial tandem lines.

One year of output from the six-line site is enough cells for about 7.7 million 600-watt panels, which would generate roughly enough electricity for about 650,000 U.S. homes for a year (17% capacity factor, 10,500 kWh per home; typical U.S. values, not site data). Panels keep generating for 25–30 years, so each year of production adds to that total.

#5636. Here's How Much It Can Cost To Refuel These 5 Vehicles Due To High Diesel Prices

With the national average cost of a gallon of diesel fuel having been over six dollars for several months now, as a direct result of the Trump administration's war with Iran shutting off much of the world's oil supply, it's been an expensive time to own a diesel-powered vehicle. Add to that the inflation-and-tariff-driven ballooning cost of insurance, car payments, parts, and maintenance, and you've got a perfect storm of anti-consumer policies playing out in real time. As an owner and semi-regular driver of a 2013 Porsche Cayenne diesel, these policies have hit me directly in the pocketbook. I'm managing to weather the storm well enough, but many of America's working class families have been devastated by this blow to the affordability of daily life.

Recent reports from Fortune Magazine indicate that the war has cost the average American household nearly $2,000 since it began in February, with the lion's share of that cost coming as a result of increased energy costs. We're all getting hit pretty hard right now at the pump. I wanted to take a look at just how hard us diesel drivers are getting crunched, and provide a bit of context for the people who might not fully understand the numbers.

Let's take a look together at the increase in costs to fill a tank of diesel in a handful of diesel-powered machines. We'll also look at historical diesel cost trends, what some non-Americans are paying, and how this price increase impacts other segments of the global economy.

Here's a fun one to kick off this exercise. Between 2002 and 2008, Volkswagen stuffed a giant ten-cylinder turbocharged diesel V10 into its flagship SUV, the Touareg. It was a torque powerhouse with 553 pound-feet on tap. A product of the engineering excess Volkswagen Group committed to during Ferdinand Piech's tenure as Chairman, this engine was completely unnecessary, but in hindsight, pretty frickin' cool. One major downside, however, was that it was rated at just 17 mpg combined.

The fuel tank in a V10 TDI Touareg holds 100 liters, or 26.41 gallons. With the current national average price of diesel sitting at $6.17 per gallon, if you rolled in with a completely empty tank (not recommended, by the way), it would cost a staggering $162.95 to fill it back up to the tippy top. Do you think that's expensive? Let's look at what our friends to the north are paying in Canada. The current Canadian average for diesel fuel is about 2.60 CAD per liter. That equates to about $1.84 per liter, or $184 to fill that same tank. Europe is the home of expensive fuel, right? Over in the European Union, they're paying €2.15 per liter on average. At current exchange rates, that's $2.41 per liter ($9.12 per gallon), or $241 for a diesel Touareg fill-up.

On average, Americans drive around 13,660 miles per year. If they happened to be one of the few people in the country daily-driving a twenty-year old German SUV with a Volkswagen V10 TDI under the hood, at current diesel rates they're going to pay around $4,957.78 for fuel this year. If I owned one, I think I'd be looking for something a little more efficient.

The Volkswagen XL1 wasn't sold in the U.S. market, but it's another product of the Piech era of over-engineering at VW. The goal here was to build the world's most efficient vehicle, using an offset two-seat configuration, a tiny carbon fiber monocoque, extreme lightweighting and aerodynamic advancements, and a two-cylinder 48-horsepower diesel engine mated to a plug-in hybrid electric motor. While the car was absurdly expensive and not really very good at anything but looking cool and sipping fuel — it managed to do over 100 kilometers on just 0.9 liters of diesel. That's the equivalent of about 261 mpg. It's basically the philosophical opposite of the Touareg V10 TDI.

With just enough battery capacity to travel about 31 miles on a charge, plus a tiny 10-liter fuel tank, the XL1 is hardly a long-legged touring machine. That said, topped up on both, it's efficient enough to travel around 500 miles at a go. Only 250 of these machines were built, so it's unlikely you will have a practical use for this information, but maybe you can trot it out at a party or something. Let's compare the XL1 to the Touareg.

Obviously, since the tank is one-tenth the size of the Touaregs, a fill up in the XL1 will be one-tenth the cost. I certainly wouldn't mind spending $16.29 for a full tank of diesel. That same fill-up would be $18.40 if you're Canadian, or $24.10 for our European friends. The same 13,660 miles that cost almost five grand in a Touareg would be just $322.92 (plus a few extra bucks on your electricity bill to charge the hybrid gubbins) in the XL1. It just goes to show how important fuel efficiency is for your annual running costs.

It's been a handful of years since Ford offered a diesel option for its basic F-150 pickup, but the F-series Super Duty lineup still offers the massive 6.7-liter Power Stroke turbo diesel V8 as a $12,495 option. This is one of the most popular diesel vehicles in the U.S. today.

If you opt for the long-wheelbase 8-foot bed Crew Cab configuration, the truck is delivered with a gigantic 48-gallon fuel tank. Now that's an incredibly expensive fill-up. At the $6.17 average we mentioned earlier, that's $296.16 per tank. If you happen to drive a Power Stroke Super Duty in California, where a gallon of diesel is $8.14, you're looking at nearly $400 in diesel. And don't even get me started on the cost of DEF.

Because the F-250 doesn't have to report fuel economy numbers and isn't subject to EPA reporting, it's hard to get an exact number, but Power Stroke Super Duty owners report real-world fuel economy on Fuelly around 14 mpg. At that rate over the same 13,660 miles per year, a diesel F-250 owner is paying $6,020.15 for a year of fuel. If they're Californian, you can pump that number up to $7,942. Add with the cost of a monthly truck payment and decent car insurance, and you're going to see a really high cost of ownership here.

Have you noticed that the produce in your local grocery store is getting more expensive? According to the Department of Agriculture, U.S. fruit and vegetable prices have risen nearly 5% and 3%, respectively, with further increases expected through 2027. At least some of that increase can be attributed to the increase in diesel prices, as basically every farm implement on the planet is run by diesel fuel. The Farm Bureau reports that U.S. farmers spent a combined $2.4 billion more on diesel fuel during the 2026 planting season compared to 2025.

Let's take a look at the best-selling combine harvester in the market for the purposes of this exercise, John Deere's S780. This giant machine chews up, separates, and spits out most field-grown grains, corn, soybeans, rice, and even sunflower. It also burns quite a lot of diesel.

The S780 has an absolutely massive fuel tank, taking on a full 330 gallons from dry to full up. Obviously, farmers don't pay the same price as standard road diesel, as "red dye" off-road diesel is exempt from road excise taxes. Federal taxes are levied on diesel at a rate of about 25 cents per gallon, while state diesel taxes average around 35 cents per gallon. It's hard to say exactly what farmers will pay because there are delivery fees and bulk purchase discounts to take into consideration, but for the sake of simplicity, let's just take that 60 cents from the $6.17 national average road diesel price and say farmers pay $5.57. That means filling up this John Deere will still be an impressive $1,838 bill. Back in January, when road diesel was about $3.47, a fill-up would have been just $947.10, about half as much.

If you thought farm equipment was expensive to fill up, just wait until you hear about the incredible costs of fueling a semi. And we'll use the current market leader, the Freightliner Cascadia, as our benchmark.

The Cascadia is available in a bunch of different configurations, and each configuration has its own separate fuel tank capacity, depending on engine size, sleeper length, and axle count. Each truck carries one large aluminum tank on either side of the cab, ranging from 80 gallons to 150 gallons of capacity each. For maximum effect, let's look at the largest 300-gallon long-haul trucker configuration. At today's prices, it would cost a whopping $1,851 to cram both tanks full of diesel. That really puts things into perspective, doesn't it?

The Department of Energy says semi-trucks on the road in the U.S. travel an average of 58,890 miles per year. Considering there are around 2.9 million active registered semi trucks on the road today, that's a whole lot of miles travelled and a whole lot of diesel burned. At the current average price of diesel, and with the Cascadia achieving an astonishing industry-best 10 mpg, each one of these monsters costs $36,335.13 per year to feed. If you've been wondering why prices are going up at the grocery store lately, this is a pretty big part of it. Transporting goods from manufacturer to retailer is expensive.

#5635. Environmental, Public Health Experts Testify During Public Hearings on Methane Pollution Rollback Proposal

Sierra Club staff & members highlight dangers of rolling back methane pollution standards.

Washington, DC — Today and tomorrow, environmental and public health experts, alongside community advocates, will testify during a virtual public hearing to the dangers and risks posed by the Trump administration’s proposed rollback of long-awaited methane pollution standards finalized in 2024. The hearing is part of a broader public comment period in reaction to the Environmental Protection Agency’s plan to reverse key components of the landmark safeguards aimed at reducing methane, and associated pollution, from both new and existing oil and gas equipment.

Soon after taking office in 2025, the Trump EPA suspended the implementation of key provisions from the Biden-era standards, delaying their enforcement by up to 18 months despite no widespread evidence of compliance difficulties. Now, this rollback would permanently eliminate some of the rule’s most important safeguards, including its ban on routine flaring at oil wells and its program to leverage third-party monitoring data to identify and stop particularly large methane releases known as super-emitter events.

The proposal would also shield low-producing wells from leak monitoring requirements and other key safeguards, despite consistent evidence showing that such wells do not pollute less than higher-producing wells. Nearly one in ten people in the U.S. live in a county with over a thousand low-producing wells. These sources represent nearly half of the sector’s methane emissions and are primarily owned by large, well-resourced and highly profitable corporations.

Sierra Club experts and members will be among many testifying against the rollback.

In reaction, Sierra Club staff providing testimony released the following statements:

Andres Restrepo, Sierra Club Senior Attorney said: “EPA’s authority and obligation under the Clean Air Act to control methane emissions from the oil and gas sector has long been settled law, and the safeguards that the Biden Administration put into place in 2024 rely on cost-effective, widely available technologies and practices that the industry itself has used for years. The Trump Administration’s current proposal to strip the 2024 rule for parts and leave a rump regulation in place has support in neither the law nor the facts. The agency is attempting to manufacture sham justifications to mask what is nothing more than the giveaway that Donald Trump openly promised to oil and gas executives in exchange for supporting his campaign. Sierra Club will use every resource at its disposal to fight back against this betrayal of our families and communities.”

Cyrus Reed, Legislative and Conservation Director of Sierra Club’s Lone Star Chapter, said: “No state produces more oil and gas than Texas, and no state has more to gain from strong methane regulations than our state. We already have poor air quality from ozone pollution, particulate matter and other pollutants like hydrogen sulfide, and rolling back the methane standards will only make matters worse. Texas voters went to the polls in record numbers for a non-presidential election, and for the most part, voted for change, in largely because of anger over rising prices, but also due to a politics that often favor entrenched wealthy interests. This rollback proposal does not respond to this call for change, but instead proposes to let bad corporate actors off the hook and increase pollution that leads to higher energy prices, harms our health, and supercharges climate disruption.”

Antoinette Reyes, Permian Basin Organizer, Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter, said: “As the federal government moves to weaken methane protections, New Mexico is working to strengthen its own. But pollution doesn’t stop at state lines, and neither should our commitment to protecting communities. Families in the Permian Basin already face industrial air pollution, from odors and poor visibility to respiratory health concerns. Every preventable methane leak wastes a valuable energy resource, potential tax revenue, and affects the quality of the air we breathe. Proven technology exists to reduce these emissions. State action alone cannot fill the gap left by federal rollbacks. We need strong protections at every level to safeguard our health, climate, and communities.”

Sarah Corcoran, Deputy Director of the Sierra Club Pennsylvania Chapter, said: “Pennsylvania is one of the leading states in the nation for fracked gas infrastructure. We are also one of the states with the highest pediatric asthma and cancer rates — but those numbers are increasing across the nation. The Trump Administration is not doing anyone any favors by reducing these regulations, not the industry, not the environment and not the American people who will feel the health impacts of these decisions for years to come. Policies that reduce methane waste, such as controls on flaring, quicker response times, transparent communications with impacted residents and more frequent testing are commonsense and cost effective. We need stronger protections in place for methane, not looser.”

Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that has more than 80 times the power of carbon dioxide over a 20-year period, driving approximately one-third of the warming our planet has experienced to date. Each year, the U.S. oil and gas sector emits large amounts of methane into our atmosphere. Methane is emitted from oil and gas sources alongside other damaging pollutants, such as smog- and soot-forming volatile organic compounds and air toxins like benzene and formaldehyde, human carcinogens.

According to EPA’s analysis, the 2024 standards are projected to avoid 58 million tons of methane through 2038, as well as 16 million tons of volatile organic compounds and 590,000 tons of air toxins.

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person's right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. For more information, visit www.sierraclub.org.

#5634. Scientists Are Using Your Unhinged Driving Behaviors In Grand Theft Auto To Make Roads Safer

As you're preparing to explore all of 212 GB's worth of "Grand Theft Auto VI" and go on the ultimate chaotic crime driving spree in the game's Florida-like state of Leonida, scientists are gearing up for their own run through the new game. GTA's years of detailed city streets, paired with drivers' unhinged behaviors behind the wheel have unintentionally created a solid test bed for a variety of scientific studies aimed at making real-life driving and travel safer, according to the BBC.

If scientists want to look at how humans react to dangerous situations on the road, what game has better scenarios than GTA? The game's detailed city maps and roads also help make the science cheaper.

Pavlo Bazilinskyy, a human factors engineer at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands, told the BBC that a video game with such a massive budget is "miles ahead of the average simulator setup." GTA provides a realistic environment for Bazilinskyy and his fellow researchers. It's an ideal space for them to use technology like eye-tracking, or more specifically, cyclist behavior as they head towards hazardous situations.

Intel Labs and Darmstadt University in Germany shared a paper in 2016 on how the two used Grand Theft Auto's road scenes and objects to teach AI how to detect both. MIT Technology Review wrote that using the video game's already categorized imagery and streets would help researchers save thousands upon thousands of hours trying to collect and label that street imagery. The game's addition of changes in time and weather, which can both influence the road conditions, helps models experience realities that are difficult and expensive for researchers to recreate digitally.

Institutions like the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology conduct similar research today, using GTA to help train its AI driving software to avoid dangers on the road. In the U.S., at Eastern Michigan University, researchers have used GTA to train an AI's ethical decision-making. EMU's work found that the tests helped reduce fatal accidents by 24%.

There are devices currently in development that could alert cyclists and pedestrians of upcoming hazards on busy roads, acting like a sixth sense for detecting traffic behind them. To test one of these devices, researchers at the Osnabrück University of Applied Sciences in Germany placed participants on a stationary bike with screens showing GTA V in front of and behind them. The devices successfully spotted traffic as it headed towards the cyclists, but without the inherent danger that would be a part of testing the device on a real road.

Science and road safety may be the two furthest things from the average GTA player's mind come Friday, when the sixth installment is available for gameplay. However, scientists and researchers will likely be thrilled to have a newer, even more realistic setting to play with.

#5633. OMCO Solar offers solar-powered tracker control system

OMCO Solar now offers a version of its OMCO Star Tracker Control System powered entirely by solar energy, allowing tracker controls to operate without AC power at the site.

The system, first launched last year, is designed for OMCO Origin Factory-Direct Trackers. Its tracker controllers, array controllers and sensor bridges use all-weather battery packs charged by solar modules.

According to OMCO, the technology eliminates the need for AC power to tracker control components and an uninterruptible power supply. It also allows tracker controls to operate and protects modules against wind, snow and hail before AC power is available.

“Our industry has solved so many problems as we have grown – we’re now the leading source for new electric energy capacity in the US. This addition to the OMCO Star product line solves one more – how to protect modules if there’s no AC power to the site even for a short time. We’re excited to offer this solution to our existing customers and to new partners,” said Matt Kesler, vice president of solar technology at OMCO Solar, in a statement.

The OMCO Star system uses LoRa, or long-range, wireless technology with a communication range greater than 1 mile. According to OMCO, this reduces the number of network controllers required and allows direct communication with every tracker without relying on a mesh network.

The company says LoRa is 100 times less susceptible to electromagnetic noise than Zigbee and better able to connect to distant trackers despite obstacles.

OMCO says its all-weather battery packs allow the solar-powered controls to operate reliably in cold climates. The system includes field-replaceable batteries, a phone app that eliminates the need for buttons on controllers and a remote monitoring and control portal.

The portal allows operators to move trackers for activities such as mowing, snow plowing and module cleaning. The system is developed, manufactured and supported by OMCO Solar in the United States.

“We are excited about bringing this innovation to the Utility Scale and DG tracker markets. Over the past few years, OMCO has expanded its capabilities beyond just being a US steel manufacturer to now being a true technology leader in our space. We look forward to supporting our customers/partners with the OMCO Star Tracker Control System, improving reliability, and reducing the labor and materials needed to build their projects,” said Eric Goodwin, vice president of business development at OMCO Solar.

OMCO Solar will display the all-DC tracker control system at RE+ in Las Vegas, November 17–19, in the North Hall, booth N516.

#5632. Tissue and Liquid Biopsies May Complement Each Other in Prostate Cancer

— Analysis found no significant differences in genomic alterations across ethnic groups

An analysis of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress found no statistically significant differences in actionable genomic alterations, tumor mutational burden (TMB), or circulating tumor (ct)DNA fraction across ethnic groups. The findings also showed differences in mutation detection between tissue and liquid biopsies, suggesting the two testing methods may provide complementary information.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Virginia Yuk-Chun Lam, an MD candidate at King's College London, discusses the findings and their potential implications for identifying actionable mutations and guiding targeted treatment.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

What we did this year is we looked at 350 patients with prostate cancer. They all have castration-resistant prostate cancer and had one line of ARPI [androgen receptor pathway inhibitor] and progressed.

So what we did is we looked at both the tissue and the ctDNA to check if they've got any actionable genomic mutations and looked at their tumor mutation burden and also their ctDNA fractions.

The reason we are particularly interested in this group of patients is we know that there are some ethnicity differences, and also where I'm based in Guy's Hospital, it is a very diverse population with a high number of Black [patients]. So we would like to see if there's any ethnicity differences in those kinds of actionable mutations, TMB, and also ctDNA fractions.

So what we found out is the actionable mutation BRAF is kind of numerically higher in Black patients. The highest numbers of mutations were TP53; however, there's no ethnicity differences in them. For the patients with aggressive mutations in TP53, RB1, and PTEN, there's no particular differences in the ethnicity either. But with all of these, there's no statistical differences in all of these patients, but BRAF is numerically higher.

The next thing we also looked at is the mutational burden to see if there's any ethnicity differences. And what we found out is that between the tissue and the ctDNA, they are higher in the ctDNA fractions, which we kind of expected because when we looked at the ctDNA, we know they pick up a little bit more and also when the ctDNA is taken, that is when they progress.

The last thing we looked at is to try to match the ctDNA fraction and the tissue concordances to see if we pick up higher concordances in certain kinds of mutations. In our 101 patients, they got paired samples. We found out there's high concordances in BRCA and also patients with aggressive mutations. However, in PTEN, there's low concordances, but mainly they're picked up by the ctDNA.

So that's kind of a top four of what we presented at ESMO this year. And from what we can make a conclusion of it, it is a single-center cohort, we would like to extend it to a multicenter cohort with a wider ethnicity as well. Statistically, there's no big differences amongst the actionable mutation, TMB, and also ctDNA fractions. However, numerically we know it is higher in BRCA1/2, and we also found out that PTEN, as I say, is better picked up in ctDNA.

So we hope that in the future these two modalities can help each other to pick up the most actionable mutations and can benefit to see if we can find targeted drugs for the patients who progress in this kind of cohort.

I know especially in the U.K. sometimes we don't do it together. A lot of time we do tissue at diagnosis and ctDNA when they progress. But I think we found that both modalities are important. So if we can, we can try to do both.

But I know probably in other countries, say in the U.S., you've got a little bit more resources and you might tend to do both, but in other settings, this is kind of an insight that we can consider both as a way to find the most targeted actionable mutations to targeted drugs.

Richmond, Virginia — Tomorrow, November 17, the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) will begin the evidentiary hearing for NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy’s merger proposal, which would create the nation’s largest ever utility. Sierra Club filed expert testimony last month urging the SCC to reject the merger given the way it threatens the Virginia’s Clean Economy Act (VCEA) and violates the Utility Transfers Act, posing a significant risk to energy affordability for Virginia families.

Dominion and NextEra have failed to show that customer benefits, not shareholders profits, were a motivating factor for the merger. The utilities have offered a temporary $10 per month bill credit to Virginia customers for four years to help cover any additional costs. However, the credit does not so much as cover the $30 per month Virginia families expect to pay in anticipated bill increases to maintain fossil fuel plants and meet AI data centers demand in 2027 alone.

If approved, the new utility would service 10 million customers across the Southeastern United States. Allied groups will rally outside the SCC tomorrow for the Stop the NextEra Takeover: Final Rally at the SCC.

Ahead of tomorrow’s hearing, Connor Kish, Director of the Sierra Club Virginia Chapter, issued the following statement:

“Throughout November, Virginians have shown up in droves at public hearings to oppose Dominion and NextEra’s proposed merger. Utility customers, independent policy experts, and local leaders have cited sky-high energy bills, AI data center demand, and abandoned climate goals as reasons to be wary of Dominion and NextEra’s bid to become the country’s largest ever utility.

“Meanwhile, the utilities have yet to prove the merger will result in any tangible benefits for customers. Their offer of a temporary $10 monthly bill credit for customers is nothing in comparison to the $10 billion in profits shareholders are anticipated to receive should the SCC approve the merger. Virginia deserves utilities that prioritize families, not shareholders out for bonuses. To keep the lights on and make bills affordable, it’s critical that SCC fulfill its duty to the public and reject the merger.”

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person's right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. #5630. The Smallest V10 To Ever Power A Car Was The Size Of Most 4-Cylinders

V10 engines are the ultimate metaphors for what gearheads love about performance cars — relics of a bygone era where noise, power and absolute combustion were the go-to recipes of kings. The Lexus LFA and Porsche Carrera GT – arguably two of the greatest road-going supercars ever – used them. So too did the Sesto Elemento, which was Lamborghini's answer to the very essence of track-day hoonery. They even featured in the E60-generation BMW M5 – a perhaps ugly but elegant grand tourer that made a mockery of purpose-built, seven-figure unobtanium thanks to an unrestricted 200-mph-plus top speed.

But aside from the actual cylinder count, what these cars all have in common is big displacements. The LFA's V10 is the smallest of the bunch, and even that measures in at 4.8 liters. You'd think, then, that all V10s must surely have to be meaty by nature to work, but you'd be wrong. Say hello to the Connaught Type D concept: a sports car conceived in 2004 and equipped with a pipsqueak 2.0-liter V10. Yes, two liters.

For some perspective, many passenger cars these days use 2.0-liter four-cylinder engines, including the Honda Civic hatchback, which is the platonic ideal of economy cars. Now imagine constraining yourself to such a small surface area, with the added complication of having to manage an extra six cylinders. The result would be ... amazing, actually.

The standard Connaught used a naturally aspirated V10 and a Lynch electric motor for 162 hp. Yes, hybrid technology was being tested as far back as 2004 with this car, long before the hypercar Holy Trinity was formed and crowned. However, in the top-spec "Syracuse GT" version, the Type D's V10 engine was instead paired with a supercharger for a healthy 300 hp. The Connaught Type D Syracuse GT's 0 to 60 mph was projected to be in the low-four-second range, and popular publications cited a top speed of roughly 171 mph. This thing also tipped the scales at just 1,874 pounds.

Those are some serious numbers and would be enough to trouble many four-cylinder sports cars that, dare we say, could be called super. Even today's fleet of racey four-banger metal wouldn't be safe. The Honda Civic Type R, which is a rowdy teenage dirtbag, takes about a second longer to get to 60 mph, while the 2026 Ford Mustang RTR (with its 2.3-liter engine) only just edges it by two-tenths of a second (via Car and Driver). Unfortunately, the Type D never made it past the concept stage and into production due to funding issues.

The brand was acquired in 2016 by a British automotive design company called Bevan Davidson International (BDI), and in 2021, it came up with a wild idea to revive Connaught with a 20-cylinder supercar called the X20. We'll give you a moment to rub your eyes and re-read the final part of that sentence.

That 20-cylinder engine would be made up of two horizontally opposed and mid-mounted 2.0-liter V10s. It would also blow its waste gases out of no fewer than 20 exhaust pipes, rev all the way up to 10,000 rpm, and, as far as the company's calculations go, produce more than 500 hp. That sounds less like a car, and more like a miniature steam train from the 17th century, but no word on whether any have been produced yet.

Whether BDI chooses to also bring the original Type D back to life remains to be seen, but just think about it for a second: A tiny-displacement, supercharged V10-powered sports car built to comply with the ever-growing regulations posed on the industry by lawmakers. Wouldn't that be just marvelous?

#5629. 'He Should Talk to His Primary Care Doctor About That'

— We should treat the patient in front of us whenever possible

One spring day during my neurology rotation, a man in his nineties came to our clinic. He was walking with a cane but otherwise remarkably independent, with the air of distinguished gentlemanliness a brown tweed jacket lends. We had an instant connection. Talking for just a few moments, we realized he hailed from my own family's ancestral town. As I spoke with him in his native language, he soon began calling me "pota" for "grandson." Quickly though, my resident and I also realized our patient was with us by mistake. Perhaps due to a miscommunication, or an administrative error, he thought he was at his primary care physician (PCP). He had been experiencing constipation.

After we clarified the confusion, my resident -- someone who taught me a great deal -- asked me to walk our patient out to the front desk and help him schedule a primary care appointment. The front desk said the next PCP appointment wouldn't be available for 7 weeks. I went to ask the resident if we could do something to help our patient; after all, while constipation may turn out to be a complex symptom either due to a serious condition (colorectal cancer, sigmoid volvulus) or as a precursor to downstream pathology (diverticulosis, fecal impaction), it is also quite common among older adults.

Both the resident and I had rotated on internal medicine and knew the questions to ask to identify any red flags and suggest a bowel regimen. And we had the time -- our patient didn't have a neurological concern, but he still had the appointment slot. Yet, when I returned to the clinic room to ask my resident if we could give our patient the relevant advice, he looked up from the queue of notes he was finishing and replied: "He should talk to his PCP about that."

Economics tell us that workforce efficiency is maximized when everyone spends time on what they are uniquely best at doing: labor arbitrage. As a management consultant prior to medical school, I spent years evangelizing this concept of "top of license work" to clients -- mostly large academic and nonprofit hospital systems. And I still believe in the principle broadly, albeit with perhaps a bit more reticence and understanding more nuance than before.

Top-of-license work in medicine doesn't only apply vertically across levels of training; it also operates horizontally, across fields. Patient outcomes are generally maximized when neurologists focus on diseases of the nervous system and gastroenterologists the digestive system because each specialty is doing work only they can do. Yet, that day in the neurology clinic taught me a nuance to this perspective.

At the end of the day, all physicians should consider themselves doctors first, and specialists second. Medical specialization shouldn't absolve specialists of the duty to help the patient before them -- especially when doing so requires minimal time and resources -- even if the patient's concern is not directly within their field.

Of course, there are challenges to this perspective. I can empathize with the medico-legal concerns of a neurologist who is served a subpoena and deposed by a lawyer: "Firstly, why did you manage this constipation? And why did you not order XYZ tests for this patient with constipation who turned out to have colorectal cancer?" And I recognize the confusion medical teams may feel when checking charts and seeing who prescribed certain medications: "Why is the prescribing doctor for this patient's cetirizine (Zyrtec) an orthopedic surgeon?"

These concerns are real. But primary care is a limited resource too. The dumping of basic tasks on primary care -- a field with its own specialized expertise that is often not recognized -- has been discussed ad nauseam; specialists should help relieve this burden when possible.

Labor arbitrage and top of license work still apply when specialists help patients with "primary care problems." However, because of the design of our healthcare system, there is little structural incentive for physicians to work outside of their typical scopes. If, for instance, we financially incentivized all of a patient's physicians by the same quality metrics, specialists would be incentivized not just in their field, but across the spectrum of the patient's health. Or even if we had less insurance churn, payers would perhaps better leverage incentives within their networks to promote overall health.

Responding to incentives does not mean physicians have moral failings. It shows they are human. But if we continue to depend on our system as currently designed, we will continue to have rampant "moral alibis" -- a term coined by Sachin Jain, MD, MBA, to highlight how physicians at times emphasize problems with the system to escape responsibility for personal decisions -- that limit the impact of our care.

The vast majority of physicians enter medicine to help patients. It is the design of our system that has forced practice to occur in unnatural ways. But perhaps while we solve these structural problems, we can start changing things by treating the patient in front of us -- one case of constipation at a time.

#5627. 2027 Toyota GRMN Corolla Cranks The GR's Fun Factor Up To 11

Toyota shook up the compact performance car space when it introduced the GR Corolla back in 2022, and perhaps even more remarkably, it has continuously improved the car each year since. I had the distinct pleasure of hucking the 2026 GR Corolla around Sonoma Raceway last year at the press launch, and in a rare turn of events, I actually got to compare its driving dynamics to a 2025 car as well as a 2024 model.

That comparison showed me how the GR team's gradual tweaks positively impacted the experience of driving a GR Corolla, and last week I got the chance to try out their latest creation. Toyota let me loose the limited-production 2027 GRMN Corolla around Eagles Canyon Raceway in Texas to experience what is the ultimate Corolla — for now, at least. Again, the changes are small, but the resulting improvements are immediately palpable.

Full disclosure: Toyota wanted me to sample an array of its new offerings for 2027 so badly that it flew me out to Texas, put me up in a hotel for a few nights, and kept me fed so I could drive its cars. I only got to drive the GRMN Corolla on the track, so I cannot offer on-road impressions.

The GRMN Corolla earned those last two letters while lapping arguably the most iconic race track on the planet, the Nürburgring. The MN in GRMN represents the fact that this version of the GR Corolla was tuned by the "Meisters of the Nürburgring," and that's not just marketing jargon. The GR team made suspension, aerodynamic, cooling, and drivetrain tweaks. They also swapped some metal body panels for carbon-fiber ones, all with the goal of making the GRMN Corolla the most track-focused GR Corolla yet.

Suspension-wise, Toyota changed the bump stops because it found the GR Corolla's standard suspension would hit the bump stops on certain corners of the Nürburgring, causing sudden understeer. Aerodynamically, Toyota added a larger hood duct, bumper side splitters, fender ducts from the Super Taikyu hydrogen-engine GR Corolla development car to reduce front-end lift, and that adjustable rear spoiler for increased stability. The entire hood, both front fenders, and the rear spoiler are made from carbon fiber, and the rear seat was removed in order to save weight, making the GRMN weigh 66 pounds less than a standard GR Corolla.

Moving to the drivetrain, Toyota added a supplemental AWD transfer case oil cooler that will also be available for other GR Corollas but comes as standard on the GRMN, which keeps the system cool even after repeated laps in high temperatures. There's also a standard intercooler sprayer to keep it and the turbo working hard in high temperatures, too.

Engineers retuned Track Mode in the GRMN's GR-Four all-wheel-drive system to make it more rear-biased, and they managed to increase the turbocharged 1.6-liter three-cylinder engine's torque output by 7 pound-feet while also making maximum torque available at lower engine speeds, so it now produces 300 horsepower and 302 lb-ft. The changes are definitely palpable on the track, with my favorite upgrades being the GRMN's sticky Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires, the retuned steering rack with increased feedback, and the close-ratio transmission from the Morizo Edition, all of which heightened the GRMN Corolla's dynamics.

Toyota so graciously let the media go hog wild on Eagles Canyon Raceway before, which I had never seen or driven before, and luckily I was in the perfect car to attempt to learn the 2.7-mile "Italian Canyon" course's 15 corners, 20 apexes, and 150 feet of elevation change. We weren't allowed to do any consecutive laps — we had to enter the pits on each lap — but we were allowed to do as many laps as we pleased. I drove both the GRMN Corolla and a 2026 GR Corolla to see if I could tell the difference, and the answer was a resounding "hell yeah!"

Taking off from the pits, the GRMN Corolla's inputs immediately felt more taut and communicative, from the snickety shifter to the talkative steering. Once I left pit lane and got to wring out the powertrain, the GRMN's extra mid-range torque and lighter weight made it feel like it had noticeably more shove than the standard GR. Cornering is where the GRMN really shined, though.

When I first entered a corner, the GRMN's reworked steering felt sharper and more direct, and the more rear-biased all-wheel-drive tune in Track Mode made its nose feel like it could change direction like a greyhound weaving through the slalom at the AKC National Agility Championship. Compared to the GR, the GRMN felt markedly more agile and more eager to rotate rather than understeer.

The GRMN's retuned engine pulled its lighter weight out of corners stronger than the GR, and its Cup 2 tires made it cling to the road with what felt like merciless ferocity. Naturally, since this was my first time on this track I made my fair share of corner misjudgments, but even when I overcooked a decreasing radius turn, a dab of brakes made the GRMN dive toward the apex, expertly turning "oh crap" moments into drama-free learning experiences. Chief Engineer for the GR Corolla Naoyuki Sakamoto called the GRMN, "a car you can confidently push the limits in," and Sakamoto-san was absolutely correct.

The GRMN Corolla is an extremely limited-production vehicle, with just 730 units planned globally, so the U.S. market will get even fewer than that. Exclusivity paired with the GRMN Corolla's other driving experience enhancements and proven track-oriented capabilities make it a rare special edition that truly feels special. That said, it's set to cost $65,665, so it had better be pretty damn special to make you pay $65k for a freakin' Corolla.

The interior is all Corolla, but at least it has more aggressive bucket seats and a flocked instrument panel and A-pillars. You also forgo the opportunity to bring more than one passenger along for the ride, since the GRMN has what looks like a lap bar from a roller coaster rather than a back seat. Perhaps the biggest issue I had with the GRMN Corolla was that its rear windows do not roll down. The driver's window control panel has just two switches, one for the driver's side front door and one for the passenger side window, which I can imagine will cause horrendous wind buffeting for anyone who enjoys driving with the windows down.

In case you couldn't tell, I was totally taken by the GRMN Corolla. I already loved driving the GR Corolla, but the GRMN Corolla's sharpened inputs, hardcore style, and delightful driving dynamics take that love even further. I truly hope this was not the last time I can drive one.

#5626. Driving The Scion By Toyota KEI-01 Will Make You Giggle And Jiggle In Places You Didn't Know Could Jiggle

I was just as shocked as you all were last week when Toyota announced the launch of the Scion by Toyota brand in the United States with a right-hand-drive kei truck. The KEI-01 is limited to 25 mph in order to conform to low-speed vehicle (LSV) regulations, and as of now it's exclusively limited to fleet buyers. Though final details about the dinky little hauler remain slim, I did get a briefer-than-brief chance to whip around a prototype KEI-01 while attending the press event in Texas at which the truck was revealed, and the experience left me exceedingly tickled and slightly baffled.

I was baffled by Toyota's choice to bring such a niche product in the United States, its choice to do so under the name "Scion by Toyota," and by its choice to make it available to fleets only. I was tickled by the opportunity to contort my comically long limbs in order to squeeze my 6-foot-8-inch tall body behind its wheel and take it for a spin. The result? A truly unique automotive experience that is all but guaranteed to make you giggle.

Full disclosure: Toyota wanted me to sample a smattering of its new and updated models, so it flew me out to scenic Frisco, Texas, kept me fed and housed in a hotel for a few days. I got to witness the announcement of the Scion by Toyota brand there, and drive the KEI-01 a few hundred feet.

The KEI-01 is not a brand new vehicle — in fact, it's based on the Toyota Pixis Truck, which is a rebadged 10th-generation Daihatsu HiJet Truck that itself was introduced 12 years ago now. We are only getting the "extended cab" version of the kei truck, generously called the Jumbo on the Daihatsu HiJet, which adds a taller roof and about an iPhone's length of room behind the two seats for storage — I used that space to store my shoes, since I couldn't fit behind the wheel while wearing them.

In its U.S. specification, the dinky KEI-01 will only be offered with a mid-mounted 660cc three-cylinder engine that sends its power to all four wheels via a CVT automatic transmission. Toyota didn't make power figures public, but it's almost certainly the same 660cc three-cylinder used in the other kei trucks that share the platform, which produces about 50 horsepower and 47 lb-ft of torque. The standard four-wheel-drive system features a lock mode that should make this little pickup rather capable on unpaved roads, but that's only if your spine is up to the task.

They will all come standard with a weird mix of modern and throwback features, like dual front airbags, automatic emergency braking, push-button start, traction control, parking sensors, and an engine start/stop system. The standard climate controls are operated using horizontal levers like the ones in my grandfather's 1991 F-150, and the overall appearance of the interior looks like it belongs in a car that's being shown at Radwood, minus the big tacked-on infotainment screen. I didn't get to experience any of these technology features on my abridged drive, except the start/stop system that I instantly turned off because it cut the AC and was unsurprisingly annoying.

This was my first time driving a kei car, and I solely got to drive the KEI-01 on a short gravel loop, but the instant I started moving I was aware that it was not a refined vehicle. The suspension that gives it a 600-pound payload capacity also felt like it faultlessly transmitted even the smallest surface detail of every single piece of gravel I drove over directly to my butt. It jiggled parts of me that I didn't know could jiggle, and sounded very crashy going through dips and bumps. I wouldn't want to ride in one if I had a bad back. Though Toyota didn't release a spec sheet for the KEI-01, the Daihatsu Hijet has a truly puny wheelbase of 74.8 inches and laughably small tires, so no one should expect it to ride like a limousine.

As for its powertrain, the three-cylinder engine and CVT combination were more than enough to get the KEI-01 to its top speed of 25 mph, but the truck I drove did not have the limiter yet, so I saw as high as 40 mph. The CVT created a typical momentary lag between throttle pedal inputs and actual engine response, but discussing powertrain responsiveness in a kei truck that'll be limited to 25 mph is about as useful as discussing a new hyperpop album with an octogenarian.

If you didn't catch it upon first mention, I'm 6-foot-8, so I drew a bit of a crowd when I first tried inserting myself into the KEI-01. I'm all legs with a 40-inch inseam, and my first entry attempt was foiled by the immovable steering wheel. Once I took my shoes off and swung my left knee under the wheel first, I was able to finagle myself into a comfortable driving position, with about an inch left between my right knee and the hard plastic cupholder.

Headroom in the KEI-01 was downright impressive, though. Using the automotive industry's standardized headroom measurement, I had room to put one, maybe even two magician's hats on top of my head and still fit comfortably in the KEI-01. The cargo bed strangely protrudes a bit into the cab space, so the floor of the extended cab's rear storage area sits at about the same spot where the rear side window ends. It's a diminutive and awkwardly shaped and accessed space, but it allows for a bit of seat recline and is better than nothing.

Annoyingly, Toyota hasn't released pricing for the KEI-01 as of yet, but as we already know it will be limited to fleet buyers initially anyway, so it's not like anyone can go to a Toyota dealer and buy one off the lot. Car and Driver estimates that the KEI-01 will cost around $28,000, though, which would be a really tough sell. I love that American fleet buyers are getting access to a brand new genuine kei truck — especially one that's built in the U.S. — but I am left to grapple with the point of it, especially considering that anyone can go out and find a derestricted imported kei truck for a rather low price.

The so-cute-it-hurts Fiat Topolino is another recently announced U.S.-bound LSV, and I think it makes more sense than the KEI-01 since it will mainly be a cheeky electric neighborhood runabout for rich people. Its only competition are golf carts, where the KEI-01 will compete with a sea of UTVs that have served U.S. campuses, ranches, and other all-terrain hauling needs for ages. Who knows, maybe the fleet market will fall in love with the KEI-01, jiggles and all.

#5624. Chemicals in Many Everyday Items Pose a Growing Threat, U.N. Report Says

— Health-related costs from exposure is estimated to exceed $1.1 trillion annually worldwide

Chemicals in many everyday items that tinker with a body's hormones are a growing threat to human health and the environment, and science now better understands the harm they cause, a new United Nations report said Tuesday.

Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are found in many plastic items, personal care products, pharmaceuticals, toys, household goods, electronics, and pesticides. The new report, written by scientists, estimates the health-related costs from exposure to these chemicals exceed $1.1 trillion annually worldwide. It calls for urgent, coordinated international action to protect human health and the environment.

The policies and regulations to transform the products and sectors causing widespread exposure to these chemicals remain "fragmented and insufficient," it says.

The U.N. Environment Program (UNEP) and World Health Organization issued the report.

"This report is an important step towards a safer world, free from exposure to EDCs," the two U.N. bodies wrote in the foreword. "Solutions do exist. Some safer alternatives are available. The task for policymakers is to ensure that these solutions and alternatives are deployed -- to protect human, animal and planetary health, and save trillions of dollars each year."

The "state of the science" report describes what scientists have learned about exposure to EDCs and their effects since 2012. Previous reports assessed the science on EDCs in 2002 and 2012 to inform policymakers and guide action.

Jacqueline Alvarez, PhD, chief of the UNEP Chemicals and Health Branch, said the new report builds on those assessments, while reflecting a field that has advanced substantially in the breadth of health effects documented, in the sophistication of exposure science, in the development of testing and assessment methodologies, and in a growing understanding of the socioeconomic costs of regulatory inaction.

Report Says There's Strong Evidence These Chemicals Harm Health

Humans and wildlife are exposed to a wide range of these chemicals, and the evidence linking exposure to diseases and disorders "is strong and continues to grow," the report says. People can be exposed through ingestion, skin absorption, inhalation, and direct contact with medical devices during procedures. Children can also be exposed by putting toys containing these chemicals in their mouths and through skin contact with the toys.

Prenatal and early-life exposure to EDCs affects neurodevelopment, cognition, and behavior; EDCs are linked to cancer, cardiovascular disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic liver disease, according to the report. Reproductive organs, fertility, and thyroid functions are also disrupted.

When the 2012 report was published, there was a lot of evidence these chemicals harmed health, but it was not necessarily pointing in the same direction at the same kind of health effects, said Laura Vandenberg, PhD, one of the lead authors for Tuesday's report. Vandenberg also contributed to the 2012 report.

Now, there's "essentially a statement of irrefutable evidence linking EDCs to human health effects and also environmental damage," said Vandenberg, a professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

People Are Exposed to These Chemicals Through Some Plastics

Some countries are pushing to regulate chemicals used to make plastics as part of the negotiations over a global treaty to end plastic pollution. This report empowers those countries that are pushing for controls, said Bjorn Beeler, international coordinator for the International Pollutants Elimination Network (IPEN).

Beeler said the amount of harm from these chemicals is only going to increase in future years as plastic and chemical production is projected to skyrocket -- a "toxic tidal wave" no one is prepared for. IPEN wants a treaty that places global controls on hazardous chemicals in plastics and ends the rapid growth of plastic production. Negotiations are set to resume early next year.

Chemical additives to plastics impart flexibility, rigidity, UV stabilization, durability, and other characteristics that help products perform as intended, said the American Chemistry Council (ACC), a trade group that represents the U.S. chemical industry. The industry considers the safe use of chemicals paramount, said Kimberly Wise White, PhD, ACC's vice president of regulatory and scientific affairs.

The plastics industry opposes efforts to impose new restrictions through the treaty, arguing that chemicals used in plastics are best regulated through existing international conventions and national laws that consider all of a chemical's uses. White said comprehensive frameworks, like the Toxic Substances Control Act in the U.S. and the European Union's Registration, Evaluation, Authorization, and Restriction of Chemicals regulation, that evaluate uses of a chemical to determine risk, are the most effective way to regulate plastic additives.

The International Council of Chemical Associations, which represents manufacturers and producers around the world, has contributed $1.65 million and provided technical expertise to help countries implement chemical management systems, as well as created a publicly accessible plastic additives database.

Few Chemicals Have Been Tested for Endocrine Disruption

More than 350,000 chemicals and chemical mixtures have been registered for production and use globally, but the vast majority have never been evaluated for endocrine-disrupting properties, the report says.

There has been more effort in recent years to develop testing programs, which were highlighted as a major need in the 2012 report. However, most of that testing has not led to action to regulate these chemicals and control exposure, Vandenberg said.

The take-home message from Tuesday's report, she said, is that "in many, many cases we know enough to act. Why haven't we acted?"

Chemicals have been removed from products when people become aware and stop buying products containing a certain chemical, like bisphenol A (BPA), which has been used to make plastic containers for storing food and beverages, Vandenberg said. But that can lead to a "whack-a-mole problem," where a substitution is created but it's structurally similar or insufficiently tested, she added.

To truly reduce people's exposures to these chemicals, it must be done at a policy level throughout society, Vandenberg said.

The report says regulators should aim to protect vulnerable populations from exposure, particularly during pregnancy, infancy, and childhood; improve monitoring and understanding of exposure to these chemicals; advance the identification and testing of them; account for the costs of exposure; and strengthen regulations, among other steps.

The estimate of the annual health-related costs is a conservative calculation that accounts for the cost of health treatment and lost productivity, the report says. The $1.1 trillion price tag doesn't account for the additional costs associated with contaminated drinking water, loss of biodiversity, impacts on food production, and even human rights.

Bethanie Carney Almroth, PhD, U.N. Special Rapporteur on toxics and human rights, said she hopes the report will spur action, though international cooperation is challenging.

"This report makes clear that new regulations are needed, new testing paradigms must be adopted," said Carney Almroth, an ecotoxicology professor at Sweden's University of Gothenburg. "We need to reverse responses from reactive to proactive. We need to prevent harm from occurring, rather than merely documenting and treating it after the fact."

#5622. At $27,000, Is This 1974 Lotus Europa JPS A Smokin'-Hot Deal?

According to the ad, the first owner of today's Nice Price or No Dice Europa owned the car for more than 51 years. That's some dedication, and the car shows the love they obviously had for it. We'll have to decide if we love the price the current owner has set for its sale.

At some point in one's life, it's best to take the road less traveled. The well-beaten path may be the safest, but the less popular way might just offer unexpected, memorable adventures. The 2004 Nissan 350Z we looked at on Monday is probably not everyone's first choice when it comes to used sports cars with a semblance of panache. The easy answer is Porsche's Boxster or a Mazda Miata, but that's part of what makes the 350Z such a rogue option.

Capable and seemingly in as-new condition, our 350Z came with a six-speed stick, a top that drops, and a $12,500 asking price. That's plumb right in the middle of 986 Boxster territory, but offering more power and potentially cheaper running costs. That concept didn't escape you all. Comments on the car ranged from "not for me, but a good deal for someone," to "if it were closer to me..." In the end, the vote went the Nissan seller's way, too, earning the Z a solid 76% 'Nice Price' win.

Nissan has never offered a mid-engine car for sale here in the States. In fact, of the major Japanese manufacturers, only Toyota and Honda (through Acura) have gone the (rear) mid-engine route here.

In the early 1960s, mid-engine layouts were all the rage in racing, with F1, Indy, and GT classes moving to place the driver ahead of the drivetrain. Britain's Lotus was at the forefront of this movement, debuting the mid-engine Type 18 Formula 1 racer in 1960. That car brought Lotus its first F1 checkered flag and World Champion title.

Lotus also dallied with mid-engine GT racers, designing a chassis and body that the company hoped would be bought by the Ford Motor Company (Lotus had a close relationship with Ford at the time) for the Americans' assault on Le Mans. Ford chose the already race-tested Lola Mk 6 chassis for its GT40 racing program, leaving Lotus with significant engineering expense and little to show for it. Instead of initially building a race car from the proposed chassis, Lotus took the more lucrative route and built a road car: Hethel's first mid-engined model.

The resulting Europa leveraged a design first used on the Elan: a stiff, folded and welded center backbone with the drivetrain and suspension bolted in place, and a fiberglass body mounted atop that in saddlebag fashion. The earliest cars had Renault engines and transmissions, while later cars, like this 1973 Europa Special, used the Ford Kent-based Lotus Twin Cam engine.

Not only does this Europa have the most powerful engine offered in Federalized form, but that 115-horsepower 1,557cc four-cylinder is backed by a standard five-speed manual, still sourced from Renault, originally designed for the French company's 16 model.

This isn't just a "Big Valve" (denoting a reworked twin-cam head) Europa; it's also one of 100 John Player Specials built to commemorate Lotus's 1972 F1 Championship win. The cars were wrapped in black paint with gold trim, emulating the cigarette pack design of the racer's sponsor, Nottingham, England's John Player & Sons. It's an iconic bit of 1970s chic, and very British. This car still wears its commemorative dashboard plaque, indicating it's number 90 of the 100 cars built.

While the basic Europa design is a bit odd with its bread van back end, this one appears to be in exceptional condition. Also, being a later edition (dubbed Type 47 by Lotus), it has a reworked engine cover and rear end providing better visibility out the back and slightly improved proportions.

Not only does this Europa appear to be in near-show car condition, but it comes with extensive documentation from the moment it was built (March 1973) to the present day. That paperwork details title transfers between all three owners (the second owner held on to the car for more than half a century), along with all the work that has gone into keeping it on the road and winning awards at car shows. As far as turnkey classics go, there's not much to complain about with this Lotus.

On the exterior, the black-and-gold color scheme still looks as elegant as ever, right down to the original gold anodized alloy wheels. All the badging, lights, and chrome are present and in excellent shape, which is a plus since parts are getting increasingly hard to find. The interior is just as nice, showing just some scuffing on the driver's seat side as evidence of the car's age.

According to the ad, the engine underwent an extensive rebuild and documentation just 2,000 miles ago, and now runs well when warm. Both the engine and gearbox are numbers-matching for the car. How cool is that after all these years?

The ad notes a clean title and mileage documented at 34,526. It also touts the car as a "once in a lifetime chance to own a fully documented Lotus." It should be noted that, while advertised in the Los Angeles Craigslist classifieds, the car is actually located a few hundred miles away on the California/Oregon border.

Some classic cars come with a story. Some come with a past veiled in mystery. This Europa comes with a dossier that would make a CIA agent proud. Not only that, but it's a prime example of a significant model in its final, some might argue, most desired form. What might something like that be worth?

The seller has set a price of $27,000, and since the ad for the car has been posted for almost a month, we now need to give that asking price some thought. What's your take on this original mid-engined marvel out of Hethel and the seller's cash-and-carry price? Is it really worth $27,000? Or is a fairer price yet to be documented in the car's records?

Los Angeles, California, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

XPENG just reported 3rd quarter financial details today, while also forecasting what will happen in the 4th quarter. Everything is looking quite rosy at the moment.

As far as 3rd quarter financials go, on the back of strong sales, the company logged 24.28 billion yuan ($3.643 billion) of revenue. That’s a new quarterly record for the company. It’s 19% more than in Q3 2025 and 23% more than Q2 2026.

That said, despite strong revenue, the company still scored a net loss. It had a significant 870 million yuan ($130.5 million) net loss, in fact, which was up 128% from 380 million yuan in Q3 2025 and down 35% from 1.34 billion from Q2 2026. XPENG made a small profit in Q4 2025, and since then has again been trying to get its finances into the green again instead of in the red.

Good news going into the 4th quarter is the company expects even better. XPENG is forecasting 169,000 to 174,000 vehicle deliveries, which would mean year-over-year growth of 45% to 50%. Expected revenue is 30.4 billion yuan to 31.8 billion yuan, which would mean growth of 37% to 43%.

We’ll see. The company is still not expected to get another net profit quarter, but perhaps the quarter could surprise and XPENG could log its second quarterly profit. One thing making that unlikely, though, is that XPENG’s R&D costs were up significantly, 17.5%. Also, general and administrative expenses were up 11.4% year over year. We’ll see what the 4th quarter brings.

It's official: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond. He's genuinely not who I expected, an older and whiter actor than I figured the studio would go with, but I expect him to do spectacularly in the role. I also hope he's a different type of Bond, campier and more fun than Craig got to be as 007. Most importantly, though, this casting brings us to the key question of the franchise: What car will this new Bond drive?

James Bond has driven all manner of cars in his years, from the Sunbeam Alpine of "Dr. No" to the various Aston Martins of "No Time to Die." He's usually driven British cars, particularly his Astons, but he's had his fair share of BMWs too — even Porsches if you dive into the video games. Bond had AMCs for a little bit! He drove a Ford Mondeo that one time! So, with the entire automotive world a possibility, what do you think Pattinson's Bond should drive?

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk

This is maybe the hardest question I've had to answer for QOTD, because I'm so intent on getting it right. An Aston is the easy answer, maybe a new variant of the DB12, but I don't want this new Bond to just be more of the same. A Longbow Roadster would be sleek and techy, fitting Bond's love of gadgets, and an updated TVR Griffith would show a return to how things used to be for both brands. Maybe neither of those two cars ever actually come out, though. So, to settle things, I'm going to pick a car I think fits: The Morgan Supersport.

The Supersport is a British sports car, as befits an MI6 agent. It's a bit out of time, a bit of a modernized vintage design, as befits a Cold War-era spy whose box office draw has outlasted the Cold War and its espionage heyday. Most crucially, though, it's weird and impractical and fun — characteristics I hope befit Pattinson's Bond, who I hope will follow more in Pierce Brosnan's quippy brogue-prints than Daniel Craig's tactical bootsteps.
