#5619. FDA Wants Liquid Statin Off Shelves

— Missing annual reports put simvastatin oral suspension on thin ice

The FDA wants a liquid formulation of simvastatin (FloLipid) withdrawn from the market, though the agency is giving the drugmaker an opportunity for a hearing.

Approval of simvastatin oral suspension is at risk because Salerno Pharma "has repeatedly failed to file required annual reports" to the FDA, according to a notice in the Federal Register.

According to FDA policy, these annual reports are supposed to convey labeling information and technicalities, such as a current list of approved chemistry, manufacturing, and control information.

Initially approved in 2016 for a host of indications, simvastatin oral suspension is marketed as the first LDL cholesterol medication in liquid form for U.S. patients. The product was developed for patients who have difficulty swallowing pills, and the recommended usual starting dose is 10 mg or 20 mg once a day in the evening on an empty stomach.

Regarding safety, an increased risk of myopathy, including rhabdomyolysis, has been observed in patients taking an 80-mg dose of the oral suspension. Other patients unable to hit their LDL cholesterol goal taking the 40-mg dose are advised to initiate alternative LDL cholesterol-lowering treatments. In 2020, the drug label for the liquid simvastatin formulation was updated with a warning of rare reports of immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy associated with statin use.

According to the Federal Register notice -- which came from Michael Davis, MD, PhD, the FDA's top drug regulator -- Salerno is being given a shot at requesting a hearing if it wants to argue why the approval should not be withdrawn.

Salerno's simvastatin suspension was previously manufactured for Rosemont Pharmaceuticals, a Perrigo company.

Oral suspension atorvastatin (Atorvaliq) is an alternative liquid statin on the market.

#5618. SolarEdge unveils U.S.-made optimizer for C&I solar

By Marie DeFreitas, Contributor | November 17, 2026

SolarEdge’s new Duo Power Optimizer promises to simplify commercial and industrial solar installations with 50% fewer optimizer units, independent module-level power tracking, and enhanced safety features.

The commercial and industrial (C&I) solar market is getting a new hardware option aimed at making installations simpler without sacrificing system performance. SolarEdge Technologies has unveiled its new Duo Power Optimizer, a U.S.-manufactured solution designed to deliver module-level energy harvesting and monitoring while cutting the number of power optimizers in half.

Announced November 16 ahead of RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, the new product introduces a 2:1 architecture that allows one optimizer to connect two solar modules. Notably, each module retains its own independent maximum power point tracker (MPPT), which preserves the module-level performance benefits associated with the traditional one-to-one optimizer configurations.

For developers, EPCs and installers managing large-scale rooftop and distributed generation projects, the value here lies in fewer components to purchase, wire and install, with no trade-off in module-level optimization.

Simplifying installation without sacrificing performance

SolarEdge’s optimization tech addresses the challenge of conventional string inverter systems, which is that an underperforming module can affect the output of an entire string. But by allowing each module to operate independently, the system limits the impact of shading, degradation or performance differences between panels.

The Duo brings demonstrates that capability in a two-module configuration. By reducing the number of optimizers by 50% compared with one-to-one designs, SolarEdge is targeting an opportunity to streamline balance-of-system requirements and reduce the installation labor.

SolarEdge’s U.S.-made Duo Power Optimizer connects two solar modules while maintaining independent module-level power tracking for commercial and industrial solar installations. Credit: SolarEdge

The hardware also incorporates design changes intended to improve jobsite efficiency. Each optimizer features two input pairs: a shorter connection for the nearest module and a pre-extended connection for the adjacent module. The arrangement reduces excess wiring and eliminates the need for field-made jumpers.

The configuration also accommodates modules with different orientations, making it particularly relevant for east-west and dual-tilt racking applications.

Beyond installation efficiency, SolarEdge is emphasizing electrical safety as a central feature of the new product.

The Duo extends the company’s Sense Connect technology to its input and output connectors, monitoring connector temperatures to identify developing issues before they potentially escalate into overheating or electrical arcs.

Also, the optimizer introduces what SolarEdge describes as an industry-first approach to arc fault detection: every optimizer acts as an individual arc sensor. Rather than relying exclusively on detection at the inverter, the system distributes monitoring throughout the array, allowing potential arc faults to be identified closer to their source.

SolarEdge says the technology provides coverage across strings with up to 3,280 feet of total cable length between the inverter and optimizer. It can also help pinpoint problems to the optimizer area, potentially making troubleshooting and maintenance more efficient.

Manufactured at SolarEdge’s Florida facility, the Duo is designed to meet U.S. Domestic Content and Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements, according to the company. SolarEdge says its domestic-content eligibility levels are consistent with those of its previous U.S.-manufactured power optimizers, subject to applicable tax guidance and project-specific requirements.

For SolarEdge, the Duo represents an effort to combine three priorities that are becoming more and more important in commercial solar: installation efficiency, system-level safety, and domestic manufacturing.

The technology does not fundamentally change the value proposition of module-level optimization. Instead, it looks to make that architecture more economical and easier to deploy at scale.

SolarEdge will showcase the Duo Power Optimizer at RE+ 2026.

#5616. BMW In South Carolina: A Free Trade Success Story

I recently attended BMW’s “Beyond The Machine” event in South Carolina. The largest facility of the German company globally is Plant Spartanburg in Greer, South Carolina. As part of the event, I saw the opening of BMW’s new battery plant in nearby Woodruff. We stayed in the nearby city of Greenville, which was transformed by BMW and the businesses that followed.

Beyond the vehicles and manufacturing, which I plan to cover in more detail in future articles, one of the most striking aspects was the human impact. From the “Woodruffian” Mayor fighting back tears at the opening of the battery plant to the plant employees to the people I met exploring the town, they clearly appreciate what BMW has done for the community. Throughout the presentations and discussions, there was support for free trade along with the local benefits. People in the area pride themselves in their resilience. They have reason to be proud. And they were optimistic about the growth of the increasingly clean manufacturing and electrified products from this global company.

The area around Greenville, South Carolina the rose to prominence in the 1870s on the textile industry. Cotton from throughout the South that had previously been shipped to other areas for processing was processed in Greenville and Spartanburg counties. However, as global competition increased in the 20th century, the mills became less competitive. The last textile mill closed in Greenville in 1977, although a few textile operations continued in the region into the 1980’s. As that industry left, the local economy declined. If the story ended there, many might use it as an argument against free trade.

When BMW came to South Carolina in 1992, they saw a lot of potential. Michelin had already started making tires there in 1978. Local leaders were enthusiastic to work with BMW. The people were also enthusiastic to receive training for the new jobs. The deep-water port of Charleston on the other side of the state facilitated shipping, while nearby rail links connected to much of the US.

Since 1992, BMW has invested over $15.8 Billion. The new Woodruff battery plant is their most recent major investment. In the process, an area that could have been considered a casualty of global trade became one of its greatest beneficiaries.

The first model, an E36 3 series, rolled off the line in 1994. BMW also produced the Z3 in the plant, including the first “German” car driven by James Bond on camera. However, the big breakthrough came with the introduction of the X5 in 1999. At the time, relatively few SUVs were being sold in Europe. BMW Spartanburg as the center of SUV production was intending to largely for the US. However, global markets shifted.

Now, Spartanburg is the “Home of X.” It currently produces the X3, X5, X6, X7 and XM, including electrified versions. It is the sole manufacturing plant for a number of those SUV models globally. A little over half of their production is exported, which also makes it consistently the top US overseas automotive exporter. Export volume topped $9 Billion in 2025 over roughly 200,000 X vehicles.

BMW designed those vehicles to be able to use ICE, PHEV and BEV powertrains. While some may want them to make just pure BEV, the approach gives BMW the ability to shift rapidly with the market. The different models also give the plant a level of market resilience. However, to fuel that resilience they need a very flexible supply chain that can respond quickly. Suppliers being close to the plant creates greater resilience.

BMW is designing its vehicles to be globally competitive. While 400+ miles of EPA range and charging speeds approaching 500 kW may be at the top of the US market, they are also competitive in global markets. While BMW developed the cells and packs, they use multiple suppliers to manufacture the cylindrical cells to their specifications. Packs at the plant currently use AESC cells, but they will shift to LG in the future and use other suppliers in other markets.

BMW also worked with the state of South Carolina to develop people. Nearby Clemson University provides a source of engineering talent, and BMW partners with the university on the Clemson University International Center for Automotive Research, where both students and BMW benefit from the development of new innovations. They are also developing potential future suppliers with the BMW Venture funds. One such company will be supplying flax-based composites to future M models.

A heavy emphasis is placed on technical training at the factory. In addition, they collaborated with community colleges to provide technical training. But the development programs start much earlier, with a heavy emphasis in middle school and sponsoring the First Robotics Competition for elementary school students.

BMW also worked with the South Carolina Department of Transportation to build infrastructure to support the plant and its suppliers. Moving forward, that infrastructure will increasingly include electrification and EV charging. BMW also worked with the SC Ports Authority to develop an “inland port,” which is essentially a direct rail link to the Port of Charleston. By moving freight by rail, emissions are greatly reduced. In addition, a lot of emphasis is going into transferring freight quickly, as every minute a truck sits idling is also wasted emissions.

While BMW employs 11,000 workers, over four times as many jobs are supported by the plant, according to a Clemson economist. That multiplier is much higher than most companies due to how BMW operates. Part of the impact on the local economy beyond employee count comes from the strategy behind the manufacturing. Overall, more than 70% of the value of the vehicles comes from outside suppliers.

Plant Spartanburg receives 3.3 million parts per day delivered by 1200 truckloads and 50 sea containers, 6 days per week. All those parts then go into over 1500 vehicles produced per day. The plant is laid out a bit different than some other manufacturing plants to facilitate the supply chain. Multiple fingers go up off the main line, along which parts are delivered to be assembled nearby. There isn’t much in the way of warehousing. Trucks come to the plant each day and the parts can end up on vehicles driving off the line the same day.

In the initial stages of manufacturing, more of the supply base came from overseas. However, as the plant established itself, more suppliers localized. That growing supply chain then attracted additional companies to the region, like Mercedes, Volvo and Scout. Those companies then create greater scale for the suppliers, who can reduce costs and expand operations.

Overall, for heavy, bulky components, localization will tend to  happen naturally. For a company that relies on suppliers to consistently and almost constantly deliver parts, that localization tends to increase. The more localized the supply chain, the more capable it becomes to respond to market dynamics. Once scale is attained for heavy, bulky components like batteries, that production will naturally become more localized.

BMW has a growing supply chain footprint across the Americas and especially across the Southeastern US. There will be over 850 Tier 1 supplier locations in the Americas by 2027, with multiple times as many Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers providing materials, parts and components. BMW focuses on value creation, competitiveness and collaboration in their supply chain. In addition, while they are bringing economic benefit, they are also focused on decarbonization.

Of course, all this economic activity has brought “green” in terms of money to the local communities. As I was stranded in Greenville due to flight interruptions, I had time to walk around the town and speak to some of the locals. Streets that were once desolate and unsafe are now vibrant with shops and restaurants. An area that people once wanted to leave is now growing rapidly and attracting people from around the world. I started conversations  with several friendly people in town about trade. I heard stories of transformation from past struggles to current successes.

Even though it was clear that they were benefitting from the economic impact, I was still surprised how strongly and openly they supported free trade and realized the benefits. A local guide pointed out major buildings and businesses that were new. Downtown is now pleasant and walkable. Part of that is due to the restoration of a river that runs through the city, surrounded by shops and artwork, where I saw some locals fishing in the clear water. This gets to the other kind of “green.”

While there are a lot of trucks transporting materials and components, shortened travel distances and efforts to streamline intermodal transfers reduce emissions. The proximity enables packaging to typically be sent back to the supplier to be reused. BMW is also putting a lot of effort into reduced CO2 emissions steel produced locally, which I plan to follow up on. Over half the steel in their vehicles is reduced CO2. Solar panels and landfill gas provide power for their facilities.

As the company relies heavily on its supply chain, the supply chain is a major focus of its decarbonization strategy. While EVs reduce emissions overall, the proportion of emissions from the manufacturing phase tends to be higher than for ICE vehicles, adding emphasis to decarbonization of manufacturing. At the same time, they strive to create regional strength, resilience and value creation while reducing emissions. Close collaboration is the key to meeting these goals. BMW plans to have net zero CO2 emissions throughout their supply chain by 2050 at the latest.

The new Woodruff plant will produce their sixth-generation battery. BMW develops the batteries first and then outsources the cell manufacturing, but they will now be manufacturing the packs locally. Initially, this will be for the iX5, to be delivered domestically and to global markets. However, additional EV models may benefit in the future.

Overall, politicians in the 1970’s could have tried to block global competition to protect the textile mills. That might have extended the life of those plants for a few years. However, in the process, those plants would become less globally competitive and less globally relevant. Protectionism would have only extended a slow, painful decline.

However, by keeping the market open and staying open to new business opportunities, Greenville, Greer, Spartanburg and Woodruff created the circumstances for their current success. People were open to new companies from other countries. They were open to industries that were new to the area. And they were open to investing in retraining to better take advantage of the new opportunities.

In the initial site selection, South Carolina could have imposed strict regulations and tried to force localization before the factory was built, production was ramped up and scale was attained to support that localization. If that happened, the plant would have undoubtedly been built elsewhere, and the economic benefits would have gone to someone else. By taking a more collaborative approach, rather than being confrontational, both BMW and local suppliers benefitted greatly. Building on that approach, more companies came to the region, building scale and amplifying the benefits.

BMW is not being hypocritical in their support of free trade. They are not promoting free trade just when it benefits them and then putting up barriers for other competitors. They are not shying away from global competition. They are seeking to make globally competitive vehicles for global markets. While global competition is fierce, by facing that competition, rather than hiding from it, their products become more competitive.

In the process, one of the brightest spots in US automotive trade globally, as well as one of the leaders in electrified product and supply chain decarbonization, comes from a German company.

Change and globalization can be scary things. Especially in the short term. The transition to EVs can also be scary, especially for those tied to the past. However, hiding behind political and trade walls rarely works out in the long run. A willingness to be open and collaborative with people who might come from within different lines on a map or sound different than you can have long term benefits. And the courage to engage with the technology transition and compete globally can put you ahead of many established competitors. That cannot only transform how we power our vehicles, but also transform the lives of people in communities for generations to come. As Woodruff Mayor Kenneth Gist put it at the battery plant opening:

BMW and the City of Woodruff wanted the same thing. Success in business, success in our community, and success in building the next generation of BMW electric vehicles to be the best in the world…

…When I think about this plant, I think about our children, our grandchildren. Educational partnership that will open the doors for them, the career that will be waiting for them, and a Woodruff they would be proud to call home for decades to come. BMW, you have been a true partner to me personally, to every person in this community.

Larry lives in Queens, NY, with his wife and cats. While he has spent much of his professional career leading global marketing efforts, his passions focus on clean technology and the automotive industry. He believes in Green Free Trade and the potential for the application of engineering talent to create solutions to the world’s most challenging problems.

#5615. Peanut Peptide Injections Promising for Allergy Immunotherapy

— A novel route to immunotherapy for peanut allergy passes phase II test

A novel peptide-based immunotherapy for peanut allergy appeared safe and modestly efficacious for reducing children's symptoms over the first 12 months, a phase II trial showed.

For the primary efficacy endpoint, the higher of two monthly PVX108 shot dosages significantly boosted the maximum tolerated dose of peanut from baseline to month 12 by 2.4-fold, compared with a 1.2-fold change in the placebo group, reported Brian P. Vickery, MD, of Emory University and chief of the Division of Allergy/Immunology at Children's Healthcare of Atlanta, at the American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology annual meeting.

In terms of safety, there were no cases of anaphylaxis or other treatment-related allergic or severe adverse events with the shot. Only six of the 71 trial participants reported any adverse event (13% with the higher dose tested), largely local administration site reactions.

At an oral food challenge at 1 year, 39% of patients on the higher dose tolerated at least 300 mg of peanut protein compared with 17% in the placebo group (the equivalent of one peanut). "This is more than double, on average, what causes accidental reactions in the field when people are exposed accidentally while they're trying to avoid peanut. And it's been shown in previous work that ... is probably clinically meaningful for most patients with peanut allergy," Vickery said. But he acknowledged it "is probably less than what you'd expect in a study of oral immunotherapy, where the participants are swallowing about 300 mg of protein daily as part of their treatment."

While efficacy needs to be confirmed in a larger trial, "there's also a big safety difference and a difference in burden in terms of daily versus monthly therapy," he added, pointing to adverse events in most immunotherapy patients with other routes of administration and anaphylaxis in 10-15% of trial participants in some studies.

Immunotherapy shots offer an advantage of fewer office visits than the typically once-every-2-week schedule for oral immunotherapy up-dosing and also not requiring kids to consume peanut products daily, commented Jay Lieberman, MD, of the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis. With peanut protein, though, "you can't do it the same way we do allergy shots to cat or oak tree pollen, because it is too dangerous. It caused too many reactions," he said.

PVX108 comprises seven short peptides representing immunodominant T-cell epitopes of major peanut allergens rather than intact peanut proteins that interact with the immune system and can lead to reactions. "This is designed to get around that problem by formulating fragments of peanut proteins that are too small to interact with IgE [immunoglobulin E] and the allergic components of the immune system and instead interact directly with T cells, which are thought to be kind of the driving force behind the allergy," Vickery said.

"We have made some progress in being able to treat peanut allergy with oral immunotherapy and now FDA-approved omalizumab [Xolair] as the two most commonly used options," Vickery said in an interview monitored by media relations for drug developer Aravax. "But there are millions of patients out there with peanut allergy, and most of them are not being treated due to limitations in care and also limitations in access to these treatments and because of limitations in the treatments themselves."

"The scientific community believes that there is plenty of room for new forms of immunotherapy to be developed," he added, "because we don't think of peanut allergy as a one-size-fits-all condition where one treatment will solve the problem."

While the only FDA-approved peanut oral immunotherapy product recently left the market as clinicians rely on off-the-shelf commercial products, Lieberman agreed that PVX108 could find a place: "Bringing an [oral immunotherapy] FDA-approved thing to the market when people are already just using PB2 powder [commercially available peanut flour], that was the problem."

The trial included 71 peanut allergy patients ages 4 to 11 years at 14 trial sites in the U.S. and Australia in the primary efficacy and safety cohort. They were randomized to double-blind treatment with 5-nmol or 50-nmol PVX108 or placebo given monthly by intradermal administration over 12 months. At the end of that period, a double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge was done following the PRACTALL guidelines.

After 6 months off treatment, a follow-up food challenge was conducted at month 18. It showed evidence of maintenance or improvement in clinical effects compared with month 12, indicating disease-modifying potential, Vickery said, although this needs further confirmation.

The optimal length of treatment isn't clear yet, but immunotherapy shots for other allergens typically take 3 to 5 years of treatment, Vickery noted. "So it's likely that longer-term treatment might be necessary or even might be more optimal."

#5614. The BLUETTI Apex 200 Expandable Portable Power Station — CleanTechnica Tested

BLUETTI continues to innovate, finding new ways to move its portable power station technology into meaningful new formats that provide owners with additional capability, portability, and utility.

They recently reached out about a new stackable portable power station format based around the Apex 200 power station. It packs in a meaningful 2.5 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of storage capacity by itself, but the real magic is that it was built to be modular and can be linked up with additional storage modules to be stacked underneath, connecting directly to the main unit.

Disclaimer: BLUETTI provided the Apex 200, B300K, and a pair of solar panels to the author for the purposes of this review.

This modular format is a game changer because it means you don’t need an installer to bolt 300 pounds of batteries to the wall of your house. Instead, you can order them in manageable formats and add more as you need them. Among other things, this capability allows the owner to assemble and disassemble the battery pack that meets their needs when they need it.

If you’re heading out to camp for a week in your RV, you can grab an Apex 200 and one of BLUETTI’s B300K expansion batteries and bring 5.5 kWh of capacity with you on the road. When you get home from the trip, you can put them back into the garage and add that back into the battery capacity for your home.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 serves as a head unit or master controller for the battery stack, while the other battery modules are effectively servants to it. For example, when you’re setting the unit up to charge from a wall outlet or from a set of BLUETTI’s solar panels, which can wire directly into the Apex 200 with MC4 connectors, you simply plug one set of connectors or one AC charging cable into the Apex 200 and it automatically balances the energy storage across however many additional battery packs are plugged into the unit.

That really simplifies the charging structure and allows you to use the battery exactly how you want to. If you want to just head to the park with two solar panels that are portable, you can do that and have a much more manageable power system, effectively bringing a mini-grid with you on the go.

We tested the BLUETTI Apex 200 out on a wall charger and, much like most of the other portable power stations on the market, it effectively maxes out the capacity you can actually draw from a wall outlet, which is around 1,600 watts continuous. Even with the best charging cables, you’re going to notice some heat building up in the cable, and BLUETTI has made some concessions for this. The Apex 200 has a switch that allows you to select from different charging modes:

When it comes to solar, the BLUETTI Apex 200 can plug in to solar arrays through either an XT60 connector or the MC4 connectors that wire directly into the unit on the side. Between the MC4 connectors and the XT60 solar input, the unit can pull down 3,000 watts of solar, though you will need to make sure the voltage on your panels lines up with what each of the ports on the unit can handle. When we initially wired our two Bluetti 100-watt solar panels into the unit, we had them wired in parallel, which resulted in just 40 volts being pushed into the unit.

Stacking them in series gave us 80 volts, which pushed it over the minimum 60 volts for the MC4 connectors and allowed the BLUETTI Apex 200 to start charging from the panels. Pushing 2,000 watts maximum of solar power into a 5.5 kWh battery stack is going to take some time to get it charged up, but it’s easy to manage scaling the input power system up to an impressive 2,000 watts to really deliver some meaningful power.

The flexibility is pretty impressive, because it means you can dial the system in to exactly what you need, whether that’s bolting an array to the top of your RV or installing solar panels on the side of your house and then wiring them in a way that’s the most convenient for you.

BLUETTI also makes a larger B500K battery, so you can really pick and choose exactly the right level of storage that you need for your house and the right size battery packs that you want to be able to move around.

The MC4 connectors for solar panels are a little bit troublesome on the BLUETTI Apex 200 because they require a special tool to release the locks that connect the male and female ends of MC4 connectors together. That means if you have your solar panels wired up and plugged into the unit, you’ll need an MC4 connector release tool to disconnect the solar panels from the Apex 200 before you move on. Alternately, you can wire the solar panels up through an XT60 connector, which is a simple plug-and-play adapter for lower voltage solar setups.

When it came time to use the stored power from the BLUETTI Apex 200 and the B300K battery pack, we had to pick up some more high-draw appliances to really put them the the test. We bought a 1,500-watt electric fireplace and 1,500-watt portable heater for a total draw of around 3,000 watts by. We also grabbed an an Instant Pot from the kitchen to pull a bit more juice from the battery stack.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 handled both of the heaters running full blast without a problem. It shared a continuous power output capacity of 3,200 watts. This gets bumped to 3,600 watts when you attach a B300K extension battery. Beyond that, you can even pull a little bit more power, pulling peak usage up to 4,800 watts for a few seconds, because of its peak power handling capacity.

Keeping the larger heater unit attached, we added an Instapot to the the mix, and again the unit had no issues no matter what power levels we used. It’s a solid stack with impressive stats that actually deliver when you need them to the most.

BLUETTI has really built an impressive system here with the Apex 200 and its different expansion battery options. A single BLUETTI Apex 200 can be expanded up to 33.3 kWh, and they can even go bigger than that if you need something with more storage.

BLUETTI allows you to link three Apex 200 battery stacks together through their Hub 1 accessory for a total of just under 100 kWh of storage capacity. That can be accomplished by stacking three Apex 200s with a bunch of BLUETTI’s 5kWh B500Ks and then linking them all together through the Hub 1.

It’s a massive system that shows BLUETTI isn’t just building products for a quick sale, but building a much more comprehensive, flexible storage system that you can build at home into the right configuration for your needs with components that act more like LEGO building blocks.

The ability to wire in solar via XT60 connectors and MC4 connectors is exciting, giving homeowners even more options to produce power from the sun for them to run their lives on. The BLUETTI Apex 200 retails for $1,399 USD.

For more information about the BLUETTI Apex 200, the B300K, B500K expansion packs, or their solar panels, head over to their official website.

#5613. Bentley Torcal EV Is Already Sold Out Through 2027

Good morning! It's Tuesday, November 17, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, Bentley's Torcal EV is sold out all the way through 2027, Tesla is going to invest over $3.3 billion in expanding its German factory so it can build Cybercabs, General Motors wants to add a lot more robots and automation into its facilities and BMW wants the U.S. government to cut it some slack on tariffs.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

Bentley's first all-electric vehicle might have a bit of a silly name and slightly polarizing styling, but it would seem that's not enough to keep buyers away. Initial demand for the Torcal is shockingly strong, with the electric crossover already sold out through 2027. Now, if you want one, Bentley is taking orders for 2028. You'll be lucky to get one before you vote for the next President.

One caveat to all of this is that Bentley hasn't said how many Torcal build slots were actually available for 2027, and it hasn't indicated any sales volumes, so theoretically, it could have sold like 5 of the Cayenne-sized EVs, but I sort of doubt that. A spokesperson for the British luxury automaker said it was "very pleased with the response and the position we're in" following the Torcal's reveal in September. From Automotive News:

Based on orders, the S variant has been the most popular Torcal so far, [Bentley CEO Frank-Steffen] Walliser said. In general, Bentley has seen the Torcal attract new and younger customers to the brand.

The Torcal, based on Volkswagen Group's Premium Platform Electric, is slotted beneath the Bentayga, Bentley's first crossover.

It will become Bentley's fourth nameplate alongside the Bentayga, Continental GT coupe and convertible, and Flying Spur sedan. The rest of the Bentley lineup is offered with gasoline and plug-in hybrid powertrains.

The Torcal has a range of up to 375 miles from a 113-kilowatt-hour battery and offers fast charging at 400 kilowatts. Power is rated at 810 hp and 881 pound-feet of torque for the Torcal and 876 hp and 996 pound-feet of torque for the Torcal S, making it the most powerful Bentley to date.

U.S. pricing starts at $222,495 for the Torcal, $262,695 for the high-performance Torcal S and $300,995 for the Torcal First Edition.

Bentayga pricing starts at $231,150, the Flying Spur starts at $254,850 and the Continental GT starts at $288,750. All prices include shipping.

The EV market is sort of an unknown in the ultra-luxury space. Sure, Rolls-Royce brought out the Spectre in 2023, and that has been a success; the Cadillac Celestiq is doing alright and the Ferrari Luce is selling well, despite its deeply polarizing design. However, Lamborghini killed its Lanzador EV earlier this year.

The Torcal's success is paramount for Bentley in the coming years. It invested $463 million to upgrade its factory in Crewe, England to build the EV, and it has spent even more than that on R&D and supply chain preparations. That's a lot of money to make back for a low-volume automaker like Bentley. It's doubly important because the automaker's global sales fell 17% through September, and the brand's profits dropped by over half to $54.1 million through the first nine months of 2026. This thing needs to be a sales success, and luckily for Bentley, it's looking that way.

Tesla is about to drop $3.31 billion to add a new facility at its Berlin-Brandenburg factory in Germany in an effort to boost production of CEO Elon Musk's latest pet project: the Cybercab. The news comes just days after Tesla opened direct sales to select customers. The plan is for production to officially begin in 2029, and it'll eventually ramp up to 1 million vehicles per year, according to factory lead Andrew Tierig. Construction is slated to begin in the first half of next year.

That's quite an expansion. The German factory, which first opened in March of 2022, makes hundreds of thousands of Model Ys and millions of battery cells, but it doesn't exactly produce a million vehicles per year. From The Wall Street Journal:

The group said on X Friday that "select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use" at an estimated purchase price of $29,990 and a $299-a-month subscription to Tesla's autonomy software.

Tesla started adding Cybercabs to its Austin fleet of robotaxis in September, and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation to determine whether the steering-wheel-free vehicles comply with safety standards. Tesla told the regulator that the Cybercab meets all applicable standards, the NHTSA said in a filing.

Musk recently said the company would wind down production of the Cybertruck at its gigafactory in Texas next year to make room for increased production of the self-driving Cybercab. Adding a dedicated facility in Germany would allow Tesla to make the Cybercab on both sides of the Atlantic.

As Tesla's sales in Europe started regaining strength earlier this year after declining in 2025, the company has sought to boost output in Germany. In May, Thierig said the group would invest $250 million into its German factory to increase production of EV battery cells.

I'm skeptical of the scale of this project, but if it works, it would be good news for Germany's struggling automotive industry. Local automakers are having a tough time right now and cutting tens of thousands of jobs as they look for ways to remain competitive against Chinese rivals. Obviously, building out Tesla's factory and then staffing it would create a lot of theoretical jobs.

General Motors is looking to increase the use of robots and other automation by 20% at its factories in North America by 2028 as it looks for ways to deal with higher labor and onshoring costs.  The General is said to be developing its own robots and assembling them at its Kokomo, Indiana, plant, according to unnamed sources who spoke with Reuters. It's focused on using autonomous mobile robots to move parts around its plants. Unsurprisingly, the United Auto Workers union is rightfully worried about this plan.

Currently, GM is buying robotics equipment from outside suppliers while developing its own in-house, and it's asking parts suppliers bidding on new contracts to submit automation plans for their own operations. GM is using a scorecard to rate suppliers' automation efforts and even considering the scores in contract decisions. From Reuters:

GM said it uses automation to improve safety, quality and ​efficiency. "As competition intensifies globally, we continue to put these technologies to work in ways that support our manufacturing teams," its statement said.

US automakers have increased automation ​to contain manufacturing costs since the United Auto Workers won record contract gains in 2023 and President Donald Trump's drive to bring more factory work home put pressure on production costs.

The UAW, as you may have imagined, is not a fan of this.

The UAW won the contract gains from GM and its crosstown competitors Ford Motor and Jeep-parent Stellantis. GM said the contract would add about $575 ​in labor costs per vehicle; Ford pegged its added cost at $900 per vehicle.

At the time, analysts said the companies likely would increase automation as a ​way to defray the higher labor costs. GM last year said it had about 100 roboticists, AI engineers and hardware specialists working on advanced robotics systems.

US automakers have long ‌said their ⁠labor costs exceed those of foreign rivals and newer competitors such as Tesla, whose US factories are largely nonunion.

The companies face another round of potentially contentious negotiations in 2028, when the contracts are scheduled to expire. UAW President Shawn Fain already has warned that AI and increased automation pose a threat to workers.

"The fruits of our labor have multiplied like never before, but workers aren't reaping the harvest. That's theft," Fain said at a UAW convention in ​June. "And if AI continues to be used ​as an accessory to that ⁠crime, it has to be stopped."

Automation is nothing new at vehicle factories, but automakers are exploring more ways to integrate AI and robotics into their plants. At the end of the day, a robot is less expensive and less needy than a person, and if a company can save even a dime by using a robot versus a human, it's going to do it 10 times out of 10.

BMW is sick and tired of being sick and tired over these tariffs, and it wants some relief. It's the latest in a group of foreign automakers that are currently in talks with the Trump administration that are trying to catch a break on import duties by investing billions in new U.S. factories. Last year alone, BMW ate more than $1 billion in U.S. import tariffs, according to Robert Engelhorn, CEO of BMW Manufacturing.

The German automaker is pointing toward the $1.7 billion it spent on expanding its U.S. footprint for EV production at its plant in Spartanburg, South Carolina. The company produces more than 400,000 vehicles per year there, and ships about half of them to 120 countries. From Automotive News:

BMW's status as the largest auto exporter by value in the U.S., as well as its recent investments, are worthy of consideration for tariff relief, as company officials see it.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster said he would like to see lower tariffs for a company bringing outsized economic benefit to the state.

"Over time, I've had conversations with the people in Washington about that very thing," McMaster told Automotive News at a Nov. 13 event celebrating the opening of BMW's battery pack factory. "Nothing moves real fast sometimes, but it's all going to work out just fine, and this is more proof of it right here."

Last year, it imported about 215,000 vehicles to the U.S., most of which were sedans like the 3 Series and 4 Series. I'm not sure if it'll be enough to sway the Trump administration, but it's worth a shot. I'm sure having McMaster, a character we saw during Trump's first administration when he served as the National Security Advisor, in its corner is helpful, though.

The thing is, Rich, you were a bit of a crook in this one regard. Listen, I know everyone was out to get you, and you're one paranoid son of a gun, but I'm pretty sure you did that stuff, man. What gets lost in all of this is that Nixon made this proclamation at Disney World, and that really tickles me. Anyway, if you want to learn more about Crooked Rich, head over to History.com.

Fuel prices continue to tumble, as we hit another huge milestone when it comes to diesel. It's easy to see why, too. Both WTI Crude Oil futures and Brent Crude prices are down, sitting at $86 and $94, respectively, at the time of publication. We should enjoy these good times while we can, because who knows how long they're going to last.

Here's where national average prices stand right now, according to AAA:

This all shakes out to the average price of a gallon of gas dropping another 3 cents overnight to $3.78, according to AAA. Diesel is the big winner, though. #5612. Acura ZDX Recalled For Temporary Loss Of Braking Like Its GM Brethren

General Motors issued another recall intended to address temporary loss of braking in several of its Ultium-platform models late last month, and now we know the problem plagues 2024 Acura ZDXs, too. You're forgiven if you forgot about the brief existence of the Acura ZDX EV, so allow me to refresh your memory. The ZDX was Acura's first EV, and beneath its sharp and aggressive exterior it was based on the Chevrolet Blazer EV, sharing that crossover's powertrain and technology. According to the NHTSA Recall Report, 14,648 all-wheel-drive 2024 Acura ZDXs need a software update to correct the same temporary loss of braking issue plaguing GM's EVs. Rear-wheel-drive ZDXs are not affected by the recall.

The temporary loss of braking only arises under very specific conditions, and it corrects itself after the driver releases the brake pedal and presses it again, but any loss of braking is a scary and dangerous situation. In GM's recall of over 67,000 EVs, it was aware of 20 minor accidents due to the fault, two of which resulted in minor injuries; Honda is unaware of any warranty claims or injuries related to the recall.

As with the GM recall, the only time the Acura ZDX's temporary loss of braking occurs is under very specific circumstances. According to the recall report, "the software logic used to calculate vehicle reference speed (Vref) may become unstable when wheel slip associated with turning and light braking occurs together with travel over a road disturbance and release/reapplication of the brake pedal. On a high-friction surface, the unstable calculation may incorrectly determine that the wheels are in deep slip and command an inappropriate reduction in brake pressure."

To fix the condition, Honda will update the Electronic Brake Control Module software. Owners who have accepted the terms and conditions to accept over-the-air (OTA) software updates can download the updated software remotely, but all owners can take their ZDX to the Acura dealership to have the update installed, too.

I attended the first drive event of the Acura ZDX Type S back in 2024, and I wasn't the biggest fan of the car. It drove fine, but the interior didn't feel any more upscale than the much cheaper Blazer EV, and considering that Acura canceled the model after just one year on sale, I expected sales numbers to be much lower. Check out NHTSA's website for more recall information.

#5611. Groups Decry Trump EPA’s Decision to Grant Louisiana Oversight of Toxic Coal Ash

Testing at all Louisiana coal plants found unsafe groundwater contamination.

BATON ROUGE, La. — The Sierra Club, Earthjustice, and the Alliance for Affordable Energy Louisiana decried the Trump administration’s final decision today to put the State of Louisiana in charge of oversight of toxic coal ash waste. The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ) has repeatedly allowed coal plants to violate federal coal ash protections.

Coal ash is generated when coal is burned, and massive quantities are stored at coal-burning power plants near Baton Rouge, Alexandria, and Shreveport.

At all three active Louisiana coal plants (Big Cajun 2, Brame Energy Center, R S Nelson), and the state’s one retired plant (Dolet Hills), monitoring data shows that coal ash is contaminating groundwater at levels above federal safe drinking water standards. These toxic chemicals include arsenic, boron, cobalt, lead, lithium, radium, sulfate, and thallium. More than 61% of Louisiana’s population relies on groundwater for all or part of their drinking water supply.

“Louisianans know all too well that we can’t trust our state regulators to hold polluters accountable, so it’s nonsensical that the Trump Administration just gave LDEQ even more authority to handle something as dangerous as coal ash,” said Darryl Malek-Wiley, a Sierra Club senior field representative in Louisiana. “It’s clear this decision is meant to favor wealthy coal-owning utilities at the expense of our health.”

“The Trump administration chose polluters over the people of Louisiana,” said Earthjustice senior attorney Mychal Ozaeta. “An alphabet soup of toxic chemicals from burning coal is contaminating groundwater in locations across the state. The right thing to do is make the polluters clean up their toxic mess, and protect sources of drinking water. Instead, the Trump administration is handing over authority to Louisiana’s state government which won’t lift a finger to clamp down on the concerning levels of contaminants poisoning the state’s groundwater.”

“Our state regulators are dangerously inadequate in their oversight and enforcement of polluting industries, which has already cost Louisiana our safe air and water. We simply don’t think LDEQ can handle even more responsibilities they won’t take seriously,” said Logan Burke, Executive Director of the Alliance for Affordable Energy.

Public interest groups submitted formal comments to EPA urging the administration to reject Louisiana’s request to handle coal ash oversight in the state.

Coal ash contains arsenic, mercury, chromium, lead, lithium, radium, and other heavy metals, which have been linked to numerous types of cancer, heart and thyroid disease, respiratory illness, reproductive failure, and neurological harm.

As an example of the state’s abysmal track record on coal ash, LDEQ has allowed power plants to close coal ash dumps with ash in groundwater, ensuring that the dumps will contaminate groundwater with toxic chemicals indefinitely. LDEQ should not be in charge of issuing permits that let coal plants continue to violate the law. These permits will shield power plants from federal enforcement and prevent Louisiana residents from stopping coal ash pollution.

LDEQ is a severely understaffed and extremely lenient environmental regulator. In addition to its coal ash failures, its air monitors are far away from Louisiana’s heaviest air-polluting facilities, and the agency has for years been criticized for approving permits for wealthy polluters, including LNG terminals and a massive Formosa plastics factory. Louisianans know all too well that LDEQ does not protect low-income communities of color, and creates a lax regulatory environment that has enabled disasters like the recent Smitty’s Supply explosion and spill.

Please see the Earthjustice Louisiana coal ash page.

#5610. Trials Raise Questions About Perioperative Immunotherapy in Bladder Cancer

— Experts weigh negative KEYNOTE-866 and ENERGIZE findings against positive NIAGARA trial

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three expert leaders in the field of bladder cancer discuss the latest research presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress.

Moderator Matthew Galsky, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, is joined by David Aggen, MD, PhD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and Stephanie Berg, DO, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

In this second of four episodes, they examine the disappointing results from the KEYNOTE-866 and ENERGIZE trials, how those findings compare with the positive NIAGARA trial, and what they mean for perioperative treatment decisions in muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

Click here to watch all episodes of this roundtable series.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Galsky: Okay, so let's talk a little bit about the next set of studies. And we saw two studies at ESMO, really along the same theme, and that is should we add immune checkpoint blockade to cisplatin-based therapy for cisplatin-eligible patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer? We saw the results from KEYNOTE-866 and the ENERGIZE study, and I might add the long-awaited results from both of those studies. Previously, we saw the results of a similarly designed study called NIAGARA, which showed an improvement in essentially every endpoint, path CR [pathologic complete response] rate, event-free survival [EFS], and overall survival [OS].

But these studies were disappointing. There were some improvements in path CR rate versus the control arm. However, there was not an improvement in the time-to-event outcomes. And that raises some questions about cisplatin-based chemotherapy plus immune checkpoint blockade in the perioperative setting.

And now we have data with these different regimens that are mixing and matching components, so it's harder to say that it's just the class of IO [immunotherapy], PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade, or it's harder to say that it's the duration of treatment because duration of treatments were pretty similar. So, Dr. Berg, what do you make of these studies?

Berg: I agree. I kind of forgot they were around until when they were presented at ESMO. And I think ENERGIZE was really interesting because I didn't really know a lot about that compound. But in the end, they both were kind of negative and really aren't going to change practice in my mind.

But I think it was something where we saw, like you mentioned, some path CR gains, but it's also with the design of the studies and what's going to actually happen in current practice compared to what we were just discussing within ADC [antibody-drug conjugate] and IO. I'm not sure they're not going to really change practice, but it was something that, again, they were finally out and we are definitely abandoning cisplatin chemo.

Galsky: So these studies might not change practice themselves, as you point out, but there is another study that showed benefit with this type of approach, which is NIAGARA. And that really makes one wonder if all three studies were presented at the same time, whether or not the general interpretation of the studies would be different than having the positive study come out first and well before the others.

So, Dr. Aggen, what do these studies tell you in terms of how to interpret NIAGARA in retrospect?

Aggen: I think you can't compare because these trials sort of happen in different eras. Perhaps in the control arm of the more contemporary studies like ENERGIZE, there was more use of adjuvant IO that may have narrowed the difference. It's also quite striking in ENERGIZE, it enrolled a very high percentage of patients who had clinical T2 disease. And so maybe it was a slightly lower-risk population as well.

I think the question though is sort of obsolete given the striking results from KEYNOTE-905, KEYNOTE-B15, and now VOLGA that say that you should probably be giving ADC-IO to patients. I think that there may be a small subgroup with either variant histologies or other tumor features that needs durvalumab [Imfinzi] in combination with cisplatin. We don't really have the granularity of who that is.

And so at the moment I still think ADC-IO is our backbone of perioperative therapy. It is an interesting academic question though that you have two phase III trials with chemo-IO that show perhaps higher path CR rates than NIAGARA, but not the same benefit in terms of EFS and OS. And I don't think we're going to get crystal answers as to why those differences exist.

Galsky: So, Dr. Berg, Monday morning, any patient walking in the door who is going to be an appropriate candidate for cisplatin-based chemotherapy plus immune checkpoint blockade versus EV [enfortumab vedotin (Padcev)] plus immune checkpoint blockade?

Berg: I do agree with Dr. Aggen. I think the non-bladder or non-urothelial histology, perhaps even upper tract urethra, since they weren't enrolled on these studies, you would really discuss about cisplatin perioperative therapy. Even though those other studies too with variant histology, we normally go right to cystectomy.

But again, we can consider a perioperative therapy for them and I think it's still appropriate and active in those subsets, but I think more is going to come out with ADC and the non-urothelial histology. So there's some work being done in that center, but I think that's what I would use right now. I would still consider it pretty appropriate.

#5609. A Smaller Electric Land Rover Defender Is Coming In 2027

Rumors of a smaller, electric Land Rover Defender have been swirling for quite some time now — we first reported on it three years ago — and now we're finally getting some concrete information on when we'll be seeing the compact SUV. Jaguar Land Rover CEO PB Balaji says the battery-electric Defender is set to be sold alongside the existing combustion-engine model sometime in 2027, according to Automotive News.

From the spy shots we've seen, the so-called Defender Sport will be quite a bit smaller than the current five-door Defender. We know it'll be the second model underpinned by JLR's brand-new 800-volt Electrified Modular Architecture platform, the first being the Range Rover GT that should be revealed in just a couple months. When production spins up in Halewood, England, it will also mark the end of the Range Rover Evoque and Discovery Sport. The baby Defender will be powered by the same battery pack as the Range Rover GT, which JLR said will have up to 450 miles of range on the European cycle, but the boxier shape of the Defender will certainly cut down on that number.

Those who are into the idea of a smaller Defender but who aren't sold on an electric drivetrain needn't worry. Like the GT, the Defender EV is being developed with hybrid powertrain options as well. However, those buyer is going to have to wait a little while, because the hybrids aren't going to be on sale until 2028 at the earliest. Balaji told AutoNews that they are "fully underway" but "won't catch next year's timelines."

The Defender EV is set to be JLR's fifth electric vehicle, sitting alongside the aforementioned Range Rover GT, as well as the electric versions of the full-size Range Rover and Range Rover Sport, and the Jaguar Type 01. Yes, there was also the Jaguar I-Pace, but that's long dead. While pricing for the Defender EV hasn't been revealed or hinted at yet, AutoNews expects it to be fairly close to the current Defender 110. That means both will be priced significantly above the Evoque and Discovery Sport, a clear sign that JLR is continuing its move upmarket while leaving entry-level luxury behind.

The one caveat to all of this is that JLR's EV timelines have been a bit fugazi of late. The Range Rover Electric was only just officially revealed in September, two years after it was initially slated to go on sale. Keep in mind, the fifth-generation Range Rover was first revealed all the way back at the end of 2021.

This new model will be the first in a proposed series of vehicles meant to establish Defender as its own brand within Land Rover, according to Car and Driver. It's part of JLR's "House of Brands" strategy that we first told you about all the way back in 2023. I'm not sure if that's a play that'll work, but who am I to tell a brand how to run. You've got to think the Defender EV will be a solid off-roader. It has the Defender name to uphold after all. It really cannot get away with being mediocre when the going gets rough, can it?

#5607. When Less Is More: Rewilding as a Strategy for Nature Recovery

Can we bring nature back from the brink of collapse? That may sound melodramatic, but the evidence is sobering: the Planetary Health Check 2026 shows that we have crossed 7 of the 9 science-based planetary boundaries;[1] the Living Planet Report 2026 finds that wildlife populations have declined 73% on average since 1970;[2] and around 1 million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, with 75% of the land surface having been significantly altered by human activity, according to the IPBES, the leading intergovernmental body for assessing the state of biodiversity.[3]

In fact, with vertebrate extinction rates up to 100 times the natural background rate, some scientists believe we are at the onset of a sixth mass extinction.[4] But perhaps we should not be surprised at this precipitous decline in the health of our living planet. After all, around $7.3 trillion is spent every year on activities that harm nature ($4.9 trillion by companies and $2.4 trillion in government subsidies), while only $220 billion goes towards protecting or restoring ecosystems (2023 figures).[5] In other words, for every $1 we spend on taking care of nature, $33 is spent on activities that degrade the environment.

The drivers of nature loss are many, including climate change, overexploitation of resources, pollution and invasive alien species, but the largest is land-use change, primarily for agriculture.[6] Research by UNEP and Chatham House goes so far as to identify agriculture as a threat to 86% of species at risk of extinction.[7] So, is regenerative agriculture the answer? That is certainly one approach that would help, as I explored in a previous CleanTechnica article. But there is another, more direct—and some would say more radical—solution that is gaining popularity: rewilding.

As with regenerative agriculture, rewilding is more a collection of ideas and practices than a well-defined science. Nevertheless, experts convened by the IUCN define rewilding as the process of rebuilding a natural ecosystem, following major human disturbance, by restoring natural processes and food webs.[8] The Global Rewilding Alliance puts it even more simply, as “helping nature heal”.[9] In practice, this can mean anything from leaving areas of nature undisturbed to actively introducing keystone species such as beavers, bison and wild boar.

Perhaps the most cited rewilding experiment is the reintroduction of wolves into Yellowstone National Park in 1995–96, after they had been eradicated there by 1926. This resulted in a so-called trophic cascade, whereby elk numbers fell, scavengers such as eagles, ravens and bears gained a year-round food supply, and willow and aspen began to recover in places.[10] The strength of that recovery, and the extent to which the wolves were the primary driver, has been contested,[11] but few dispute the overall positive effect on biodiversity and the ecosystem.

The Yellowstone case is rewilding on a large scale, but it is still dwarfed by the rewilding work of Tompkins Conservation, created by the late Doug Tompkins, co-founder of The North Face and Esprit, and his wife Kristine McDivitt Tompkins, former CEO of Patagonia. Working primarily in Chile and Argentina, they have helped create or expand 16 parks protecting over 45 million acres of land and sea, and reintroduced 14 species, including around 50 wild jaguars.[12] Besides the ecological benefits, ecotourism is boosting local economies.[13] In Chilean Patagonia, every dollar the state invested in the national parks along Chile’s Route of Parks in 2024 returned US$6 to local communities,[14] while visitors to Argentina’s Iberá Park, partly degraded by cattle ranching in the past, have doubled in a decade to 60,000 a year.[15]

At a more local scale, the Knepp Estate in the UK has become another well documented case of rewilding. In her book Wilding: The Return of Nature to a British Farm, Isabella Tree tells the story of how she and her husband, Charlie Burrell, converted their 1,400-hectare farm from intensive dairy and crop agriculture, which was losing money, into a thriving “wild farm,” with free-roaming herbivores such as cattle, ponies, pigs, and deer.[16] A 20-year review shows an incredible rejuvenation of biodiversity, including a 916% increase in breeding bird abundance in the southern block, a 132% rise in bird species richness, a near-ninefold increase in dragonflies and damselflies, and a doubling of butterfly species in some areas.[17] There are climate benefits too, with 5.2 tCO2e/ha/yr sequestration, comparable to new native woodland.[18]

Critics of rewilding often frame it as a trade-off: more nature means less food; more wildlife means fewer jobs; more biodiversity means lower economic growth. These arguments can (and should) be tested, for in many (but not all) cases they will prove to be a false choice. My view is that it should be about balance. I saw this pragmatic approach at a rewilding site in Norfolk, England, called Wild Ken Hill, where they have designated separate areas for regenerative farming, coastal conservation, and rewilding—including 30 or so wild Exmoor ponies, 6 very inquisitive and vocal Tamworth pigs, and a small herd of Red Poll cattle.

My conclusion on rewilding is that it can certainly help us to reach the global goal of reversing biodiversity loss and becoming nature positive. It is by no means the only strategy, but it is one of the most direct and impactful. As I noted in the chapter on nature restoration in my book Thriving: “We know that nature is on the ropes, bruised and battered by dumb agriculture and dumber economics. But another thing we know is that, given half a chance, nature bounces back. Ecosystems are resilient and designed to flourish. The most powerful and effective action we can take is to step back and give nature space and time to recover.”[19]

This article is adapted and updated from content in Wayne Visser’s book “Thriving: The Breakthrough Movement to Regenerate Nature, Society, and the Economy (New York: Fast Company Press). For more information, see waynevisser.com.

[2] WWF (2026). Living Planet Report 2026: The Science of Hope. WWF, Gland, Switzerland (with ZSL)

[3] IPBES (2019). Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services. IPBES Secretariat, Bonn

[4] Ceballos, G., Ehrlich, P.R., Barnosky, A.D., García, A., Pringle, R.M. & Palmer, T.M. (2015). Accelerated modern human-induced species losses: Entering the sixth mass extinction. Science Advances, 1(5), e1400253. doi:10.1126/sciadv.1400253

[5] IPBES (2026). Methodological Assessment of the Impact and Dependence of Business on Biodiversity and Nature’s Contributions to People (Business and Biodiversity Assessment). IPBES Secretariat, Bonn

If that nameplate sounds familiar, the Aston Martin Dreadnought was originally a digital-only vehicle exclusively designed for "Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4."

The two-time F1 world champion won't be heading out into the desert alone. He will reunite with his previous Dakar co-driver, Marc Coma. Few competitors are as accomplished and experienced as Coma. The 50-year-old won the Dakar five times with KTM and briefly served as the rally's race director between 2016 and 2018. As a pairing, Alonso and Coma finished 13th in the 2020 Dakar Rally with Toyota. Alonso said his return was driven by a desire to challenge himself. Honestly, F1 isn't much of a challenge at Aston Martin this season. The Spaniard is just trundling around, hoping to finish races. He said in a release:

"After deciding to continue racing in Formula One with the Aston Martin Aramco, I thought carefully about Dakar. In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely and take on both Formula One and the Dakar Rally in the same year."

The version of the Aston Martin Dreadnought won't feature a carbon-fiber chassis, military-grade armor plating or weapons storage like its Call of Duty counterpart. This Dreadnought is based on the Prodrive-designed Dacia Sandrider. The machine is fitted with the same three-liter, twin-turbocharged Nissan engine. The starkest difference is the bodywork, styled after the digital-only combat SUV, most evident in the square headlights and the louvered rear window.

The Prodrive-run effort will also include another usual suspect at the wheel of a Dreadnought: Nine-time World Rally Champion Sébastien Loeb. The living legend has never won the Dakar Rally, but has finished second on three occasions. The third Dreadnought will be driven by Lucas Moraes. The Brazilian joined the Dacia-Prodrive effort after winning the World Rally-Raid Championship with Toyota in 2025. The vehicle's origin may seem ridiculous, but Aston Martin has a legitimate chance of winning the Dakar in January. Prodrive is the returning winner after Nasser Al-Attiyah took the 2026 victory in a Dacia Sandrider.

#5604. China’s Electric Heavy Trucks Are Taking Sales from Diesel and LNG

In September 2026, battery-electric trucks captured 49.8% of China’s new domestic heavy-truck registrations. Of 65,800 trucks registered, 32,800 ran on batteries. Another 36 used hydrogen fuel cells. Battery electric accounted for more than 99% of the broader new-energy category. China’s freight operators are buying batteries at a scale that puts diesel and LNG suppliers under pressure.

The shift has gathered speed. Battery electric accounted for about 13% of domestic heavy-truck registrations in 2024, 28% in 2025 and nearly 38% in the first nine months of 2026. The figures come from compulsory-insurance registrations for trucks sold into the domestic market, excluding exports. China’s total domestic truck market remains below its pre-pandemic levels. Battery trucks are gaining share while the market for new heavy trucks remains constrained.

From May through September, new-energy heavy trucks exceeded 40% of new registrations for five straight months. The category reached approximately 226,400 vehicles in the first nine months, up 64% from the same period in 2025, and nearly 99% were battery electric. Tractor units that pull semi-trailers are leading the change. In September, 64.48% of new domestic tractor registrations belonged to the new-energy category. Electric trucks are moving freight on ordinary commercial routes, including work beyond ports and industrial yards.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing traces China’s heavy-truck sales from 2015 through 2026, examines real freight costs and charging choices, and assesses the consequences for manufacturers, logistics companies and fuel demand.

The operating economics explain much of the appeal. Trucks earn money by carrying cargo, so annual kilometres, payload, electricity prices, charging stops and vehicle availability matter as much as the price on the invoice. High-mileage routes make electricity and maintenance savings more valuable. A costly grid connection or charging queue can eat into those savings. Fleet operators need to evaluate the truck and its route together.

Recent ICCT case studies document how those economics play out. A Guangdong warehouse fleet of 28 electric trucks had estimated five-year ownership costs 16% below comparable diesel trucks. In Yangtze River Delta express delivery, 50 electric tractor-trailers working routes of 300–500 km achieved a narrower 3% advantage over six years without purchase incentives. Another operation covering 900 km a day with strategically placed high-power charging showed estimated ownership costs 19% below diesel. The differences reflect route, utilization and charging arrangements.

Those three operations offer a more useful procurement lesson than a single quoted range figure. The operator starts with cargo, schedules and energy access, then selects equipment. The narrow 3% margin in express delivery also shows why financing and charging costs can determine whether a viable electric route makes money.

Battery swapping has carved out a sizable part of this market. In September, 20.09% of newly registered battery-electric heavy trucks were classified as swap-capable. That compares with 22.92% across January–September 2026 and 30.39% for all of 2025. The number of swap-classified trucks continued to rise, while conventional charging gained a larger share of the expanding electric market. China’s registration classification also includes some trucks with leased batteries that are recharged rather than exchanged.

Swapping fits dense, repeatable freight operations such as steelworks, ports and bulk-material haulage. Fleet operators and station owners can standardize vehicles and use stations often enough to pay for batteries held in inventory. Conventional charging serves a wider range of routes and can fit scheduled stops, overnight parking and depot operations. Both approaches depend on predictable truck traffic and reliable electricity connections.

China is building infrastructure around those freight patterns. Yunnan commissioned 3,350 km of heavy-truck charging corridors in 2025, with 113 stations and 869 connectors. Fujian opened a 649 km coastal corridor in October 2026, including 15 charging stations and eight swapping stations. The IEA’s 2026 charging review describes the concentration of heavy-vehicle charging around freight corridors and industrial centres. Long-haul coverage still has gaps, but the network is expanding where trucks already have work to do.

Hydrogen has found little traction alongside this expansion. China registered 689 fuel-cell heavy trucks in the first nine months of 2026, compared with more than 223,000 battery-electric trucks. LNG has a much larger installed customer base, although its advantage over diesel has narrowed as gas prices change. Battery trucks offer a different cost structure built around drivetrain efficiency and lower maintenance needs. That makes the competition increasingly difficult for equipment and fuel suppliers dependent on combustion engines.

Sales changes take years to work through the operating fleet. Kpler projects that new-energy trucks, predominantly battery electric, will account for about 8% of Chinese heavy trucks in service at the end of 2026. It also estimates they will displace about 230,000 barrels of diesel per day compared with moving the same freight using diesel trucks. Freight vehicles with high daily utilization can have a large effect on fuel demand before they become a majority of vehicles on the road.

China’s June 2026 heavy-truck programme joins purchasing incentives, grid access, charging corridors, financing and logistics planning. Its 2030 targets include a 40% share of new-energy heavy-truck sales, a 20% share of the operating fleet and 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors. Monthly new sales have already surpassed the sales-share target. Building and replacing enough vehicles to reach the fleet target will take longer.

Other countries have different electricity tariffs, road networks and freight routes, but the procurement method travels. Start with the actual jobs trucks perform. Identify routes with strong electric economics, plan the charging and grid connections those routes require, and finance vehicles and infrastructure as one programme. Other drivetrains can compete where their operating costs or performance are better. The evidence from China’s largest commercial freight applications increasingly favours batteries.

The complete TFIE Strategy Briefing includes the historical registration series, the ICCT ownership-cost cases, charging and swapping corridors, and fleet-turnover analysis. TFIE Strategy works with fleets, utilities and policymakers on freight-electrification scenarios and investment decisions.

#5603. Electric BMW M4 Convertible Is Coming To Silently Mess Up Your Broccoli Haircut

It seems like only a few months ago that we told you BMW is working on an electric i4 convertible (and a new 4 Series coupe, too) to sit alongside the already revealed i3 in the lineup, and that's because it was only a few months ago. Now, just hours after the first prototype reviews of the electric M3 have been published, our spies in Germany have caught the i4 droptop testing in high-performance M4 guise. Its quad motors and 800-plus horsepower will be perfect for silently messing up the broccoli haircuts of the M4 convertible's typical owners and the three friends they bring along for the ride.

We have yet to see the regular i4 convertible make its debut, but since the four-door M3 is almost here and this M4 prototype looks fairly close to production-ready, once the standard model is revealed we shouldn't have to wait too long for the M4 to be shown off. We know the electric M3 will be sold alongside an M3 with a gas inline-6, and the same should be true for the M4, though as of now internal-combustion prototypes haven't been spied.

This prototype is still covered in camouflage, and it doesn't seem like the M4 bumpers has been fitted because it's missing things like the M's square LEDs in the corners, but there are a few tells we're looking at an M4. There are wider flares tacked onto the front fenders, and the rear fenders seem wider than the ones on previously spied i4 prototypes. The wheels look massively wide, and this car is fitted with pretty big drilled brake discs with blue calipers. It has camo paneling on the hood, which is probably to obscure the vent we've seen on the M3.

Like its four-door counterpart, the electric M4 convertible should get a quad-motor powertrain with well over 800 horsepower that will make it drive and feel like a proper M car. There will be fun noises that you can turn off if you're boring, simulated gear shifts and other performance technology features, alongside actual mechanical changes like upgraded suspension and better steering. We don't yet know how much of a range hit you'll take when going for an M4 instead of an i4, but given how fast the Neue Klasse cars charge, long road trips should be no problem.

We don't have concrete details on when the i4 will be revealed or go on sale, not to mention the timeline for the M versions, but it seems like a sure bet that the standard model will be shown at some point in 2027.
