#5601. The Rising Tide Of Distributed Energy Resources

Centralized power plants can trip widespread brownouts or blackouts when under stress. They make fat targets for enemy weapons, too. In contrast, distributed energy resources (DERs for short) can improve overall resiliency in the face of both natural and human-made disasters, while also enabling ratepayers to take advantage of utility discounts, and even earn revenue from their personal energy assets. The DERs field includes — but is not limited to — rooftop solar, EV charging stations, and home batteries. And, we ain’t seen nothing yet. DERs stakeholders have also begun moving into the distributed computing field as well.

DERs first surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar in the early 2000’s during the Obama administration, when the US Department of Energy began promoting decentralized, home-and community-based energy resources as the leading characteristic of a modernized and more resilient electricity grid. Made possible by the falling cost of solar, wind, and energy storage, the agency’s embrace of small-scale, localized electricity generation was a sharp contrast with the traditional emphasis on large centralized power plants for energy security (see more DERs background here).

Nowadays the DERs field embraces practically any non-centralized power generation resource, regardless of size or type. The DERs field can include, for example, a new gas power plant commissioned to run an adjacent AI data center.

To get some perspective on the journey of DERs since the early 2000’s, consider the case of the leading rooftop solar installer Sunrun. After launching in 2007, Sunrun segued into energy storage and virtual power plants, with “virtual” referring to smart grid technology that coordinates thousands of far-flung energy producing (and consuming) devices to balance supply and demand at peak periods of consumption.

For the record, Sunrun now presents itself as a storage-first company. The company’s focus remains on renewable energy but the storage field is source-agnostic, embracing practically every energy resource on the planet.

Sunrun CEO Mary Powell also prefers to use “distributed” instead of “virtual” in reference to decentralized power systems, to emphasize that hardware is the foundational element. As of this month, Sunrun ranks as the biggest distributed power plant in the US, with solar and storage assets spread among 164,000 enrolled households.

Back in 2021, Sunrun entered into an installation partnership with the home energy management startup SPAN, known for its next-generation home electrical panels among other products, and that layed the ground work for a partnership on distributed computing systems. Earlier this year, SPAN introduced XFRA, a new product consisting of computer nodes to be staged at homes and smaller commercial spaces to form a distributed data center. The model is similar in concept to the familiar Internet-enabled citizen scientist platform, except that XFRA deploys its own nodes instead of using a participant’s personal computer.

This past September, Sunrun announced its selection as an authorized installation partner for XFRA with a focus on new home developments, aiming for gigawatt-scale distributed computing networks beginning in Texas and other selected markets. “Sunrun’s battery-plus-solar systems will maintain reliable electricity for both the homes and the XFRA compute nodes, while preventing the overloading of local distribution infrastructure—allowing SPAN to maximize node deployment.,” Sunrun explains.

“By pairing home energy generation and storage with XFRA compute nodes, we are unlocking new economic value for our customers and for Sunrun, while also solving certain speed-to-power constraints that would otherwise limit AI deployment,” Sunrun CEO Mary Powell elaborated in a press statement.

Arch Rao, founder and CEO of SPAN, also chipped in his two cents. “We can now drastically increase our penetration of XFRA compute nodes by pairing them with Sunrun energy systems to deliver cost-effective AI compute capacity at unprecedented speed while also reducing compute cost for certain AI applications,” Rao said.

Back when the Energy Department initially began promoting DERs as a function of the energy transition, the agency used the term “prosumer” to describe ratepayers who are empowered to engage with their local power grid as a renewable energy producer, not simply as a passive consumer. The distributed data center adds another layer of engagement to the prosumer mix.

At a personal appearance during Climate Week in New York City in September, Powell referenced distributed computing as the latest demonstration of the company’s ongoing dialog with its customers and other stakeholders, leading to innovative new products that put more power management tools in the hands of ratepayers.

Powell reiterated the point during an appearance at the 2026 “DERVOS” summit at the Brooklyn Navy Yard on November 5, and the DERVOS gathering itself provides further insights into the widening scope of DERs activity.

“DERVOS” is a play on Davos, which is shorthand for the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum. Like the World Economic Forum, DERs stakeholders have emerged in force upon the global economy as well as here in the US, stretching far from its do-it-yourself roots in the off-gridder movement of the 1970’s.

The event itself is the brainchild of the collaborative trade organization DER Task Force. The group formally launched in 2019 but it claims roots much earlier, in the 1970’s-era New York City activist organization Energy Task Force, whose activities were highlighted by the installation of a wind turbine in the city — illegally, of course.

By the time DERVOS 2026 rolled around, the DER Task Force had become an organization with a reach far beyond New York, and it has also embraced the size-doesn’t-matter ethos  under the slogan, “Everything is DER.”

“That’s what we mean by Everything is DER: not that everything is small, or even literally ‘distributed,’ but that the center of gravity is shifting toward energy resources that are closer to load and controlled by those who need the power,” the Task Force explains (emphasis theirs).

“Sometimes that shift is bottoms-up, sometimes it’s centrally planned, but either way, DERs aren’t the sideshow anymore. They’re the main event,” they add.

I’ll have much more to report from DERVOS 2026 in the coming days and weeks, but for the time being let’s go back to the foundational idea of improving grid resiliency and security. Climate change aside, in recent years Russia and the US have both provided textbook cases for transitioning out of energy systems that involve building fat, juicy infrastructure targets for attack, alongside precariously long energy transportation systems. If you have any thoughts about that, drop a note in the comment thread.

Image: The renewable energy “prosumer” envisioned by the US Department of Energy in the early 2000’s has become the sophisticated distributed energy resources manager of today (graphic by Sara Harman courtesy of US DOE).

Tina has been covering advanced energy technology, military sustainability, emerging materials, biofuels, ESG and related policy and political matters for CleanTechnica since 2009. Follow her @tinamcasey on LinkedIn, Mastodon or Bluesky.

#5600. Are There Any V12 Engines That Could Be Called 'Dependable?'

A V12 engine under the bonnet is a symbol of automotive decadence, telling the world that you've made it and who cares about fuel consumption. Sure, there are plenty of engines that deliver as much performance, but few that exude extravagance and luxury in quite the same way. Still, can V12s be dependable? You might assume not, given their specialized nature and low-volume production.

V12s are installed in high-end sedans and limousines, in mid-engined supercars, and in a handful of opulent SUVs and 4x4s. But they're not that numerous in the grand scheme of production vehicles.

One of the first uses of the V12 came in 1913, when, in the UK, Louis Coatalen, the chief engineer of Sunbeam Motor Car Company, stuffed a new type of aircraft engine called the Mohawk into one of the company's race cars. Subsequently, "Toodles V" was born: a machine which, after a few hiccups, went on to set eight world speed-over-distance records at Brooklands racetrack.

After Toodles and before WWII, V12s grew in popularity for their smoothness and power, with the North American auto industry providing the bulk of them, even during the Great Depression of 1929: think Packard Twin Six, the Auburn 12, the Cadillac V-12, and the Lincoln series K.

But when Lincoln ceased production of the V12 in 1948, that was that for American V12s. No car company has made one in the U.S. since, and production was mainly left to Europe. Ferrari made its legendary "Colombo" V12, Lamborghini's 1963 V12 would eventually underpin the gorgeous Miura, and even Jaguar brought a 5.3-liter V12 engine to the E-Type in 1971.

There are still a few V12s in production today that you can buy with a new-car warranty, which are likely reliable, but what about those of yesteryear? Here's a look at the most dependable.

If you're after a V12 that's about as widespread and dependable as can be, then the Mercedes M120 is the one to seek out. Mercedes had been working on the idea of a passenger car with a V12 since the 1950s (and considered putting one in its 600 Pullman limo), but it was beaten to the punch by BMW's adoption of the 5.0-liter V12 in 1987's E32 750i. Mercedes didn't get its M120 V12 to market until 1991 in the W140-series S-Class. The 600 badge was given to the W140-series S-Class, the related CL coupe, and the R129 Mercedes SL due to the engine's displacement.

The M120 was a considerably more advanced engine than BMW's V12. It featured an aluminum-alloy block, a forged crankshaft, and LH-Jetronic fuel injection, along with dual throttle bodies, mass airflow sensors, and ECUs. Producing 402 horsepower and 428 pounds-feet of torque, the M120 had enough grunt to push the heavy 600 SE and SEL models from 0 to 60 mph in around six seconds.

What makes the M120 so desirable today, though, is its dependability. There are a few known weak points, such as oil leaks around the valve covers, the front timing covers, the lower oil pan, and the front crank seal, along with worn engine mounts. But aside from these relatively minor issues, this V12 is known for its reliability and solidity. Furthermore, owners of such high-end Mercs are likely to have kept up with their maintenance.

One final seal of approval comes in the form of the M120's subsequent use in the middle of the Pagani Zonda, a supercar classic we'll always love: a 7.3-liter development of the V12 powered various iterations, culminating in a near-800-hp final edition.

Japan is a country that has not wholeheartedly embraced the V12 engine. In fact, it has made but one road-going engine of this configuration in history, although it turns out to be one of the most reliable V12s you could imagine. It's called the 1GZ-FE, a naturally aspirated 5.0-liter lump with variable valve timing, two ECUs, and enough redundancy built in that it can run on one bank of six cylinders if necessary. The engine powered the second-generation Toyota Century.

A big plus point of the 1GZ is that it's not what you'd call a stressed V12. In its original 1997 incarnation for the Century model, the Japanese "gentleman's agreement" put in place to prevent a horsepower war meant that Toyota claimed a peak power output of just 276 horsepower, with torque rated at up to 355 pounds-feet. It was never going to be one of the most powerful JDM engines ever made, even if its horsepower was higher than the domestic advertising suggested.

If that's not a big enough perk, know that like so many Toyota engines, the 1GZ-FE would accommodate a heck of a lot of tuning. In fact, the notorious Smokey Nagata – founder of Top Secret and the man who pushed a Supra to 194 mph on a British motorway in 1998 – later built another Supra with a Century's V12 in it. Only that was adorned with a pair of HKS GT2540 turbos, liberating 930 hp and a top speed of over 220 mph.

When the engine was launched, Toyota published an engineering paper stating, amongst other things, that the 1GZ-FE was more reliable than its competitors, and though the sample size is small, it has been proven to be a dependable V12, with nothing other than age-related failures of minor parts generally reported.

The original BMW V12, the M70, started an entire line of engines that went into the 7 Series as well as the 8 Series. BMW's M70 successor, the M73, was employed by Rolls-Royce starting in 1998 with the Silver Seraph. Rolls began using a V12 in its Phantom III (1936-1939), but after trying that 7.3-liter monster out for size, it eventually dedicated itself to inline-6 and V8 engines. Rolls-Royce did not use a V12 again until the 1998 Silver Seraph.

Perhaps the most famous application of a BMW V12 was the S70/2, designed by Paul Rosche, which was the incredible engine that powered the legendary McLaren F1 with 627 horsepower. Though maintenance costs are high, the engine itself is robust.

Both Ferrari and Lamborghini's V12s are highly tuned, and of course, they're installed in the sorts of cars that command huge fees on the used market. Nonetheless, the 5.5-liter engine in the Ferrari 456 GT, for example, is supposed to be fairly dependable, as long as it is subjected to regular (and expensive) maintenance.

Aston Martin has been making production V12s since the DB7 Vantage of 1999, and while these "AML" units were not just two Ford Duratec V6s welded together, there was plenty of Ford-derived DNA in the British engine courtesy of Ford's advanced powertrain division. It's generally dependable, so long as owners keep up with maintenance. Oil starvation to the crankshaft is one of the more common issues.

Finally, Jaguar had a good array of V12s in such cars as the E-Type and XJ models. While the mechanicals are reasonably durable, these engines are frequently let down by their electrics.

#5599. BYD E6Y Odyssey

A couple of friends embark on a road trip to pick their EV purchase, and it turns into an Odyssey.

The BYD E6 is a BEV classic. Globe-trotting friends have ridden in them as taxis in Singapore. Majella and I even took one for a test drive (it reminded me of a ’70s Chrysler Valiant). It was the best selling pure electric car in China in 2016, with about 600,000 sold globally, and it is viewed by many as ahead of its time. So, when one showed up at our coffee and cake morning tea, I had to interview the owner, Joanne, and her road trip friend, Meredith. What they shared with me was truly an odyssey of determination to get Jo’s car home. Please note: this story took place 6 years ago. Charging availability has improved and so has Joanne’s knowledge of living with an electric vehicle.

Joanne told me that she had been looking for an EV for two years when a search on carsales.com found an ad for an E6Y (the taxi version of the BYD E6). It was a pre-COVID import and had been mothballed at Sydney airport after the company importing the vehicles had decided not to go ahead with taxis. Photos of all the BYDs at the airport were widely circulated as evidence that no one wanted to buy an EV. The cars were being “sold by a mate out of the back of the factory.” At the low cost of AU$32,000, claiming a 400 km range from its 83-kWh battery and only 100 km on the odometer, Joanne saw it as a bargain.

There was some consideration of putting the car on a flatbed and having it shipped, but in the end, the two friends decided on a road trip.

Jo informs me that: “They only brought 120 of the BYD E6Y taxi versions into the country. BYD sold some GLX versions, which had more bells and whistles.”

She was soon to find out that all is not as it seems. Her lack of knowledge of EVs meant that her trip in the car from Sydney back to Brisbane would be an odyssey of Greek tragedy proportions. Jo reminisces: “Meredith reminded me our original plan had been to spend just two days driving back to Brisbane with the one overnight stay. I thought I could ‘fast charge’ the car and make it back to Brisvegas on the second day. Hahahaha. Lesson learned the hard way.” They expected it to be just a twelve-hour trip. Meredith adds, “I told her we would laugh about it one day.”

Joanne contacted the seller and planned her flight to Sydney. Meredith got excited and joined the “road trip” in Newcastle. Jo paid the money and took ownership of the car. “It took two hours to get out of Sydney.” To be fair, that wasn’t the car’s fault — just Sydney’s congested traffic. However, the fact that the previous owner had only charged the car to 50% didn’t help. She was able to charge the car to 80% on the outskirts of Sydney. “But I had no idea that I wouldn’t get the expected range at highway speeds.”

Another learning curve was the state of charging points — sure, there were plenty listed on PlugShare, but many were unavailable or broken. Again, dear reader, I must emphasize this was 6 years ago.

Her next planned stop was accommodation she had booked at Newcastle. She got to within 2 km when the battery readout said “zero.” She was unable to find a place to charge — the car had not come with a granny charger. Jo clarified her Newcastle experience by email: “the Uni in Newcastle was the first I tried to charge. My friend Meredith and I tried three other places to charge all with no luck. I found out later that the Newcastle chargers were notorious for not working.” She confided to me that she now knows that the car can go a little further even when it says zero battery. She also had to learn the difference between AC and DC charging. The BYD she had bought could only handle AC charging.

With the battery reading zero, she felt she had no choice but to leave the car at a nearby garage. The owner of the accommodation she had booked kindly came and picked her and her friend up. The next day, the BNB owner dropped them back to the garage and a tow truck was ordered. The tow truck took them and their car to a local winery where they trickle charged next to the golf carts. The winery also had a Tesla level 2 charger for customer use. It was charging when they arrived. “We left a note on the windscreen of the Tesla that was using the level 2. During breakfast the Tesla owner rang and said the charger was available. We left the winery fully charged and off up the highway.” Not a bad place to get stuck, methinks.

280 km up the road to Kempsie, there was access to free charging in the council carpark, but no available accommodation! That’s what happens when you travel on the Queen’s Birthday long weekend. “We were checking out the back seat of the car as a place to sleep when a friend of a friend told them he had a farm in area. ‘Have I got a place for you!’ he told them. After we finished charging, we had to drive down this dark farm track. We couldn’t plug the car in because we still didn’t have a granny charger!” They made themselves comfortable in the available beds in the barn. The next morning in the light of day they found they had driven alongside of a lagoon! “We could have easily driven into that!”

Meredith adds: “I didn’t think I’d be sleeping in a shed with a tractor and then I couldn’t sleep because of the smell of diesel.” The trip was not just a challenge, but torture.

Their next adventure was just a few kilometers up the road at Gladstone NSW. Low on juice, they contacted people through PlugShare and got a message from a local café owner. You can check out the café here. He already owned a Hyundai Ioniq, and so had a granny charger to lend. The café owner knew a fellow who was visiting his mum in town. This friend had ordered an Atto 3 from BYD and was waiting on this first shipment of BYDs to arrive. Jo took him for a ride around town in her car. “This was his first ride in a BYD.”

He arranged for them to leave their car at his mother’s home in the next town (Smithtown). Jo and her friend were now in a hurry, as both had to get back to Brisbane to go to work the next day. Leaving the car charging, “We belted back to Brisbane in this horrible little roller skate hire car.” Home in Brisbane, Jo had to plan how to retrieve her BYD purchase. Meredith did not want another “road trip.”

This time, Jo travelled south by train. Even this trip was not without drama. She missed her stop. Thankfully, she was able to get off at the next stop and change to the northbound train to make it back to where her car waited faithfully for her. She took a taxi to her car, returned the borrowed granny charger, and began her journey home. She was so keen that she ended up with a speeding ticket.

Joanne arrived at her motel in Balina with 10 km of range showing on the dashboard. But the available ocular charger soon filled up the car. By 9:00 pm, with a full battery, she couldn’t wait to go home. The fireworks display in town was a fitting sendoff for the final leg of her journey.

Jo would like to acknowledge all the good advice and offers of help she received from fellow users of PlugShare, as well as all those referred to above. She is now a confident and competent driver of her BYD E6Y and has made many trips back and forth to Sydney from Brisbane with less drama. The BYD E6Y Facebook group has been a great help. She says she would not part with her green E6Y Singapore taxi — “a comfortable and solid basic car.” Rumour has it that there are about 250 on Australian roads, with the record distance travelled over 1 million km.

Another owner commented: “This unstoppable tank will outlive me I’m sure, best of all its super basic … no internet, no lane assist, no self-driving and plenty of new and used cheap parts available. This is why it seems like there are so few … they are so good NO ONE who has one is selling them.”

Jo has even taken her car camping. “The camping trip was to Yandina up the coast. I did sleep in the back of the car on that trip very comfortably. But that time I had a mattress and bedding. I did take out the bottom half of the back seat from the car so I could get a completely flat rear area for the mattress. When I returned from the camping trip, I popped the rear seat bottom back in the car. It’s just two bolts and a couple of plastic clips that hold it in.”

And in the future, I asked? “It will be hard to part with my E6. I am waiting on the first solid state 1000km BEVs before I would consider parting with it. I just love the two-tone paint job.”

Jo is another happy battery electric vehicle owner, sharing her learning experience “odyssey” and having fun. “Thanks for the opportunity to immortalise the odyssey,” she told me in her latest email. The future is bright and electric as we learn to live with our new vehicles.

David Waterworth is a retired teacher who divides his time between looking after his grandchildren and trying to make sure they have a planet to live on. He is long on Tesla [NASDAQ:TSLA].

#5598. Slate Sells 'Screenless GPS' For Its Trucks, Which Is Just A Map

Slate, maker of the barebones $26,400 electric truck that I desperately want to see succeed despite my worries about its competition, is all about simplicity. Simple truck, simple purchase price, simple construction, simple accessories. So what happens when buyers want something more complex — something like GPS, which requires satellite connections, maps, screens, and code? Well, the company does it the old fashioned way by stamping its brand on a Rand McNally Road Atlas and selling it as "Screenless GPS."

The automaker is selling these atlases for $30, and on the website it's currently marked as sold out. The product description reads, "This is the original navigation system — no signal required. Spiral bound, large print, and ready for wherever your Slate takes you. Covers the US, Canada, and Mexico. Limited edition." This particular book is the 2027 Rand McNally EasyFinder Road Atlas, and it includes "7 curated Rand McNally road trips."

Rand McNally, for the younger readers out there, makes books of maps that it calls its road atlases. I grew up with a road atlas wedged between the driver's seat and center console of my mom's car, and I certainly remember thumbing through its pages while bored — behavior my mom encouraged, so I'd know how to read a map by the time I started driving myself. It's certainly a skill the average Slate buyer has, and maybe the folks that appreciate a simple truck will likewise appreciate a simple way to navigate it around.

Paper maps have had a bit of a renaissance as we all get ever more tired of our constantly-increasing screentime. Backcountry Discovery Routes has worked with Butler Maps for years to create paper maps of its BDR routes for those looking to go screenless on the trails, and it seems Slate is hoping to bring the same enthusiasm to road maps with its Rand McNally tie-in. I'm just hoping the promotion Slate is doing for its map, like the Instagram post above, is all tongue in cheek. If the company really means "analog pinch to zoom" is a feature, it comes off a bit I HATE WIFE AND PHOEN.

For most of us, a phone mount suction-cupped to the windshield will make a better navigation solution than a Rand McNally shoved next to the center console. For Slate's target market, buyers who actively miss simpler, older cars and want a return to that kind of design, the bent and worn pages of a worn Road Atlas may provide a bit of the nostalgia they're looking for in an all-electric truck. After all, they probably had one in their old Ranger all those years ago.

#5597. It's Official: U.S. Loses Measles Elimination Status After 25 Years

— Vaccine rates have fallen as cases rise

The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread -- largely among the unvaccinated -- at the highest rate in more than 30 years.

Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) declaration has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but it marks a sharp turnabout in a disease largely controlled through decades of scientific advances. It also may be seen as the beginning of an era in which diseases of the past become deadly problems for the modern world.

"Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf," Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, PAHO's director, said at a news conference. "It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community."

PAHO expects the U.S., Bolivia, and Mexico to submit plans "in the coming weeks" for how each country will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, Daniel Salas, MD, the organization's executive manager for immunizations, told reporters.

Measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024. The outbreaks in North America started in close-knit Mennonite communities and have since spread to areas with low vaccination rates. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998.

International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months.

Tuesday's announcement signals an erosion of public health preparedness.

Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the U.S. and globally. And as one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine, measles was seen as likely to be one of the first vaccine-preventable diseases to reemerge when vaccinations falter.

That means others are likely to follow, some experts said.

"It can be the canary in the coal mine to other things," said Susan Kansagra, MD, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials.

Measles vaccines have safely stopped the virus' spread in the U.S. for 30 years.

It takes a community vaccination rate of 95% to prevent outbreaks, experts say. But as fewer parents vaccinate their children and federal leaders sow doubt and confusion about the importance of getting vaccinated, the virus has found footholds in communities across the U.S. All but three states have reported a confirmed case of measles this year.

The last 2 years have been the worst in a generation in the U.S., with more than 7,000 cases and 13 reported deaths. Nearly all of those people were either unvaccinated or didn't report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10% of those infected had to be hospitalized.

The illness typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it's one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults over age 30.

Ten measles-associated deaths have been reported in the U.S. this year, making it the deadliest in more than three decades. Health officials haven't released detailed information on each death, but at least five of the dead were children.

Major Outbreaks in Texas, Utah, South Carolina, and Pennsylvania

Since the U.S. eliminated measles in 2000, public health officials usually logged fewer than 200 cases a year, most of them tied to international travel.

But since 2025, measles has sickened thousands. It started with a major outbreak in the Southwest.

In Texas, more than 760 people got sick and two children died. In New Mexico, about 100 people got sick and one adult died. Then measles exploded in rural border towns in Arizona and Utah, followed by a major outbreak in South Carolina in the winter and spring that sickened nearly 1,000 people.

This year has been much worse -- the worst for measles cases since 1991. The more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that dwarfed the earlier ones.

And the outbreak tallies are almost certainly an undercount, public health experts say.

Critics Say the U.S. Response Is Falling Short

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump appointed him to oversee federal health agencies.

Kennedy and other federal leaders have argued that vaccination rates were waning for years before Trump took office a second time, that measles is not an "American phenomenon," and that the U.S. government is handling measles better than other countries. In January, a CDC leader told reporters that the loss of the nation's elimination status would be the "cost of doing business" globally.

It's true that other countries are struggling with measles, and some also have lost their measles-elimination status. But public health experts and others say the outcome in the U.S. wasn't inevitable.

"This humiliating determination is the tragic yet predictable result of an ongoing campaign by grifters, quacks, and charlatans to put their own greed and self-worth ahead of the health and safety of children," said Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.).

The government has been taking some steps. In August and September, the CDC awarded $100 million to support state and local measles-response work. And Kennedy and CDC Director Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, have made statements that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles from spreading.

"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," Schwartz said in a statement Tuesday. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities."

But state and local health officials say the cost is far higher and that the moment demands a louder federal voice -- and a bigger push for vaccinations -- than Kennedy and Schwartz are providing.

"When the people at the front of the room are not speaking loudly and frequently in support of vaccination, the program starts to falter. And that's what we're seeing in the U.S.," said Noel Brewer, PhD, a University of North Carolina public health professor who chairs a committee that presented an analysis of U.S. measles data to PAHO last week. "How many kids have to die before they start getting concerned?"

Some experts noted that neither Kennedy nor the CDC has scheduled a news conference to address their plans to fight measles. When the AP asked for Kennedy's reaction to the U.S. losing its measles-free status, an HHS spokesperson pointed to Schwartz's statement. During the PAHO news conference, the health department did issue a news release promoting the latest episode of Kennedy's online cooking show.

After hugely successful vaccination campaigns, the Americas became the first region in the world to be free of measles in 2016. Health officials estimate the measles vaccine prevented 6.2 million deaths in the Americas between 2000 and 2023.

Now, the entirety of North America faces the task of earning back the designation.

#5596. 1969 Chevy Camaro SS For Sale With 10,000 Miles Shown Boasts 396 V8 And Body-Up Restoration

While we're yearning for another generation of the legendary Chevrolet Camaro, our best bet is to look back at its golden era — and one of the most pristine restomods we've found on Hemmings. This Ontario orange 1969 Camaro SS, listed by a Clarkston, Michigan dealer for $58,900, shows 10,000 miles on the odometer and a body-up restoration. Its 396 big-block raises a fair question: How did that engine really stack up against its rivals back in '69?

Neither the Hemmings listing nor the dealer's YouTube walkaround gives horsepower or torque figures, but this clearly isn't a stock motor. The 396 wears an Edelbrock Performer aluminum intake, ceramic headers, a mild camshaft, and a Flame Thrower high-energy-ingition distributor, with chrome valve covers and an air cleaner on top. Behind it, a Turbo-Hydramatic 400 automatic sends power to a 10-bolt rear axle with 3.23 gears.

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j-bnQtJsNGQ]

For context, Chevrolet offered three 396s in the 1969 SS, rated at 325, 350, and 375 horsepower, with torque between 410 and 415 pound-feet. The 375-horsepower L78 sat at the top, peaking at 5,600 rpm. So without a dyno sheet, there's no telling where this restomod example lands among them.

On paper, the L78 outgunned most of its competition. Its 375 horsepower beat the 345 claimed for Pontiac's Ram Air IV Firebird or the 335 rated for Mustang Mach 1's 428 Cobra Jet — one of the most powerful powertrains the Mach 1 ever came with. Even the base 325-horsepower SS 396 sat within 10 horsepower of the Cobra Jet.

Testing was less flattering. Car Life's figures (per Curbside Classic), recorded in showroom-stock trim, have a Camaro SS 396 L78 reaching 60 mph in 6.8 seconds and covering the quarter-mile in 14.77 seconds at 98.7 mph. The Mach 1 428, meanwhile, managed 5.5 seconds and 13.9 at 103.3 mph. Two other 375-horsepower rivals also ran quicker quarter-miles: the Plymouth 'Cuda 440 at 14.01 seconds, and the Boss 429 Mustang at 14.09, despite a slower 7.1-second run to 60. Traction was the usual culprit, since bias-ply tires struggled with big-block torque, so gross ratings didn't settle the pony car argument.

The Camaro's paint is Ontario orange metallic with a black hockey stripe, and there are front and rear spoilers, a cowl hood, and dual chrome mirrors. The 17-inch American Racing Torque Thrust wheels are wrapped in Dunlop 255/45ZR17 tires in back and 235/40R17s up front. The car also gets tubular upper and lower control arms, an aluminum radiator, power steering, and power front discs with slotted and drilled rotors. Inside, the black vinyl interior includes factory bucket seats, a center console, a sport steering wheel, and a Retrosound radio. So while we speculate on the return of the Camaro, consider looking to the past to get the edge off with this low-mile time capsule.

#5595. HLTH 2026: Noom pushes deeper into connected health with new wearable, Noom Band

HLTH 2026: Noom pushes deeper into connected health with new wearable, Noom Band" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Noom launched its own wearable to enhance its metabolic health platform with activity, sleep and cardiovascular data insights.

The device, called Noom Band, will be bundled into Noom’s existing enterprise partnerships at no additional upfront cost starting in early 2027. The wearable is also free for Noom Health employer and health plan customers.

The introduction of a wearable is part of Noom’s broader push to build an integrated metabolic health platform combining behavior change, virtual care, diagnostics, medications and continuous health data.

Noom Band is a faceless wrist-worn wearable powered by Sensor Bio, and it will be fully integrated into the Noom app. The device will track heart rate, heart rate variability, SpO2, sleep and activity, with the data feeding directly into Noom’s behavior change platform, executives said.

Noom is providing the wearable to enterprise clients at no additional upfront cost as it sees opportunities to use continuous data on sleep, activity and other physiological signals to keep members engaged and drive better outcomes in the company's weight management and metabolic health programs, Noom CEO Geoff Cook told Fierce Healthcare.

"We are getting outcomes-based payments, so we believe we will have more people hitting their 5% weight loss goals or 10% weight loss goals, if they have the wearable, than if they don't," Cook said in an exclusive interview about the launch of Noom Band.

Integrating a wearable device into Noom’s metabolic health program fills a major data gap, Cook said.

Noom has evolved from a weight loss app into a broader preventive care and clinical health platform. The company's behavior change platform uses psychology, clinical support and structured habit design to help users build long-term lifestyle shifts. The company also offers integrated telehealth services through its Noom Med platform, combining remote clinical care and prescription weight loss medications with its core behavior change app. And the company has expanded into at-home diagnostics with its Biomarkers Test Kit.

But Noom lacked continuous physiological information, particularly around sleep and activity, Cook said. Less than 10% of members have devices such as the Oura Ring, Whoop, or newer Fitbits, he noted. Continuous physiological data enables Noom to be a more comprehensive healthcare platform.

"This is all about just boosting signal so that we can deliver the right insights, and to do that, we felt we needed to bring a wearable deeper into our program," he said.

Noom is starting with the Noom Band as a wrist-based wearable, and the company is at an “earlier stage exploring ring-based options,” Cook said. "We believe ultimately it’s important to meet people where they are, and both the wrist and the ring form factors have a role to play in generating signal to drive health outcomes, as people have different preferences," he added.

Cook sees chronic care, telehealth, diagnostics and wearable companies increasingly converging as they broaden their capabilities and move into adjacent areas of healthcare.

"Every player in preventive health, which is looking more and more like healthcare generally, is chasing this same holy grail of determining what is going on in a patient or member’s body, and then suggesting a behavioral insight or a pharmaceutical intervention, or ordering a diagnostic test based on that signal," he said.

Noom is making strategic moves to cover all of those capabilities itself.

The company focuses on whole person health that goes beyond nutrition, Cook said, with extensive data and interventions around food and activity but comparatively little insight into sleep. Sleep is an important factor for metabolic health, and the Noom Band gives the company a way to incorporate sleep alongside nutrition, activity and mindset, executives said.

Noom is betting that wearables can improve outcomes for members in its weight loss programs. An analysis of 144,000 Noom Med members taking a GLP-1 medication found that those who used a connected wearable were 34% more likely to lose 20 pounds by the fourth month in the program, according to the company. A separate sleep analysis found that, on average, members on a GLP-1 weight loss drug who used Noom Band slept 90 minutes more per week after only two months, and members who started with a sleep deficit added 150 minutes of sleep per week, the company's data shows.

Studies have shown that chronic sleep restriction or poor quality sleep significantly increases the risk of insulin resistance, obesity and type 2 diabetes.

"Bringing that dimension of health into the program, we felt, was just critically important," Cook said.

The company built a device from the ground up rather than partner with an existing wearable player, so it could own the user experience. "We didn't want to pick a partner where essentially that partner’s app would be competing essentially with the Noom application for this signal interpretation," Cook noted.

Many existing wearables focus on optimizing health and athletic performance, Cody Fair, Noom Health’s chief commercial officer, told Fierce Healthcare. Noom developed Noom Band to capture measurements related to weight management and metabolic health, he noted.

Through the partnership with Sensor Bio, the wearable platform provides the validated sensors and underlying physiological data, while Noom controls how those signals are interpreted and incorporated into the interventions. Cook cited Sensor Bio's research, validation work and focus on device accuracy as key reasons Noom selected Sensor Bio as its partner to develop Noom Band.

By investing in a wearable, Noom also aims to improve member engagement to ultimately drive better outcomes for the members as well as payers and employers, Fair noted.

Members can lose motivation when the number on the scale stops moving. Giving them other measures of progress, including sleep, steps and recovery, provides additional "wins" that could keep them engaged, he said.

Noom also plans to offer the wearable as something that members can "unlock" when they hit early milestones in the program, turning the hardware into an engagement incentive, executives said.

"We didn’t set out to build another wearable—we set out to build the ultimate metabolic health program that drives better health outcomes for members, leading to increased ROI for clients," Fair said.

"For employers and health plans, that’s the difference between a fitness perk that gets left in a drawer and a tool built to deliver health outcomes they’re already paying for and that is available to their population at no additional cost, he said.

Expensive wearables can undermine the ROI payers are looking for, Cook noted. "I essentially believe that the devices are a commodity and should effectively be given away. That’s why we're including the wearable at no additional cost to the payer," he said.

Payers and employers also want to see ROI on health programs within a shorter time frame, within 12 to 24 months, Fair added. Providing employers with a program that combines behavior change, wearables and biomarker testing also reduces the number of vendors they have to work with, he added.

Health plans want evidence that daily behavior changes translate into measurable clinical and financial outcomes, such as improvements in blood pressure and A1C, and Noom plans to study whether its wearable can help deliver that ROI over the next year, Fair said.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ ACCESS Model could serve as a proving ground for Noom to demonstrate how the combination of its behavior change program with wearables such as the Noom Band can affect cardiometabolic health.

Noom plans to participate in CMS’ Advancing Chronic Care with Effective Scalable Solutions model under the cardio-kidney-metabolic clinical track, focusing on conditions like obesity, prediabetes and diabetes improvement. ACCESS is a 10-year initiative to integrate tech-enabled care into Medicare.

"That model is an outcomes-aligned payment model. We're excited to bundle the blood pressure cuff, the wearable, along with the Noom program, to have the absolute maximum effect on the outcomes that are being measured, outcomes like A1C, blood pressure and weight," Cook said.

Cook is bullish that wearables will play a bigger role in chronic condition management as sensors are able to generate more sophisticated physiological data and AI gets better at interpreting the data.

"It should be possible, in my view, within years and maybe quicker than that to have the wearable signal itself provide a blood pressure signal that is validated, which would certainly simplify models like the CMS ACCESS model, if you didn't also have to ship a blood pressure cuff," he said. "These less invasive wearables, as they get more powerful, I think, can be transformative to healthcare generally, and I think the CMS ACCESS model is pointing the way to how they would democratize that, and at a relatively low cost to the ultimate payer."

#5594. Manhattan’s Top 2 Sales This Week Go Under Contract After Price Hikes

The top-two sales in Manhattan last week were in signature luxury buildings that have seen very strong sales and were able to raise their prices from initial launch.

The No. 1 contract, a 17th floor unit at 1122 Madison Ave., is pending with an ask of $38.75 million, a bit over its original ask of $38 million in January.

The next highest contact, Penthouse B at The Henry on 211 W. 84th St., went under contract with an ask of $28.75 million, a hefty bump over its August 2024 price tag of $24.95 million.

Both units were sponsor sales in new construction, and are full-service luxury buildings with renowned architects and designers. The buildings essentially look at each other from across Central Park, one on the upper east side, one on the upper west.

"This is a sponsor strategy," says luxury broker Michael Reisor, of the Compass-affiliated Reisor.Team in Manhattan, who is familiar with both locations. "It's escalating pricing based on absorption."

Escalating pricing can create a sense of exigency in the buyer, offering a strong incentive not to dilly-dally with an offer, as the price will likely increase over time.

"The initial release pricing will always go up as the market absorbs apartments," he says. "This gives people the urgency of, 'If we don't act now and secure the apartment, then it's just going to get more expensive.'"

However, the early release strategy "doesn't always work unless buildings are this in demand," the broker says of the two top sales. The strategy is obviously successful, as the first building has only one unit left, and the second has only four.

Both complexes have highly desired locations as well being architecturally significant with bold names attached: Studio Sofield for 1122 Madison Ave. and Robert A.M. Stern Architects (RAMSA) for The Henry.

Nor did either development spare expense on finishes, materials, appliances, or amenities. (There is one key difference, however: The Madison Ave. building doesn't have a parking garage.)

Additionally, both are boutique buildings with a controlled number of residences: 26 for the first, and 45 for the second. With buildings like this, says Reisor, there usually is no downward negotiation on pricing.

"If you're selling really well, especially on a certain line, developers are always looking to maximize what they can get," agrees Manhattan broker Lisa K. Lippman of Brown Harris Stevens, who is familiar with both buildings.

She says that once The Henry sold its penthouses quickly, it was off to the races in terms of price.

In February, the 1122 Madison building's penthouse duplex went under contract for $89.5 million, setting a record for a condo on the Upper East Side, and also giving leeway for the building to raise prices.

Lippman, who heads up sales at another Stern building, 200 W. 88th St., has just raised prices on its A line due to its popularity, thanks to it being a corner line with four-bedroom layouts.

"We sold so many of them that we felt we could raise prices there," she says.

"When a building launches and signs a significant number of contracts in a relatively short period, the sponsor may recognize that the remaining inventory is worth more than originally anticipated," agrees Michelle Griffith of Douglas Elliman, who has shown clients in both buildings.

She notes that there is a strong pricing difference between new development and resale, saying, "On the resale side, it's generally less common for sellers to raise an asking price once a property is already listed."

The 1122 Madison Avenue full-floor condo comes with five bedrooms, five bathrooms, two balconies, a powder room, a library, a home office, and a laundry room. Then there's the sweeping Central Park and Metropolitan Museum of Art views from the great room, library, eat-in kitchen, and primary bedroom suite.

Despite being built in 2026, the building has a convincing prewar look. The unit boasts European white oak Parquet de Versailles-inspired flooring in the entrance hall and entertaining spaces, and quarter sawn European white oak plank flooring in all living areas, as well as soaring 11-foot high ceilings.

The impressive amenity suite contains two floors of leisure and wellness spaces, with a squash court with a retractable basketball hoop, a fitness center programmed by The Wright Fit, a private training studio with Pilates reformer, a spa with a steam room, sauna, and cold plunge, and a sports simulator.

On the lower level is a drawing room, a residents' lounge with bar, private dining room, billiard room, media room, game room, and children's playroom.

All but one unit is sold out, yet the complex won't be completed until fall of 2027.

Griffith says the building is doing particularly well because it's a boutique, brand-new condo in a neighborhood that is "largely defined by older co-op buildings."

The sales agent, Cathy Franklin of Corcoran, told Realtor.com she not wish to comment.

Across the park at The Henry, Penthouse B offers a full-floor with six bedrooms, 6.5 bathrooms, a living room, library, and formal dining room, chef's kitchen with an eat-in area and a large pantry, and terrace with the ultimate perk of Central Park views.

Designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects, the building showcases the high quality work the atelier is known for, including "a classic facade of Indiana limestone and hand set brick," along with prewar-style touches such as "terrace setbacks, bay windows and decorative detailing—emblematic of the best Stern buildings."

The week ending Nov. 15 saw 34 luxury (over $4 million) contracts signed, 11 fewer than the week before, according to Olshan Realty. As usual, condos out sold co-ops, but at 17 condos versus 12 co-ops, the gap had slimmed considerably since the week before.

Experts say that co-op sales, which often come with an arduous board-approval process, are increasing to due to a lack of inventory.

However, there will always be those who prefer an older building with a classic New York feel. The two top buildings this week managed to convincingly create that prewar (pre-1939) feel while being newly constructed.

#5592. AI Writes Better Discharge Summaries Than Doctors, Study Suggests

— Physician reviewers gave AI summaries higher marks for accuracy, completeness, clarity, and tone

Artificial intelligence (AI) outperformed clinicians in drafting hospital discharge summaries, a U.K.-based retrospective study showed.

A higher proportion of large language model (LLM)-generated discharge summaries were signed off by a clinician reviewer with no or minor changes compared with clinician-authored summaries (92.2% versus 70.0%), meeting prespecified noninferiority criteria, reported Kathleen Goldsmith, MSc, senior data scientist at a partnership between Imperial College London and Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust in the U.K., and colleagues.

Moreover, clinician reviewers rated LLM-generated summaries higher on accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity compared to clinician-written summaries, they wrote in JAMA Network Open.

Finally, a smaller proportion of AI-generated discharge summaries contained inaccurate or incomplete information compared with ones written by clinicians (26.2% vs 45.1%), they reported.

"Together, these findings suggest that AI-assisted documentation could strengthen the quality of information transferred at discharge, an important component of safe and effective continuity of care," Goldsmith told MedPage Today.

While this research focused on discharge summaries, Goldsmith said it could be applied to other administrative tasks, but "patient safety and clinical value have to be central to how we adopt technology like this."

In an accompanying editorial, Melanie Molina, MD, of the University of California San Francisco, wrote that this research raises the question not of whether AI can produce acceptable drafts, but whether physicians can verify the information in real-time.

"Lengthy, complex, and fragmented clinical records create a verification paradox: the cases in which automated summarization is most valuable are often the cases in which verification is most difficult," Molina wrote, adding that emergency department care poses particular challenges.

Plus, AI tools have already evolved far beyond the model tested in this study, with newer, more sophisticated models less likely to hallucinate.

Molina argued that while this research shows that "a thoughtfully designed LLM pipeline can produce discharge summaries that clinicians prefer to routine documentation," this does not yet equate to a safer transition of care.

"The enduring clinical task will be ensuring that what it writes is true, complete, and actionable," she wrote.

Goldsmith and team sought to evaluate how AI tools could "free up clinician time for patient-facing care while maintaining clinical safety and accuracy" and to develop a framework for evaluating the use of LLMs in clinical settings.

This retrospective noninferiority study used Imperial Clinical Analytics, Research and Evaluation (iCARE) research data from a network of 5 hospitals in London from Sept. 1, 2022, to Sept. 30, 2023.

Discharge summaries written by clinicians and by GPT-4o mini were blindly reviewed by 12 resident physicians from the Imperial College Healthcare Trust. The primary outcome was clinician sign-off on the discharge summary with little to no edits. Goldsmith noted this endpoint reflects how the technology would be used in real-world settings.

"Having clinician input in both the co-design, use, and evaluation of healthcare AI technologies is crucial to ensure these systems are trusted, and truly deliver the benefits to clinical work," Goldsmith said.

Ultimately, there were 1,294 discharge summaries included, of which 649 were clinician-authored and 645 were LLM-generated.

Patients' median age was 46 and 56.6% were female. The median length of stay was 3 days. On average, each case required the review of 30 clinical documents, or about 4,000 words.

The researchers noted some limitations, including that de-identification may have removed clinically relevant information, that only one LLM was evaluated, and the retrospective study design; prospective assessments at the point of care are still needed.

Every Medicaid managed care plan has them.They’re the members who remain outside the reach of traditional outreach and care management after the calls, texts, letters and emails haven’t worked. Many have changed tactics and brought in outside vendors. Those approaches work for most members.But the hardest-to-reach members are still left behind.For this population, simply finding the member is often the biggest challenge. Someone moving between temporary housing, shelters, encampments or other locations may be impossible to locate using the information a plan has on file. Finding that person may require combining data and technology with local knowledge, community relationships and people on the ground.And finding the member is only the beginning.A member may not trust the person who finds them. Housing, food, transportation or an immediate behavioral health need may matter far more at that moment than making a primary care appointment. Language differences and difficult experiences with the healthcare system can create additional barriers.That’s why the distinction between contact and engagement matters. Contact means reaching someone. Engagement means listening, building trust, addressing barriers and helping the member take the next step.What It Takes to Truly Engage MembersTechnology can help determine where to look, prioritize the next best action and make field teams more efficient. But technology doesn’t create trust. This is ultimately a human effort—technology-enabled but led by people.

While finding members is often the hardest part, it’s only the beginning. What happens next is what can change outcomes.Experience with hardest-to-reach Medicaid populations has shown 25–40% reductions in ED utilization and 35–55% reductions in inpatient utilization after members were located and engaged, barriers addressed, and ongoing follow-through provided.*For plans, that’s where the financial opportunity lies. Reaching high-risk, high-cost members and helping them reconnect to care creates an opportunity to reduce avoidable ED visits and hospitalizations—and the costs that come with them.At a time when every avoidable ED visit and hospitalization matters, reaching and serving these members is more important than ever. It’s an opportunity to improve care while addressing a significant source of avoidable healthcare spending.

#5587. Cancer History Tied to Severe Maternal Morbidity During Childbirth

— Deliveries among cancer survivors have increased in recent years

More cancer survivors are giving birth, and severe maternal morbidity was increased at delivery for both past survivors and current cancer patients, a cross-sectional study in the U.S. showed.

From 2016 to 2023, hospital deliveries increased from 30.1 to 45.6 per 10,000 for past cancer survivors (average annual percentage change [AAPC] 6.3%), while hospital deliveries for current cancer patients were relatively unchanged (7.0 to 7.4 per 10,000 deliveries, AAPC 0.2%), reported Koji Matsuo, MD, PhD, of the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, and colleagues in JAMA Network Open.

Compared with a severe maternal morbidity rate of 6.8 per 1,000 hospital deliveries for people without cancer, this rate was 11.9 per 1,000 deliveries for past cancer survivors (adjusted incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.45, 95% CI 1.37-1.53) and 48.2 per 1,000 deliveries for current cancer patients (adjusted IRR 3.80, 95% CI 3.58-4.04).

Of note, the inpatient maternal mortality rate during the admission for hospital delivery was 14-fold higher for current cancer patients compared with those without cancer (273.0 vs 7.0 per 100,000 hospital deliveries; adjusted IRR 14.24, 95% CI 10.87-18.66).

"As cancer care and outcomes have improved and fertility preservation and assisted reproductive technology have become more widely available, pregnancy after cancer is an important issue in survivorship care for reproductive-aged individuals, including adolescent and young adult cancer survivors," wrote Matsuo and colleagues. "The increase in delivery hospitalizations among past cancer survivors in the U.S. may partly reflect these changes."

"These findings support the importance of preconception evaluation for cancer survivors and early referral to tertiary care centers with multidisciplinary teams, as currently recommended by multiple organizations," they added.

This study used national hospital discharge data from the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project's National Inpatient Sample, which approximates a sample of 20% of discharges from participating hospitals across 48 states and the District of Columbia.

Among 28,360,443 hospital deliveries, 0.4% were among past cancer survivors, less than 0.1% were among current cancer patients, and 99.5% were among women without a cancer diagnosis. Median age at delivery was 33, 32, and 29 years across the three groups, respectively.

Among past cancer survivors, thyroid cancer (22.3%) was the most frequent type of cancer diagnosis, followed by cutaneous melanoma (15.7%), breast cancer (11.7%), lymphoma (10.8%), uterine cervical cancer (6.6%), leukemia (4.2%), and ovarian cancer (3.6%).

The study's primary outcome was severe maternal morbidity at the time of delivery, with morbidity indicators restricted to those with a case-fatality rate of 1% or higher after an event. The most common were cardiac arrest or ventricular fibrillation, conversion of cardiac rhythm, heart failure or arrest during surgery or a procedure, and amniotic fluid embolism.

Rates of severe maternal morbidity at delivery varied by cancer type, with greater associations seen among survivors of leukemia and lymphoma, and more modest associations with breast, cervical, and thyroid cancers.

Most hospital deliveries (57.6%) for past cancer survivors were full term, while only 39.6% were full term for current cancer patients.

Matsuo and colleagues acknowledged that the study had several limitations. For instance, they pointed out that unmeasured confounding factors were possible since they did not have access to information on cancer stage, histologic type, familial cancer syndrome, treatment history, duration of remission, residual organ dysfunction, or detailed disease status.

How did your organization do in terms of seeing its chosen candidates elected?

Things went even better than expected. Kennedy Jr. -- the vaccine delusionist -- overseeing HHS during one health crisis after another, leading to preventable deaths from measles and preventable diseases. Annie Andrews, MD, [D-S.C. senator-elect] is at the top of that list. South Carolina hasn't elected a Democrat statewide, I think, in over 20 years. I was having coffee this morning with a senator who had just met her at orientation this week, and he said he told her to "Lean in and make sure your voice is being heard because we really need you right now." I think that that is true coming from the senator's mouth, but I think it's also true coming from the voters' mouth.

You mentioned the vaccine issue and the Affordable Care Act tax credits. What other healthcare issues are you hoping to see acted on in the new Congress?

We were promised [by the current administration and Congress] to see a reduction in healthcare costs, and we've seen the exact opposite. Premiums continue to skyrocket. Out-of-pocket costs and deductibles just keep going up, and there doesn't seem to be much relief on prescription drug prices either.

This is at a time when we're having record numbers of foodborne illness outbreaks and measles deaths and spread. The threshold for herd immunity is 95% for measles, and most kindergarteners' classes are below that at this point. So it really does call to have strong health leaders leading with facts and evidence and their values to protect Americans' health and make healthcare more affordable.

We are looking for action on healthcare affordability and accessibility, and holding the administration accountable for what, to say the least, have been questionable choices such as the approval of candy-flavored vapes, so we do expect that Congress should be able to deliver on both.

I was a chemist and worked in breast cancer research and drug discovery, and I worked on creating an antibiotic to combat superbugs. #5584. HLTH 2026: Calibrate, Withings study finds wraparound care boosts GLP-1 weight loss by more than 60%

HLTH 2026: Calibrate, Withings study finds wraparound care boosts GLP-1 weight loss by more than 60%" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As health plans and employers continue to evaluate the costs and outcomes associated with GLP-1 weight loss drugs, a new study found that wraparound clinical care and behavior change support can make expensive GLP-1 treatments more effective and durable.

A two-year real-world study from Withings Health Solutions and Calibrate Health suggests that pairing GLP-1 medications with Calibrate’s integrated obesity care program produced substantially greater weight loss than GLP-1 treatment alone, and Calibrate members sustained more of their weight loss.

The study followed 4,961 U.S. adults who began GLP-1s between 2022 and 2024, comparing 3,422 Calibrate members with 1,539 Withings users taking GLP-1s without the program. After adjustment for differences between the groups, Calibrate members lost 17.3% of their starting weight at two years versus 10.7% for the GLP-1-only group, a more than 60% relative difference.

The study was a real-world observational analysis, not a randomized controlled trial. Because Calibrate members chose to join the program, the two groups differed at the start. Before comparing, a statistical adjustment made them comparable on age, sex, race, BMI, health conditions and GLP-1 treatment, according to the study. Weight was followed for over 24 months.

The study findings, shared first with Fierce Healthcare, underscore that GLP-1 treatment may work better when medication is paired with personalized clinical management, behavioral coaching and continuous monitoring, rather than being treated primarily as a prescription benefit, according to Calibrate, a digitally integrated obesity management solution.

The study results also reinforce that obesity should be treated as a disease, another chronic metabolic condition requiring intensive, ongoing support, rather than a medication-only problem, Linda Anegawa, M.D., Calibrate Health’s chief medical advisor, told Fierce Healthcare.

“With any chronic disease, like hypertension for example, you won’t get as good outcomes if you just hand someone a medication and don’t support them across other pillars of health, like self-monitoring blood pressure, physical activity and stress reduction. Type 2 diabetes is another good example; you can give high doses of insulin, but medication can’t do the job alone without nutrition education and support,” she said.

“[The study results] make it very clear that treatment [for obesity] shouldn’t stop at just drug coverage,” she added. “As we envision the future, I’d like to see obesity care looking very similar to diabetes care, with insurance covering the full range of necessary services from medication treatment to nutrition education and overall lifestyle support. Obesity is a complex, chronic disease deserving of the same coverage parity as any other."

Treating obesity as such not only prevents health complications and improves quality of life, but it will also lower overall long-term health systems’ costs of care, Anegawa asserted.

The advantage of the integrated care program persisted despite weight regain, the study found. While both study groups regained some weight after reaching their lowest point, the Calibrate members remained about 16.6% below their starting weight, according to the study results. The GLP-1-only group reached a best point of 12.6% weight loss and was about 9.2% below baseline at the peak of its rebound.

There was a body-composition benefit as well. In a subgroup of 974 participants followed for body composition, the muscle-to-fat ratio improved 49.3% for Calibrate members versus 39.9% for GLP-1-only users at 18 months, roughly a 9-point difference.

The study data is based on two years of daily weigh-ins from Withings-connected scales, analyzed with causal-inference methods. Body composition was followed over 18 months in 520 Calibrate members and 454 Withings users.

The study reinforces the importance of evaluating body composition, rather than weight alone, in obesity treatment, Anegawa said.

“We know that abnormal visceral fat accumulation and dysfunction is what drives most of the metabolic conditions we treat, so if we aren’t equipping members to maximize visceral fat loss and preserve muscle, we can actually end up making people sicker. Losing muscle has severe consequences—it isn’t just scaffolding. Muscle is a critical metabolic organ that regulates energy balance, hormonal signaling and insulin sensitivity,” she said.

Adding the insights of body composition to Calibrate's clinical and metabolic data allows the company to better monitor trends and adapt care based on quality evidence, she noted.

There are several key factors that make an integrated obesity care program more effective than a medication-only program, Anegawa said.

"Physician-led personalized care that includes medication optimization for each member’s needs, tailored wraparound support, and features that drive continuous engagement—all of which are designed to maximize clinical outcomes," she said.

"Breaking this down, we start with a comprehensive clinical evaluation for each member, vs. other programs, which only require a questionnaire for a prescription. This helps us get to know each member’s medical and weight histories in detail. We analyze comprehensive lab data to understand their baseline metabolic profile. This information is then used by our expert clinicians to personalize clinical care from day one," Anegawa said.

Live one-to-one coaching support focuses on four pillars of healthy weight maintenance: nutrition, activity, sleep and mindset shift. Tailored education and anticipatory guidance help members manage side effects and stay on treatment, while connecting members to their personal motivations helps sustain engagement through challenges and supports lasting improvements in metabolic health, according to Calibrate.

Calibrate Health has been working with connected health device maker Withings for over five years. The company's members use Withings devices regularly as a required part of the program, according to Anegawa.

"We were already getting body composition data that gave us additional insights into individual members’ health. That data led to additional questions, such as are there significant differences that we can see in aggregate? If so, how large are the differences, and are they changing clinical outcomes? Can we use these data to inform and improve the evolution of our protocols and clinical care? So in asking these types of questions, it became clear to both the Calibrate and Withings teams that we should formalize this into a collaborative study," she noted.

The use of smart devices, specifically Wi-Fi or Bluetooth-connected scales, provides continuous data to help identify weight loss patterns that might not have been apparent through traditional clinical measures, noted Antoine Pivron, vice president of Withings Health Solutions.

"Today, most people on a GLP-1 are monitored through a keyhole. A patient whose primary care doctor prescribes the drug might be weighed a few times a year, and each reading reflects one day: what they ate, the time, the clothes they wore. Between visits, nobody knows whether they plateaued in month three, started regaining in month five, or stopped the drug altogether," he said.

"Specialty programs do better, but many rely on self-reported weights from whatever scale the patient owns. And people tend to stop reporting exactly when things go wrong, which is the moment the care team most needs to know," he added.

Body composition is the biggest blind spot, Pivron asserted. Withings' smart scales track weight and detailed body composition metrics to help identify whether the weight coming off during treatment is fat or muscle.

"In the study we did with Calibrate, two years of data let us see the full shape of the journey: the drop, the low point, and the partial regain that follows. We could also see the quality of the weight loss, not just the quantity. Program members improved their muscle-to-fat balance more, but part of their extra weight loss was muscle. That tells a program exactly where to focus next: protein and strength training," Pivron said.

Withings, a French consumer electronics company, launched its B2B health solutions division in 2019 to meet the growing market around virtual care and remote management in the U.S.

Pivron expects connected health devices like smart scales to play a growing role in GLP-1 treatment programs and broader chronic disease management.

"A GLP-1 prescription isn’t a care plan. The programs that work combine three things: the drug, the clinical and coaching support around it, and the data that shows whether it’s working. Miss one, and real-world results rarely match what we see in trials," he said.

Body composition will become standard in GLP-1 care, Pivron asserted: "That’s where the clinical definition of obesity is already heading."

Connected devices provide the data layer—continuously tracking weight and body composition, predicting when patients may be veering off course and identifying additional risks such as hypertension.

"But a risk score is not a diagnosis. A notification with no next step just creates anxiety. These signals belong inside a care program with a protocol: confirm with a cuff, see a clinician, treat if needed," he said. "Employers and payers are moving toward paying for outcomes. Connected devices are how a program proves it delivered them."

Employers face rising healthcare costs—projected to climb 9.5% next year—and GLP-1 treatments are a major contributor to that cost growth.

The study provides evidence of better outcomes with wraparound care, but it did not evaluate the impact on healthcare spending.

Anegawa contends that improvements in markers associated with high metabolic risk, like Hemoglobin A1c, the liver enzyme ALT and lipids, would point to meaningful cost savings.

Calibrate data from separate evaluations show substantial improvements in these markers among Calibrate members.

“Among Calibrate members who started the program with diabetes or prediabetes, 80% reached normoglycemic status at one year. Among those with abnormal ALT, 79% shifted to the normal range, and 68% of those with abnormal triglycerides were normal at year one," she said.

Withings' body composition data builds on Calibrate's prior data and gives the company another lens on the whole picture, "suggesting that lower healthcare spend is likely,” Anegawa said.

Greater treatment persistence could also ultimately reduce costs. An integrated approach helps keep members engaged so they stick with treatment and get the full benefit of therapy, she noted.

Along with weight loss and metabolic improvements, Calibrate members also report compelling health and productivity outcomes, Anegawa said. Among members with a high work-related burden at intake, 82% no longer reported it at one year.

“My favorite evidence of all is that 90% report that Calibrate improved their overall quality of life, and 94% say that their health is better than a year ago - the most clinically meaningful to me overall,” she said.
