#5583. Landlord With Dark Past Is Charged With the Murder of Disabled Tenant Who Was ‘Late on Rent’

A New Mexico landlord accused of murdering his disabled tenant and burying the body beneath the porch of the victim’s home gave conflicting accounts about whether he had evicted the man over purported unpaid rent, according to court documents.

Jonah Jeter, 33, was charged last week in Albuquerque with murder, aggravated burglary, and three counts of tampering with evidence in the death of Robert Debeary, 51, whose remains were discovered in October, more than two months after his family reported him missing.

For nearly five years, Debeary, a four-time stroke survivor, lived in an apartment at 233 Alcazar St. NE, where he received housing assistance through the federal Section 8 program, according to the criminal complaint filed in Bernalillo County Metropolitan Court.

Debeary, who walked with a cane after becoming paralyzed on one side of his body, regularly kept in touch with his loved ones, so when a week passed without hearing from him, his family grew concerned, according to his future daughter-in-law, Latajanae Evangelista, who spoke with Realtor.com®.

In mid-August, Debeary’s brother contacted Albuquerque Community Safety to request a welfare check, but was told that he had been evicted from the apartment the previous week. His family questioned that account, saying he had never mentioned facing eviction despite complaining of “ongoing issues” with Jeter.

“He was just a man, a disabled man living in his home, and he would never just go missing. He would never leave his family,” Evangelista tells Realtor.com in a phone interview, her voice breaking as she struggled to find the words. “And then he’s just found buried under his own porch where he lived, where he was supposed to be safe.”

Throughout the investigation, questions emerged about an apparent dispute between Debeary and his landlord. When confronted by the family, Jeter allegedly told them that he had evicted Debeary for failing to pay rent for several months, then later denied the claim, according to court documents.

The family later discovered that Jeter had previously served time in prison for a fatal stabbing in 2014, which left them questioning how he could be allowed to rent to a disabled tenant receiving federal housing assistance when he has a violent crime history.

Evangelista says she believes Debeary's death could have been prevented and wonders whether more stringent background checks on landlords might have protected him.

“So basically I can't be a tenant with an eviction, but I can be a landlord who is a murderer,” Evangelista notes. “It doesn't make any sense. All I know is that this was a tragedy—a tragedy that was 100% preventable.”

While Jeter claimed Debeary had fallen behind on rent, his family insisted the payments had been made—and questioned whether he had even been evicted.

Jeter told investigators that Debeary was late on his last two rent payments but admitted that he had never initiated formal eviction proceedings, according to the complaint.

There is no evidence that formal eviction proceedings were initiated, and authorities have not established whether the rent dispute played a role in Debeary's killing.

Evangelista and her fiancé, Micah Debeary, who is Debeary's son, both disputed the claim that the elder Debeary had stopped paying rent, explaining that he received Social Security benefits and rental assistance through a housing program. They claimed that they had reviewed bank records showing his monthly rent payments were being withdrawn.

“He was getting Social Security, and housing paid the rest, and he paid about $200, and the $200 came out every month,” Evangelista says. “So he was paying every month.”

Evangelista says the family contacted the Albuquerque Housing Authority and was told that no eviction proceedings had been initiated and that the agency had not received any reports of unpaid rent.

“They did not file any evictions, so he was not kicked out,” she says. “He was never evicted.”

She alleges that Jeter then moved his own relatives into Debeary's apartment roughly three weeks after he disappeared, while his family was still desperately searching for him.

“Three weeks after my father-in-law went, quote unquote, missing, his family moved in,” she claims, adding that she believes Jeter may have wanted the apartment for his relatives. Authorities, however, have not publicly identified a motive for the killing.

Meanwhile, investigators uncovered other inconsistencies in Jeter's account. When Debeary's family entered his apartment in August after not being able to reach him, they discovered a “reddish/brownish stain that they assumed was blood” on his bed, according to the complaint.

But when they returned to the property at a later date, the bed was gone. Jeter denied removing furniture or cleaning out the apartment and allegedly told detectives that Debeary did not have a bed at all, contradicting the family's account.

Debeary was last seen on surveillance footage leaving his apartment on Aug. 12. Over a month later, a tip about suspicious activity in the backyard of his rental home offered a grim new lead.

On Sept. 18, a neighbor called police and reported that, around the time Debeary disappeared, they had seen Jeter working in the backyard, “specifically digging up dirt and burying boards and other objects,” according to the complaint.

Investigators searched Jeter's car and discovered multiple firearms. He was arrested on Oct. 21 and charged with unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon.

Six days later, investigators returned to Debeary's home with a search warrant and cadaver dogs. The dogs alerted the team to the area beneath the porch, which had loose soil and what appeared to be newly installed turf, according to the complaint.

The area was excavated, and 2 feet below the surface, investigators discovered Debeary's body wrapped in a blanket and buried along with his bed frame and mattress. He had been shot at least once in the head, the autopsy revealed.

Jeter told police that he had done some landscaping in the backyard but denied burying Debeary’s body or the bed. He remains in custody at the Bernalillo County Metropolitan Detention Center. It was not immediately clear whether he had retained an attorney.

Jeter had previously served time in prison for another killing. In 2014, he was sentenced to five years in prison for fatally stabbing Oliver Yazzie at a truck stop when he was 17. He was released from probation in 2020.

It was Jeter's criminal past that has raised questions from Debeary's family about how he was even able to work as a landlord, particularly one renting to vulnerable tenants who rely on federal housing assistance.

It remains unclear what screening, if any, Jeter underwent before renting to Debeary or whether the local housing authority was aware of his criminal history.

Evangelista tells Realtor.com that she contacted the Albuquerque Housing Authority shortly after her father-in-law's disappearance to ask whether landlords were required to undergo criminal background checks.

“When Robert first went missing, I asked them, I said, ‘So, do you guys do background checks on your landlords? Because he's a convicted felon,’” she recalled. “And they were like, ‘No, we don't. We only do the background checks on the tenants.’”

She questioned why renters with past evictions struggle to find housing while landlords with violent criminal records may still be allowed to be part of housing assistance programs.

“Some people have been evicted because of hardships. They can't get an apartment. But someone can be a murderer, a rapist, a child molester, whatever, as long as they're a landlord, then somehow it's OK,” she says.

For Evangelista, the issue extends beyond the tragic fate of her future father-in-law.

“You're placing kids and mothers and elderly and people who are disabled in these homes, and that's dangerous," she says. “If I can help other people to change that, then I want to make it happen, because I would hate for this to keep happening—here in New Mexico, or anywhere else.”

Evangelista described Debeary as a devoted father and grandfather who had worked hard to regain his independence after suffering multiple strokes that left him partly paralyzed.

Despite needing a cane to walk, Debeary had planned to walk Evangelista down the aisle when she married his son, stepping into a role that held special meaning after her own father died in a car accident in 2022.

“All he wanted to do was live a normal life. That's all,” she says through her tears. “He wanted to be with his grandbabies. He wanted to spend all his time with his family.

“But I guess time wasn't on our side, unfortunately. I really wish it would have been.”

#5581. FDA Adds Another Player in ALK-Positive Lung Cancer

— Among the indications, neladalkib approved in second-line after alectinib

The FDA granted accelerated approval to the third-generation ALK inhibitor neladalkib (Nelkarmi) for previously treated advanced ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), making it the seventh approved agent in a crowded therapeutic field.

The approval limits use to patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC previously treated with alectinib (Alecensa) or at least two prior ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors and platinum-based chemotherapy.

Support for the conditional approval came from 222 patients in the phase I/II single-arm ALKOVE-1 trial.

In the cohort of 67 patients who had only received alectinib in the metastatic setting, neladalkib induced responses in 49%, with a duration of response (DOR) of at least 6 months in 76% of the responding patients. For the cohort of 155 patients previously treated with two or more ALK inhibitors and platinum-based chemotherapy, 32% responded, with a DOR of at least 6 months for 69% of the responders. The proportion of responders with DORs of at least 12 months was 52% and 51% for the two cohorts, respectively.

"Patients with ALK-positive lung cancer are often treated with multiple targeted therapies over many years," said investigator Alice Shaw, MD, PhD, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, in a press release from drugmaker GSK. "Advances in treatment have brought us closer to the goal of managing ALK-positive lung cancer as a chronic condition, but balancing disease control and long-term tolerability remains a significant challenge. The approval of neladalkib provides an important new treatment option for patients."

An analysis reported at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) meeting showed a response rate of 26% among patients with exposure to lorlatinib (Lorbrena), the only other approved third-generation ALK inhibitor, versus 46% in patients not previously treated with lorlatinib. DORs of at least 6 or 12 months in the lorlatinib-treated subgroup occurred in 68% and 54% of responders.

In the full cohort of patients presented at the meeting (median three prior lines of therapy), landmark analyses of progression-free survival (PFS) showed a 6-month PFS of 50%, 12-month PFS of 33%, and 18-month PFS of 28% for patients treated with neladalkib. Median PFS was 5.7 months, increasing to 14.5 months in patients not previously treated with lorlatinib. Additionally, a third of patients with brain metastases had objective responses with neladalkib.

At the ASCO meeting, invited discussant Angel Qin, MD, of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, said the ALKOVE-1 results suggest neladalkib has potential as an option in the post-lorlatinib setting, albeit with relatively modest activity, and a manageable side-effect profile.

The most common adverse events (AEs) were elevated liver enzymes, which occurred in almost half of patients and was grade ≥3 severity in 15-20% of patients. Other AEs occurring in at least 20% of patients were musculoskeletal pain, constipation, dysgeusia, peripheral neuropathy, edema, and fatigue. Prescribing information for neladalkib includes warnings and precautions for hepatotoxicity, renal toxicity, ocular toxicity, creatine phosphokinase elevation, and embryo-fetal toxicity.

The ongoing phase III ALKAZAR trial of neladalkib in the first-line setting may provide more information about the drug's potential as upfront therapy in advanced ALK-positive NSCLC. A preliminary analysis from ALKOVE-1 at ASCO showed an objective response rate of 86% for patients with no prior ALK-targeted therapy.

The federal public health body also lists 591 hospitalizations (11% rate) and six deaths—though it has been hesitant to outright confirm states' reports of measles-associated deaths, of which there have now been 10.

Health groups and public health professionals have pointed to lagging vaccination rates and checked endorsement of routine childhood vaccines from current leadership at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, namely Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as fueling the country's outbreaks.

The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

#5577. Erectile Dysfunction Drug Shows Mixed Results in Alzheimer's

— AR1001 missed the primary endpoint in one population, but slowed decline in another

Mirodenafil (known as AR1001), an oral phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor approved in South Korea to treat erectile dysfunction, showed mixed results in people with early Alzheimer's disease in the phase III POLARIS-AD trial.

The treatment missed the primary endpoint in one prespecified group but showed positive results in another, reported Sharon Sha, MD, MS, of Stanford University in Palo Alto, California, at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston.

In the overall study population, AR1001 showed a nonsignificant difference of -0.11 points versus placebo in Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores at 52 weeks (P=0.4015). CDR-SB scores measure cognitive and functional impairment and can range from 0 to 18.

In a population of monotherapy patients -- those not on an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or memantine at baseline -- AR1001 demonstrated a significant 52-week treatment difference of -0.44 points versus placebo (P=0.0266), representing a 31% slowing of decline.

Secondary endpoints of cognitive and functional measures trended in favor of AR1001 in both populations, with a nominally significant difference in Mini-Mental State Examination scores emerging in the monotherapy population.

The most frequent adverse events were diarrhea, falls, and dizziness. Adverse events led to discontinuation in 5.2% of patients in the AR1001 group and 1.7% in the placebo group.

Serious adverse events were similar in the AR1001 group (10.0%) and the placebo group (9.8%). Four deaths occurred in the AR1001 group (acute myeloid leukemia, cerebrovascular accident, suicide, and ruptured cerebral aneurysm) and three deaths occurred in the placebo group.

The CDR-SB data and safety profile are encouraging, Sha noted. "POLARIS-AD made its primary efficacy endpoint in the prespecified monotherapy population," she said. "The secondary endpoints had trends in favor of AR1001."

AR1001 is a brain-penetrant phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor that enhances cyclic guanosine monophosphate (GMP) signaling. In preclinical Alzheimer's models, the treatment improved cognitive performance and reduced amyloid and tau burdens.

"AR1001 takes a novel approach, relaxing blood vessels to increase blood flow to the brain," noted Richard Oakley, PhD, of the Alzheimer's Society in England, who wasn't involved in the study.

"AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra [sildenafil], but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer's disease. People should not take Viagra to try to treat Alzheimer's," Oakley said in a statement. "We look forward to seeing the full results from this trial and how this drug progresses."

In 2024, a study of 270,000 men in the U.K. linked erectile dysfunction drugs with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease. Those findings conflicted with data from the NIH DREAM initiative, but supported an earlier study of Medicare beneficiaries that suggested that sildenafil users were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than non-users.

The POLARIS-AD trial included 1,535 amyloid-positive Alzheimer's patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia in the overall population; the monotherapy subgroup had 604 patients. The average patient age in the study was 73, and just over half were women. Participants were randomized to receive AR1001 30 mg or placebo once daily for 52 weeks.

The primary endpoint was the 52-week change in CDR-SB score in the overall and monotherapy populations. The primary efficacy objective required a significant treatment difference compared with placebo at week 52 in at least one population under the prespecified multiplicity procedure. The prespecified plan was suggested by AR1001's phase II findings, Sha pointed out.

Biomarker tests showed that AR1001 increased cyclic GMP levels in cerebrospinal fluid compared with placebo at week 52 in both the overall (P<0.0001) and monotherapy populations (P=0.0058), supporting target engagement, Sha said.

The presentation included no data about sex differences in treatment effects and Sha said the company has not yet run those analyses. "These results are hot off the press as of Friday," she noted, adding that "continuing analysis is happening, and the open-label extension is ongoing."

#5576. Nantucket Brokerage Must Pay $1.3 Million to Buyers Who Couldn’t Expand Their Home as Desired

A Massachusetts judge and jury have ordered a Nantucket real estate firm to pay nearly $1.3 million to a couple after finding that one of its agents misrepresented whether a home could be expanded to fit their family of eight.

The yearslong legal battle centered on a twp-bedroom, 1,200 square-foot property purchased by Dr. Mary Murray and Jeff Ment. Murray, an obstetrician, and Ment, a lawyer, live in Westport, CT, but spend summers with their six children in Nantucket, MA.

Their kids “all love to be there. Every single one of them loves to be on the island, and we love to be with them,” Murray tells Realtor.com®.

Their real estate agent, Melanie Gowen, helped them find rentals in previous years, and in 2020, she represented them in their purchase of 151 Polpis Road for $1.41 million.

Murray says the home wasn’t ideal, but in the ultracompetitive Nantucket market, where the median listing price is $5,995,000, they felt lucky to buy anything at all.

And Murray says the family was reassured after Gowen, an agent with William Raveis Nantucket, told the couple they’d have no problem building an addition to accommodate their six children.

“She said, ‘Listen, I know it’s the smallest house, but it’s a great buy. The best part about this is it’s an undersized house on an oversized piece of property that you can double,’” Murray says.

According to the couple, Gowen said she went to the island’s building department and confirmed expansion was possible. She’d even sketched out the addition and sent a video of the planned build, Murray says.

In Nantucket, rules govern how many bedrooms a home can be zoned for. But Ment says Gowen openly discussed how a homeowner could get around those rules by calling an addition a den or a living room, then adding a bed.

“In writing, she had told us, ‘I know you can't call anything a bedroom, but you can do what's always done on Nantucket and call it some other room and use it as a bedroom,'” Ment says.

In early 2021, Murray and Ment began planning the addition and contacted the town about a septic upgrade and expansion and learned that “absolutely not another inch or square foot can be added to the property,” Murray says.

“That's when everything started to crystallize that it wasn't quite as advertised,” Ment adds.

Without an addition, the home was too small for their family and essentially useless to the couple.

“She tells us we're incorrect, that of course it can be doubled,” Ment says. “We say we don't think we're incorrect, but, you know, go ahead and do what you can do.”

She then called back with her colleague Kenny Hilbig on the line.

Hilbig told the couple, “Turns out it can't be expanded due to a deed restriction. And we're going to work with you to figure this out,” Ment recalls. Hilbig initially suggested that they might be able to “trade” their property for another home.

“He knew of some other properties that were coming on the market," Ment says. "He thought we could basically trade a house somehow.”

But that idea didn't come to fruition. Hilbig then suggested that the brokerage William Raveis Nantucket might give the couple a bridge loan to purchase a third home. The company nixed that option as well.

Murray and Ment claim Hilbig then told them the only way they could recoup anything from the brokerage directly was to sue.

So in June 2021, Murray and Ment filed a lawsuit in Norfolk Superior Court. The couple sued Gowen and William Raveis for misrepresentation, negligence, breach of contract, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing,  breach of fiduciary duty, and violation of the Massachusetts Consumer Protection Act, otherwise known as 93A, for willfully and knowingly making unverified misrepresentations in trade/commerce and failing to make a reasonable settlement offer after receiving a formal demand letter.

The lawsuit alleged that “Since Dr. Murray and Mr. Ment had been working with Ms. Gowen for so long, they trusted her, her opinions, recommendations, referrals, and relied on her island knowledge. Ms. Gowen had represented that she possessed experience both building and designing homes on the Island of Nantucket. Ms. Gowen held herself out as not only a real estate agent but as an interior designer and property developer.”

In January, a jury awarded Murray and Ment $1.28 million in damages.

Following the verdict, William Raveis and Gowen asked for a judicial review of the jury verdict. In June, a Superior Court judge upheld the verdict and the award.

Then in October, William Raveis and Gowen filed an appeal.

“We obviously disagree with the outcome of the case, which is why we have filed an appeal,” wrote William Raveis' lawyer, Ray Cashen, in an email to Realtor.com. “The fact that Mr. Ment testified at trial that even he does not believe that Ms. Gowen ever lied to him severely undermines the jury’s verdict and the Court’s decision on the Chapter 93A claim. In addition, eleven days before the sale was completed, the plaintiffs were provided with the exact document that prevents expansion of the home, and they had two lawyers review that document (including Mr. Ment). They apparently did not understand the restrictions contained in the document, yet somehow expected their real estate agent to recognize its impact.

“Moreover, they always knew that the home could not be expanded to contain more than two bedrooms due to septic restrictions,” the email continues. “In fact, the plaintiffs attempted to have the sellers of the home waive the two-bedroom septic restriction, but the sellers refused and these plaintiffs bought the house anyway, then later sold the house for several hundred thousand dollars in profit. There was no actionable misrepresentation and we feel confident that the Appeals Court will see things our way.”

In 2021, Ment and Murray sold the home at 151 Polpis Road for $1.95 million, which was $540,000 over the price they paid the prior year. They then purchased a five-bedroom property on the island for $3.1 million.

Murray says they took out a home equity loan and had to borrow against their 401(k) accounts to raise the money for their new Nantucket home.

“We are way more in debt but also have a house for our family now, which is great,” she says.

When asked why they didn’t hire a lawyer to review Gowen’s claims before purchasing the home, Ment says: “We never asked our lawyer because we already knew from Melanie, who said she was at the building department. We hired a guy to close the deal. We didn't hire a guy to assess the expandability because in our minds, that was already resolved.”

Murray and Ment hope others can learn from what they went through. “Should you trust a real estate agent to tell you certain things about a property? And should you fact-check them or back-check them if they tell you something? Or would it be better if they just don't tell you anything and tell you to do all the research?” Ment asks.

“I always tell my patients, you should get a second opinion," Murray says. "If you're not sure about what I tell you, please get a second opinion. I want you to feel really confident. Really, it’s the same with this.”

Gowen did not respond to a request for comment from Realtor.com.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5575. HLTH 2026: CVS Health, Cigna and Abridge collaborating with OpenAI to test computer-use agents

HLTH 2026: CVS Health, Cigna and Abridge collaborating with OpenAI to test computer-use agents" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

OpenAI is expanding computer-use agents for healthcare, enabling AI to navigate electronic health record systems, payer portals and other software to tackle repetitive and manual tasks.

Computer-use agents, also called computer-using agents, are AI systems designed to interact with software interfaces the same way a human does—by viewing a screen, moving a cursor, clicking buttons and typing text.

Research teams at OpenAI have been exploring how computer-use agents can assist healthcare teams with fragmented clinical and administrative workflows while keeping people in control, Karan Singhal, head of Health AI and Artificial General Intelligence at OpenAI, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Around six months ago we set a research bet that we thought that the abilities for agents to use computers would end up being helpful and reliable enough in healthcare to help people with clinical and administrative workflows," Singhal said in an exclusive interview sharing evaluation results on OpenAI's early work with computer-use agents in healthcare.

In an interview with Fierce Healthcare, Singhal also shed light on how OpenAI is working with CVS Health, Cigna Healthcare, Abridge and Ambience to apply computer-use agents to specific workflows, including referrals, prior authorizations, discharge planning, specialist consults and care manager preparation.

Healthcare systems are often disconnected, forcing administrative staff and care teams to manually move information from one system to another before a patient can get care. If a clinician orders an MRI, for example, the insurer may need information from the patient’s medical record, but a staff member still has to pull that information and enter it into a separate portal to request authorization, Singhal noted.

OpenAI executives and researchers framed computer use as the next step in healthcare AI, moving beyond copilots that draft or summarize information to agents that can actually work across EHRs, payer portals and other applications on a user's behalf.

Computer-use agents can bridge healthcare's fragmented software environment, especially where application programming interfaces (APIs) and other integrations don't exist or don't connect an entire workflow, Singhal noted.

"We have been working with health systems on things like ChatGPT for Healthcare and our integration with Epic, but there are still limitations in how useful AI agents can be today. Computer use is really a way of resolving a lot of these barriers that exist between AI capabilities and healthcare software so that care teams can deliver better care, more effectively and more efficiently," he said.

OpenAI continues to invest in APIs, plugins and MCP connectors to integrate AI with healthcare software, but the industry’s fragmented and legacy technology can make those integrations slow and incomplete, Singhal said. Computer use can help bridge those gaps.

"What we hope to do with this release is move us closer to a world where, because AI is connected to more services, AI can help more with a lot of these workflows," he noted.

Care teams, developers and individual clinicians can access computer use for healthcare through ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians and the OpenAI API.

In a research demonstration using synthetic patient data, OpenAI showed how a computer-use agent could support a clinician and an authorization specialist working on the same MRI request. In the demonstration video, a patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. The clinician then instructs the computer-use agent to review the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records and prior imaging in the EHR. The computer-use agent drafts an MRI order, an encounter note and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review.

In the same demo video, the agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review.

"The clinician and authorization specialist were both completely in control of their workflow, but the computer-use agent was able to help across different parts of the workflow and translate that into action," Singhal noted about the demo video.

OpenAI evaluated GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes. These tasks, shaped by physician input, require Astra to carry out multi-step workflows designed to test both clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient context and navigation of complex interfaces. Reviewers examined the model’s actions alongside the notes, orders and patient messages it produced, assessing whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe in the context of the task, according to an OpenAI blog post.

OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra model can perform multi-step EHR tasks such as reviewing patient records, drafting messages and notes, preparing medication refills and proposing orders, while leaving key actions for clinician review. In OpenAI's evaluation, 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated clinically safe, while physicians rated the model "very helpful" or "extremely helpful" in 93% of 646 assessments.

Clinical safety was assessed by evaluating whether inaccuracies, omissions or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm, OpenAI said.

Regarding the 1% of tasks rated not clinically safe, Singal said researchers did not identify any cases where the model created a specific, plausible risk of patient harm. "In some cases, the model might overreach and might take an action without getting the proper sign-off or authorization," he said.

"The models are not perfect today, and what we're sharing is an update on research results where we're seeing this critical point where the models seem to be useful in practice," he added.

OpenAI researchers also evaluated computer-use agents for administrative tasks, such as prior authorizations, appeals and medical equipment orders.

OpenAI says it designed its computer-use agents with robust safeguards and data security in place, according to the company. The agents can be configured with limits on system access and actions, and audit logs provide a clear record of agent actions and approvals, giving healthcare teams visibility into how each workflow was completed.

Organizations are testing out and deploying computer-use applications across different workflows and administrative tasks.

CVS Health is using OpenAI’s computer-use capabilities to automate repetitive work across clinical systems, including sending documents, processing referrals and supporting specialist consults. In one production workflow, an agent cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend, OpenAI detailed in the blog post. Another agent handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consults each day.

Generative AI company Abridge is building computer-use agents to help clinicians carry out care plans across use cases and applications they use every day, including those without APIs. The company also plans to develop an inpatient use case, adding EHR information and nurse and clinician context to identify what needs attention and to coordinate next steps, the company said. As an example, agents can work concurrently on medication access and home health coordination, using computer interaction alongside calls and messages.

Cigna Healthcare is using OpenAI’s models to pull together member information from more than 10 clinical and administrative systems, including benefits, providers, appointments and previous interactions. The goal is to reduce the time case managers spend searching across systems and give them more time to support members, OpenAI wrote in the blog post.

Companies including Assort, Bunkerhill, Forus, Gravity and Tennr are testing agents that interact directly with EHRs and payer portals for referral management, authorization checks, medication approvals and other operational tasks.

“We're continuing to invest in the models, making the models better at computer use. An important way that we think that they could continue to improve is around improved latency and costs,” Singhal noted.

OpenAI sees its role in healthcare as building foundational AI capabilities and letting healthcare companies handle the “last mile” of implementation, Singhal noted. Computer use is one example: OpenAI provides the technology and safeguards, while partners apply it to specialized workflows and deploy it within healthcare organizations.

The company also announced today improvements to trusted clinical search in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians, including how ChatGPT finds, evaluates and cites medical evidence. OpenAI also expanded its healthcare plugin ecosystem with more than 20 new healthcare plugins from companies across clinical care, care coordination and business operations.

#5572. Jennifer Lopez Celebrates ‘Freedom’ as an Empty Nester Since Her Twins Left California Home for College

Jennifer Lopez has admitted that she is enjoying the "freedom" that comes with living alone after her 18-year-old twins, Max and Emme, left their California home for college.

The 57-year-old singer and actress—who is attempting to sell her and ex-husband Ben Affleck's $50 million marital mansion—once again opened up about the realities of being an empty nester while appearing on "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon."

The singer, who shares the twins with ex-husband Marc Anthony, admitted that she "cried for six months straight" when her twins headed off to college.

Although Lopez confessed it has been "emotional," she insisted it has also been an "amazing" journey.

“It’s all the feelings. It’s like one of those moments in life where you’re just, you’re sad, you’re melancholy, but you’re excited and you’re hopeful—there’s just so many feelings that go with [it]. I cried for, like, six months straight, like, two months before they graduated until I dropped them off and then a few weeks after that," she said.

“It’s crazy ... like, I still have on my phone them on my lap, as babies," she added. "It goes so fast, just like everybody says.”

The A-lister admitted that she is now getting comfortable with the "freedom" she has living alone.

“It’s the first [time] since I was, I don’t know, in my early 20s that I haven’t been with someone, had my kids. I’m alone, I’m free—I can do whatever the f--- I want! And it’s kind of amazing, but also weird," she joked.

In October, Lopez said she was channeling that “devastation” into her music.

Speaking to Variety, the hitmaker revealed that living alone has inspired a burst of songwriting, producing material she believes could become some of her biggest hits.

“They take up such a big part of your brain for so long, and when they’re gone, which is devastating and sad and scary, you’re facing a life that’s totally different now, and you’re like, ‘What am I going to do with this space and this time?’" the hitmaker said. "For me, I just went back in the studio. I’ve written some of the best songs that I’ve ever written, and I’m really excited.

“It’s a very happy-era album. It’s some of the most joyous, beautiful songs that have just a tad of a tear in them," she added.

Her comments come mere weeks after she got candid about her kids going off to college in an emotional social video.

"My kids are going away to college," she said while going through her morning skincare regimen.

The "On the Floor" singer revealed that she made a point of soaking up as much time as possible with Max and Emme over the summer, including traveling with them before they began their new lives away from home.

"I was thinking about this summer and what a great summer it was. We got to go away together. I spent as much time with them as I could," she recalled.

Lopez revealed she was facing the reality of returning to a much quieter home—and admitted that it hasn't been easy.

"When they go away and I'm sitting here being an empty nester, and crying and thinking about them and looking at baby pictures of them and all of that stuff, these routines are the things that are going to keep me kind of sane," she shared.

For Lopez, those routines include exercising, taking care of her skin, and making an effort to prioritize herself as she navigates the newfound free time that comes with having two college-age children.

"Working out, doing my skincare routine, caring for myself, with the newfound kind of space that's in your life," she said.

But the superstar also acknowledged that the milestone comes with conflicting emotions. While she is thrilled to watch Max and Emme begin their adult lives, their departure also marks a major change for her.

"You're so excited for them to step into this new era of their life, but it's also, we have to remember, it's a new era of our lives, too," Lopez explained.

She encouraged other parents experiencing a similar transition to look at the change as an opportunity to reconnect with interests or ambitions that may have taken a back seat while raising children.

"Maybe it's time to revive some old dreams that you had," she suggested, adding that parents might return to something they "put aside during the time that you were raising your kids" or simply pursue activities they previously didn't have time for.

Still, Lopez didn't shy away from admitting that embracing such a significant lifestyle change can be daunting.

"It's a scary time. It's a transitional time. It's a new beginning, in a lot of ways, for them, certainly, but also for you," she said.

She ended her message on an optimistic note, urging others entering the empty-nest phase to continue looking after themselves and finding purpose in their new routines.

"Keep your routines going. Stay hydrated. Stay happy, stay joyful, stay productive," she said. Lopez has been preparing for the milestone for months.

Earlier this year, she revealed during an interview with "Extra" that both Max and Emme had been accepted into all five colleges they applied to, with each also receiving a scholarship offer.

The proud mom also spoke about how hard the twins had worked to reach that point, explaining that both have ADHD and have had to find approaches to learning that work for them.

Lopez also made sure to carve out plenty of time with her children before their departure. Over the summer, she documented a road trip through Italy with Max and Emme.

#5571. The Permanente Medical Group launches tech incubation company

The Permanente Medical Group launches tech incubation company" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Permanente Medical Group announced on Monday the launch of a physician-led innovation company it said will strike technology partnerships to co-develop, incubate and launch new enterprise healthcare delivery technologies.

Permanentech—a wholly owned subsidiary of the 10,000-physician medical group, which is itself part of the massive integrated nonprofit Kaiser Permanente—looks to rapidly advance potential new healthcare offerings informed by its frontline physicians and the broader organization’s focus on value-based care.

It marked the launch by announcing its first portfolio company: Wrapt Health, which offers an automated tool that predicts likely missed medical appointments for early outreach and rescheduling. In line with Permanentech’s broader thesis, it was born from a TPMG physician’s experiences, validated within the medical group and so far scaled to 22 sites in Kaiser Permanente’s Northern California region.

Those efforts will involve both home-grown tools and those developed by established or early-stage partners.

The former will champion physician-developed tools created inside TPMG’s ecosystem as an independent company launches. Starting from the concept phase, that support would include financing as well as clinical and operational validation, as was the case with Wrapt Health.

Strategic partnerships and joint ventures, meanwhile, will focus on co-development, clinical valuation and scaled deployment. Permanentech said the latter will begin with local deployments that are expanded to other TPMG sites when solutions “prove their value,” and could include additional strategic support as a partner company looks to advance their offering beyond TPMG.

Permanentech plans to add more portfolio companies and partnerships “in the coming months,” according to its announcement.

“For decades, our physicians have delivered high-quality, preventive care inside an integrated system where clinical expertise, data and incentives all point toward keeping people healthy,” Maria Ansari, M.D., CEO and executive director of TPMG, said. “Permanentech is our commitment to putting that ecosystem to work alongside the best technology from inside and outside our walls.”

Pleasanton, California-based TPMG is the country’s largest medical group, caring for 4.7 million Northern California members with about 10,000 physicians and nearly 47,000 nurses and support staff. It operates at 203 medical offices and facilities, as well as 21 hospitals.

Its parent organization, Kaiser Permanente, is the country’s largest nonprofit health system by operating revenue ($127.7 billion in 2025). #5570. Macrotroponins One Reason Not to Take cTnI Readings at Face Value

— High cTnI less of a red flag when macro-cTnI is also in the picture

Beware attempts to interpret cardiac troponin (cTn) as a cardiovascular risk marker without accounting for the presence of macrotroponins, researchers warned.

In a cohort study of community dwellers in Norway, high cardiac troponin I (cTnI; >10 ng/L) without any macro-cTnI was associated with a whopping 50.0% rate of incident cardiovascular events over a median follow-up of 8.3 years, according to a group led by Torbjørn Omland, MD, MPH, of University of Oslo and Akershus University Hospital in Lørenskog, Norway.

This was a significant jump in cardiovascular risk compared to those with high cTnI and prevalent macro-cTnI (6.8%; adjusted HR 8.5, 95% CI 3.1-23.6) or those whose cTnI readings were deemed too low to merit additional macro-cTnI testing (7.2% in the group with cTnI <5 ng/L; adjusted HR 6.1, 95% CI 3.2-11.6).

"The salient novel findings of the current population-based study are that macro-cTnI is highly prevalent in individuals in the general population with cTnI >10 ng/L by the widely used Abbott high-sensitivity assay and that macrotroponin presence may obscure the true association between cTnI and the incidence of cardiovascular events," Omland and colleagues reported in European Heart Journal.

Macrotroponins are high-molecular-weight complexes formed by cTn autoantibodies and circulating cTn molecules. These large complexes are slower to clear than cTn alone, which can cause assays to read higher.

With macrotroponin I apparently more prevalent than macrotroponin T, study authors suggested implications for interpreting cTnI results in real-world practice.

"Despite the consistent high prognostic value of cTnI demonstrated in numerous studies and individual participant meta-analyses, misclassification of risk based on high concentrations due to the presence of cTnI autoantibodies has been recognized as a potential problem. The current findings suggest that accounting for the presence of macro-cTnI may enhance the prognostic value of cTnI by reducing the extent of risk misclassification," they wrote.

Omland's team based the study on 3,703 community dwellers (median age 64 years, 49% women) participating in the Akershus Cardiac Examination 1950 Study.

Serum cTnI was initially analyzed using the ARCHITECT STAT high-sensitivity (hs) assay; the same samples were used to measure cTnT on a Cobas e801 using the STAT hs-troponin T assay. Investigators then sought samples where cTnI exceeded 10 ng/L (approximately corresponding to the study-specific 95th percentile) for subsequent detection of macro-cTnI.

Out of 108 people with such high cTnI, 81% met criteria for having macro-cTnI. Participants with original cTnI concentration <5 ng/L (n=3,256) or 5-10 ng/L (n=267) were the control groups.

The investigators found that people with high cTnI and prevalent macro-cTnI tended to have lower cTnT concentrations (9.0 vs 19.0 ng/L without macro-cTnI, P<0.001).

Beyond that, there were no significant between-group differences for age, sex, kidney function, C-reactive protein concentrations, use of cardioactive medications, prior cardiovascular disease, or risk factors at baseline.

The study's primary endpoint covered a composite of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, heart failure, coronary revascularization, and cardiovascular mortality.

Compared with people with cTnI levels under 5 ng/L, those with a high cTnI and macro-cTnI turned out not to be at significantly greater cardiovascular risk (7.2% vs 6.8%; adjusted HR 0.7, 95% CI 0.3-1.6).

Study authors cautioned that the study was limited by the complexity of the macrotroponin detection method used and the moderate number of participants with cTnI >10 ng/L, among other caveats.

"It remains unknown whether assay interference or delayed clearance of macrotroponin causes higher cTnI levels in those classified as macro-cTnI positive," Omland and colleagues added. "As such, these observations should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating, requiring validation in larger, more diverse, and higher-risk study populations."

#5569. STAT+: In a win for MAHA, FDA creates new regulatory category for the supplement NAC

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Margaret is a Washington correspondent covering the Food and Drug Administration and other federal health agencies. Reach her on Signal at margaretmanto.61.

WASHINGTON — The Food and Drug Administration is proposing a new classification for a product that’s existed in a legal gray area for years, a win for proponents of dietary supplements, including members of the MAHA movement.

The proposed rule would classify N-acetyl-L-cysteine, known as NAC and already widely sold over the counter, as the agency’s first “Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition” — in essence, not not a supplement.

The need for the legal backbending stems from the fact that the FDA previously approved NAC as a drug, and FDA regulations prohibit the agency from including approved drugs in the dietary supplement category. In 1963, the agency approved NAC to break up mucus in certain lung conditions, and in 1985 to treat acetaminophen overdose.

Allina Health, Sutter Health notch Minn. AG's approval for $26B combination" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's plans to combine have earned the blessing of Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, a key hurdle that paves the path for a Jan. 1, 2027 close.

The nonprofit systems and the attorney general's office announced Monday an oversight agreement replete with service line preservation requirements and $2.15 billion of promised capital investments. Their deal is set to create a 39-hospital cross-regional health system that would be a major player in Minnesota's increasingly concentrated healthcare market.

"My office has extensive authority to review healthcare transactions in Minnesota: we take it very seriously and with every review, we apply the lens of whether it will help you afford your life and live with dignity, safety and respect," Ellison said in the announcement. "At the end of our thorough review of the transaction between Sutter and Allina, I have determined it passes the public-interest test.”

Per the attorney general's office, the $2.5 billion be invested over five years to increase healthcare capacity in the state. That includes $150 million toward rural care, $50 million in workforce development and the scaling of virtual addiction therapy programs across the state.

The systems also agreed to maintain core services at rural locations for five years, to maintain reproductive and gender care for five years (as it complies with state and federal statute) and to continue Medicare participation and charity care. For Allina's workforce, they also agreed to retain all employees in good standing, honor all collective bargaining agreements and not enforce some noncompete agreements.

Ellison's office will enforce the five-year commitments via a 10-year period of oversight, which will include annual compliance reports from Sutter and Allina.

"In the context where the provision of healthcare everywhere is under serious financial strain and Allina is facing its own struggles, I appreciate that Sutter is entering Minnesota with a mindset of growth and an understanding that we cannot simply cut our way out of financial challenges and maintain Minnesota’s high standard of healthcare," Ellison said. "Sutter’s leadership has a history of delivering on growth and innovation and I look forward to their doing the same here."

Since the nonprofits announced their deal back in March, Minnesota and the Midwest have been the stage for substantial health system dealmaking. Sanford Health announced and closed its acquisition of North Memorial Health, while Essentia Health and HealthPartners in September shared new plans to combine and form an integrated 22-hospital organization.

Sutter and Allina, in a joint statement, thanked Ellison's office for the sign-off and said they plan to close their transaction on Jan. 1, 2027.

"From the beginning, our vision has been grounded in a simple yet powerful belief: people across Minnesota and western Wisconsin deserve a sustainable health system that provides access to high-quality, affordable health care when and where they need it," the statement reads. "With our combined capabilities and more than $2 billion in investment, we will expand access to care, improve affordability, enhance care team and patient experiences and accelerate high-impact research and innovation."

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's pending combination took a step forward this week with the signing of a definitive agreement, the nonprofit systems announced Thursday.

The agreement locks in the plans shared earlier this year in a letter of intent—namely, that the cross-market deal would bring more than $2 billion of investment to Allina's markets and that the smaller system would become the "Upper Midwest Division of Sutter Health."

Now the organizations are left with securing state and federal regulatory approvals before the deal can close, which they expect to happen before the end of this year.

“This important milestone brings us one step closer to our goal of partnering to enhance care, support our teams and expand clinical capabilities and research as a strong, nonprofit health system,” Lisa Shannon, president and CEO of Allina Health, said in Thursday's announcement. “With our combined expertise, complementary strengths and aligned missions and visions, I am confident we will be well-positioned to meet the evolving needs of our patients and communities now and well into the future.

Should the deal close, the resulting organization would span 39 hospitals as well as more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The organization would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health unveiled plans to join and form a 39-hospital, $26 billion nonprofit health system.

The pair said Tuesday that they have signed a letter of intent for Allina to join Sutter. Allina would maintain its brand and regional headquarters but operate as the Upper Midwest Division of Sutter. Under that arrangement, Sutter is also committing $2 billion to bolster care access and patient experience investments in Allina’s Minnesota and western Wisconsin markets.

“This includes establishing new ambulatory and specialty care sites to fill care gaps and meet growing community needs, as well as recruiting more physicians and enhancing AI and digital health capabilities,” Sutter Health President and CEO Warner Thomas, who would maintain those titles should the deal close, said in the announcement. “Building on our complementary strengths and combined expertise, we will build a healthcare innovation engine that accelerates how ideas move from development and design into improving the health of patients and communities.”

The systems said they plan to complete due diligence and finalize terms for a definitive agreement “over the coming weeks and months,” targeting a close before the end of 2026 should regulatory reviews run smoothly. A representative for Allina described the structure of the proposed agreement as being similar to a member substitution but noted that the deal's final structure will be outlined in the pending definitive agreement.

Alongside the 39 hospitals, the resulting organization would include more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The combination would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Among the benefits of their proposed partnership, the systems led their announcement with the synergistic technical expertise of their organizations and surrounding communities: Sutter’s immersion in Northern California's artificial intelligence and platform development and Allina’s seat in the medtech and engineering hub of Minnesota.

“The proposed combined system will be uniquely positioned to be a national leader in digital and technological advancements that meaningfully improve patients’ and caregivers’ experiences, while continuing to provide the compassionate care their respective communities have relied on for decades,” the announcement reads.

Such efforts, outlined in the announcement, include AI and digital solutions that would reduce administrative burdens for caregivers along with more convenient appointment scheduling for patients via digital consumer tools.

More broadly, the organizations said they expect the combination will help the organizations bolster physician and clinician recruitment, improve patient affordability and grow their capabilities, “particularly in clinical centers of excellence.”

“We are incredibly excited for the opportunity to harness the collective strength of our two mission-driven organizations to make a difference in the lives of our patients, communities and care teams,” said Allina Health President and CEO Lisa Shannon, who would also maintain those titles in regard to the to-be-formed Upper Midwest Division. “As one nationally leading, locally committed nonprofit health system, we will be uniquely positioned to be at the forefront of innovation, building upon the expertise of our physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses and team members to chart a new path for healthcare.”

Twenty-seven-hospital Sutter is the larger of the two organizations, with $19.8 billion reported total revenue and a $509 million operating income in 2025 (excluding impacts of the to-be-approved 2025 Hospital Fee Program). In the past year, it opened 31 additional care sites, added more than 1,100 physicians and reached 3.6 million patients.

Allina reports $6 billion of revenue with a $95.4 million operating loss and has not had a positive operating margin for the past few years. It operates 12 hospitals and more than 100 other sites.

#5564. Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute

Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Just over half of the country’s nonprofit hospitals have charity care and community benefit investments that fall short of their tax savings, according to the latest of the Lown Institute’s analyses on more than 3,000 hospitals’ tax filings.

In 2023, the most recent year in which Internal Revenue Service Form 990s were available for review, the think tank identified $38.8 billion of industry-wide tax exemptions, or $12.8 million per hospital and 3.8% of total expenses on average. About $37.1 billion was collectively spent by the same hospitals on various community benefits, as reported in the IRS forms matched to other filings such as Medicare cost reports.

While the total exemption handily outpaces the benefits investments by Lown’s measure, the group underscored that these "fair share” deficits or surpluses also vary widely between facilities, and that some of the industry’s biggest names are on the wrong side of the divide.

Here, Mayo Clinic Hospital led the pack with a $366 million deficit, according to Lown’s analysis, followed by Tisch Hospital (-$294 million deficit), Stanford Hospital (-$255 million deficit), New York-Presbyterian Hospital (-$248 million deficit) and Massachusetts General Hospital (-$219 million deficit).

"Some of America's wealthiest hospitals fall hundreds of millions short of giving back what they receive from their communities, leaving those with fewer resources to pick up the slack," Vikas Saini, M.D., president of the Lown Institute, said in a release on the new analysis, released Tuesday.

Among those leading the latter group were North Shore University Hospital ($167 fair share surplus), Rochester General Hospital ($146 million surplus) and Englewood Hospital ($142 million surplus). Lown’s analysis includes a searchable hospital-by-hospital breakdown of the tax exemptions and community investment totals.

When splitting the 52% of deficit hospitals apart from the surplus hospitals, the former group logged about $15.5 billion above their reported community benefits—a deficit Lown said could wipe the medical debt of 12 million Americans. Fair share surplus hospitals outpaced their exemptions by $13.8 billion.

Total tax exemptions were also “very unevenly distributed” among the hospitals, Lown said. The 30 hospitals, or about 1% of all hospitals, with the largest tax exemptions collectively avoided $6.8 billion, or about 18% of total exemptions. The 607 hospitals, or about 20%, accounted for three-quarters of the country’s hospital tax exemptions.

Lown’s measure of nonprofit hospitals’ tax breaks includes exemptions from federal and state corporate income taxes, state and local sales taxes, property taxes, tax-exempt bonds, tax-exempt charitable donations and federal unemployment tax exemptions. Not included are other benefits provided to many nonprofits, like Medicaid disproportionate share payments, 340B discounts or profits from indirect tax arbitrage.

Its tally of community benefit includes spending on patient financial assistance, subsidized care, payments to other nonprofits to improve health or various community health or social determinants of health investments.

Of note, it excludes Medicaid shortfall—the difference between hospitals’ costs and revenues when treating Medicaid patients—and spending on professional education and research. The hospital industry typically points to these billions of dollars of exclusions when discussing their tax breaks, with Medicaid shortfall alone accounting for nearly half of their preferred community benefit spending totals. Lown noted in its methodology that these accounting losses are often offset by other discounts and supplemental benefits and don’t always have a direct impact on community health, among other objections.

Lown said the disparities between hospitals and the outsized benefits being delivered by some are a call to amend, not eliminate, nonprofit status exemptions. The think tank accompanied its analysis with calls to increase reporting transparency and set spending targets for hospitals tied to variables such as size, exemption value, financial health and prior spending.

“Tax exemptions aren't a gift—they're an expectation, and regulators need to make sure all hospitals hold up their end of the bargain," Saini said.

Lown acknowledged the impending financial pressure hospitals will face with upcoming H.R. 1 policy changes and said such changes should be accompanied by “short-term” financial protections.

Still, the group isn’t alone in drawing scrutiny to the tax breaks. Lawmakers and policy advisors have pointed to, and questioned the justification for, nonprofits’ exemptions when questioning health system leaders on collections policies or high prices.

Academics and researchers have also called for greater transparency or other overhauls of how community benefits are reported or calculated. Of note, a research article published earlier this month in Health Affairs reviewing hospital filings between 2013 and 2022 outlined a disconnect between different hospitals’ listed charity care eligibility thresholds and their relative spending, which more closely aligned with community need than their stated policy.

#5563. Inside the Properties James Bond Has Made Famous as Robert Pattinson Gears Up to Play 007

It’s official: Robert Pattinson is stepping into the role of James Bond.

The news comes after years of speculation surrounding who might succeed Daniel Craig—who was the sixth actor to bring 007 to life, and portrayed the British spy in five films, ending with 2021’s “No Time To Die.”

The official James Bond X account shared a first look of Pattinson donning the infamous tux for the role, captioned “Identity Confirmed.”

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Director Denis Villeneuve alluded to the search for the next Bond in the statement.

“I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” the “Dune” director said. “We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007.”

Dozens of potential candidates have been floated as possibilities since Craig’s reign came to an end, including Idris Elba, Jacob Elordi, Callum Turner, and John Hardy.

Bond first walked onto the silver screen in 1962, when Sean Connery brought the iconic book character to life in the first film, “Dr. No.” There have been a whopping 25 Bond films so far, with Pattinson suiting up for the 26th.

After seven films, Connery ended his run in 1983 with “Never Say Never.” In 1969, George Lazenby became the only actor to star in a single film in the franchise, with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.”

Roger Moore held the role from 1973 to 1985, also impressively holding the gig for seven titles. Next up was Timothy Dalton, who starred in two films between 1987 and 1989.

Pierce Brosnan reinvigorated the franchise when he became Bond in 1995, holding the job until 2002. In 2006, Craig ushered in a new era, tackling 007 with a more rough-and-tumble edge.

Perhaps even more impressive than the scale of actors who have taken their martinis shaken, not stirred, is the sheer number of filming locations the franchise has made its mark on for over 60 years.

Hunting Bond, a fan site that tracks the locations, has identified nearly 600 filming spots across the world. While the James Bond universe is certainly action-packed, it’s also quite aspirational, and has often provided viewers with rich backgrounds and fascinating properties that became characters in their own right.

It would be nearly impossible to rank all of the lavish homes Bond has stepped foot in over the years, but there are definitely a handful that stand out in memory.

Even without a connection to one of the Bond films with the strongest pop culture staying power—”Diamonds Are Forever,” of course—the Elrod House in Palm Springs, CA, is an incredible dwelling.

Perched on a hillside overlooking Coachella Valley, the 8,900-square-foot home was designed by modernist architect John Lautner for interior designer Arthur Elrod.

The fascinating structure has a concrete dome-shaped roof, a circular living room, and a half-moon swimming pool that Connery’s Bond threw an enemy into during a heated fight scene.

Villa Sylva is a picturesque Greek estate that’s appeared in a handful of movies, including Moore’s “For Your Eyes Only”—although in the film, it assumed the role of the Madrid home of hitman Hector Gonzales.

The 12-bedroom luxury villa boasts unobstructed views of the Ionian Sea and is perched on an idyllic 10-acre property. Today, it can be rented as a wedding venue or a vacation home sleeping up to 18 people.

Given Bond’s important role at the UK-based M16, it only makes sense that at least some of the locations had to be local. The sprawling Luton Hoo Estate was a location in Brosnan’s 1999 film, “The World Is Not Enough” and Connery’s 1983 return for “Never Say Never Again.”

It’s also been featured in dozens of other projects, including “Downton Abbey.”

Built in 1903, the property is about an hour’s drive from London—a journey that would probably be cut in half when Bond is behind the wheel. The historic English country estate spans more than 1,000 acres and has a handful of structures—most notably, a five-star hotel and an exquisite mansion.

Craig’s Bond debut in the 2006 film, “Casino Royale,” was set in the breathtaking Ocean Club in the Bahamas.

The luxury resort has a number of sea-view villas for rent, including one that served as the perfect backdrop for a romantic scene between the spy and Solange Dimitrios, the wife of villain Alex Dimitrios.

Although Bond was just a visitor, the Ocean Club does have “67 turnkey oceanfront residences” available for ownership. The ultraprivate oceanfront abodes are available in a variety of sizes between two- and five-bedroom. Pricing begins at $7.5 million, according to the Ocean Club’s website.

It’s never been captured on screen in a Bond film, but 007 creator Ian Fleming built a bungalow called GoldenEye in Port Antonio, Jamaica.

The private estate is where the prolific author wrote all 13 of the original James Bond novels. Eventually, it was sold and turned into a resort, which is still called GoldenEye today. The property has been vastly expanded in the decades since Fleming, who died in 1964, lived there. It now includes lagoon cottages, villas, beach huts, and a spa.

The 25th Bond film, “No Time To Die,” provided a nod to the character’s birthplace. According to Architectural Digest, there’s a replica of Fleming’s desk in the opening scene of the film. Like the writer, Bond lives in a Jamaican bungalow in this installation, but it was built from scratch solely for filming.

#5561. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5560. HHS finalizes updates to HIPAA privacy rule to ease patient access to health information

HHS finalizes updates to HIPAA privacy rule to ease patient access to health information" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The final rule, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights (OCR), strengthens and clarifies the right of an individual to access their protected health information and reduces regulatory and administrative burdens, the agency said.

The proposed rule was issued more than five years ago, in January 2021. An unpublished version of the final rule is available here.

Under the final rule, healthcare organizations must respond faster to patient requests for copies of their health records. HHS said covered entities will have no more than 15 calendar days to respond to a request, reduced from the current 30-day period. Organizations are allowed one extension of no more than 30 calendar days, HHS said in the final rule.

The rule also establishes that patients can access their protected health information through personal health apps when the covered entity has the technical capacity to deliver the records in that form and format.

The rule also expands circumstances when patients must receive copies of their health records for free, requires advance notice of fees and modifies identity verification requirements.

To make it easier for healthcare organizations to share data for care coordination, the final rule clarifies that health plans may use and disclose protected health information for care coordination and case management for individuals. The rule also expressly permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations and similar third parties for care coordination and case management for individuals.

“Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr in a statement. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are putting patients in control, requiring faster access to their information, and cutting red tape that gets in the way of coordinated care. This rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and help providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy.”

Provisions in the final rule will become effective 60 days after publication in the Federal Register, and compliance will be required 180 days after that date, according to HHS in a fact sheet.

Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a "personal health app," identity verification and speed. "It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient," she said.

“This final rule provides Americans with faster and easier access to their health information, which is critical to them being able to take control of their own health and health care,” said Office for Civil Rights Director Paula M.
