#5490. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

#5489. Homebuilder Confidence Hits New 14-Year Low as High Mortgage Rates and Inflation Take a Toll

U.S. homebuilders are feeling increasingly pessimistic about the new-construction sector of the housing market amid mounting affordability concerns.

Builder confidence in new single-family home sales fell three points month over month, bringing the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) down to 25, a new 14-year low. Any reading below 50 reflects the industry's negative view of the market.

This is the lowest HMI reading since April 2012. For context, builder sentiment has now remained below 40 for 19 consecutive months.

"Strange times indeed—home prices are at record highs, the stock market has soared in recent years, employment is holding strong, and yet builders feel pessimistic about building homes," Jeff Ostrowski, a housing market analyst at Bankrate, tells Realtor.com®.

NAHB Chairman Bill Owens attributes the sharp downturn to high mortgage rates, ongoing inflation pressure, elevated energy and material costs, rising labor shortages, and sidelined buyers.

"Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy," says Owens. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."

Last week, Freddie Mac reported that the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans decreased to 7.11%, tracking lower bond yields, yet the latest hotter-than-expected inflation print could make the relief short-lived.

NAHB chief economist Robert Dietz says that mortgage rates stuck above 7%, combined with weaker consumer confidence, and broader economic uncertainty are holding buyers back from the market, but that is just part of the problem.

"The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," says Dietz.

The November HMI survey of single-family homebuilders revealed that 46% of them slashed prices in November, up from 43% in October—the highest share in the post-Covid period.

The average price cut remained at 6% for the eighth consecutive month.

Meanwhile, 68% of builders reported resorting to sales incentives, such as rate buydowns, marking the 20th month in a row when at least 60% of builders have used this strategy to boost demand.

"This could be an opportunity for homebuyers," says Ostrowski. "If you’re in the market and can swallow a 7% rate, you might be able to find a deal on a new home."

The index measuring current sales conditions shed six points to 28, while the index gauging future sales expectations slipped two points to 32. At the same time, the index charting prospective buyer traffic decreased two points to 16—its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020.

On a regional, three-month rolling average basis, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23.

#5488. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

#5487. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? #5486. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. #5485. Andrew Scott Claims He’s a ‘Bit of a Minimalist’ When It Comes to Interior Design at Home—and Reveals the Decor That ‘Freaks’ Him Out

Through the genre-spanning roles that have made him famous, Andrew Scott has proven that his skills are quite versatile. But when it comes to home design, he prefers to stay in a very specific lane.

During the Nov. 17 episode of comedian Amy Poehler’s podcast, “Good Hang,” the typically private Irish actor offered up some rare details on his home life.

Each week, the podcast opens with a brief chat with a secondary guest, who provides some additional context to the episode and gives the former “Saturday Night Live” star a question to ask during the interview with the marquee guest.

In this case, Scott’s co-star from both “Elsinore” and “Fleabag,” Olivia Colman, called in to suggest Poehler do some digging around his penchant for interior design.

Colman encouraged Poehler to ask Scott what kind of a career he would pursue if he wasn’t an actor, and guessed that he might begin discussing art or design. The Oscar-winning actress even said she’d love to see a world where Scott was an interior designer.

“I’d like to employ him to do up my house,” she said.

“I wonder if he would show me pictures of his apartment” Poehler asked, which yielded a very excited response from Colman.

“He might not, because he’s quite private,” Colman teased, adding that the actor’s abode is “f-cking amazing.”

When it came time for Poehler to ask the question, it appeared Colman was right on the money.

Scott revealed he “would for sure” be in an artistic field. “I would be drawing or painting. I like design…” he said.

The “Spectre” actor was flattered to hear Colman’s compliments, as he considers her design acumen to be pretty impressive, too. Scott explained that the two have often spent their time on set discussing design, and at one point, joked that they’d love to host their own reality television show centered on the topic.

“We said, ‘Wouldn’t it be great if we had a show together where we just slagged off other people?’” Scott laughed, explaining that the premise would be that he and Colman would circle a participant’s home and point out all of the design choices they don’t particularly agree with.

Poehler joked that the decor show could be called “I Would Not Have Done That.”

So what does Scott like? “I love design. I’m a bit of a minimalist,” he revealed.

“I don’t like the accumulation of stuff,” Scott explained. Although he noted that he’s “not crazy” when it comes to the desire to purge unnecessary clutter, he does have a few preferences that help keep a space looking neater. For example, he generally steers clear of stainless steel, as it’s prone to revealing finger prints.

Poehler and Scott also bonded over their mutual love of clean surfaces, but noted that even an intentionally sparse decor scheme needs some detail.

“Too minimal? I don’t love,” said Poehler, to which Scott agreed, “You’ve got to have some softness.”

They were also on the same page with their similar philosophies on buying things, with Poehler noting that in an “ideal world,” she would do lots of research before purchasing anything to ensure it’s the very best option.

Scott also finds pleasure in having one really great item instead of simply acquiring things: “I’ve got a bottle opener that I love. You know what I’m saying?”

He went on to note that his family says he’s “quite hard to buy for for Christmas,” even though he always makes a big show of being excited no matter what kind of a gift he opens. He’s not one for unnecessarily kitschy pieces, and expressed a distaste for “things that sort of say ‘Prosecco o’clock’ on them.”

“All those kinds of things freak me out,” he revealed.

In a May 2026 interview with The Gloss, Scott revealed that although when he “speaks of home,” he’s talking about Ireland, he’s spent a lot of time living between New York, London, and his home city of Dublin.

“One of the things that I have had to develop is how you can live in different places and think of them as home, too,” he shared.

#5484. Kevin Durant Lists Arizona Home for $13 Million—1 Year After His Trade to the Houston Rockets

Houston Rockets star Kevin Durant has listed his sprawling Arizona property for $13.9 million—jut three years after he picked up the palatial pad.

The NBA icon, 38, purchased the property in 2023 for $12.9 million from fellow athlete DeAndre Hopkins when he was traded from the Brooklyn Nets to the Phoenix Suns.

Now, following his Texas trade, the basketball star is looking to part ways with the property, listing it with Alexa Kort of The Beverly Hills Estates and Adam Bowman and Brian North of Compass, as first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Durant initially put the property on the market in September 2025 for $14.4 million. He then trimmed the price to $13.9 million, before removing it from the selling block.

The home, which was designed by acclaimed architect Jack DeBartolo, offers up 10,865 square feet and is situated on a 1.72-acre lot.

It comes complete with five bedrooms, eight bathrooms, and several other lavish amenities.

Upon entering the home, guests are greeted with poured-in-place concrete walls, gallerylike corridors, floor-to-ceiling glass, and custom finishes.

The living room offers guests the perfect place to lounge thanks to its cozy fireplace.

Although minimalist, the home offers a moody aesthetic complete with dark tones.

The chef's kitchen boasts a black marble island with matching black cabinets and state-of-the-art appliances.

The primary suite offers enough space for a king-sized bed and opens directly to the outdoor area.

The primary bathroom is certainly the crown jewel of the property thanks to its Calacatta marble bath and dual vanities.

The home also features a sleek movie theater room, a walk-in closet with custom storage space, and an office space.

Elsewhere in the home, there is a sauna and steam shower.

The property also features a 2,000-square-foot garage designed to show off spectacular vehicles.

Moving outside, guests can enjoy an 82-foot lap and reflecting pool as well as panoramic views of the Camelback Mountain, the Praying Monk and Piestewa Peak, as per a press release shared with Realtor.com®.

This isn't the first time Durant's property holdings were at the center of headlines.

In 2025, his former luxury townhome in Oklahoma City, OK, which boasts a prime downtown location, four bedrooms, two kitchens, and a private elevator—hit the market for less than the cost of a bag of groceries.

"The owner said, 'Let's just put it out there for $35 and see if someone wants to own a piece of NBA history,'" listing agent Ieasha Larkpor, of Thunder Team Realty, told Realtor.com® at the time.

The jaw-droppingly low price tag is meant to spark interest, and so far the ploy has worked, with Larkpor fielding hundreds of offers—some even in the high six figures, close to the price the owner is hoping to get.

But that hasn't stopped the occasional joker from taking the abnormally low price tag literally.

"Yes, I've gotten offers for $35," said the agent. "And I have to present them to the owner. But luckily, they can be weeded out fast."

Durant bought two three-level townhomes at 422 NE 2nd Street for $1,769,000 in 2013 while playing with the Oklahoma City Thunder.

The NBA and Olympic star put his stamp all over the four-bedroom, four-bath townhouse, including an extra-tall shower and an extra-long bathtub to accommodate his 6-foot-11-inch frame.

"Everything in the unit was designed by Kevin Durant himself or his designers according to his taste at the time," said Larkpor. The furniture and artwork could be negotiable with the sale.

In 2017, the sports legend sold one of the 3,904-square-foot units for $1.15 million to a neighbor in the complex. The neighbor happened to be a fan who kept most of Durant's stylistic choices, including the paint colors, bold wallpaper, and light fixtures.

"The new owner wanted to leave [Durant's] stamp, as it is a very nice stamp," said Larkpor.

#5480. The Future of Home: 5 Trends for the Next 50 Years

What does the future of housing design look like? Much like with homes today, trends will be tied to how people live. To predict where design is headed, we need to consider how lifestyles are changing, identify which needs have staying power, and anticipate how homes might evolve to meet them.

DAHLIN Group assembled the top trends for the next 50 years to mark the firm’s 50th anniversary, reflecting on decades of design work to determine what the future looks like. According to DAHLIN, these will be key trends:

BUILDER spoke with DAHLIN’s Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, and Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, for their insight on why these trends will endure.

Fifty years is a long time to forecast residential design trends. How did you decide on these five trends, and what’s behind their staying power?

Wagner: A responsible 50-year view should not claim to know the exact layout, style, or construction method people will use. It should identify what future design must be able to do.

The common principle is agency: giving people more useful choices without requiring them to rebuild their lives or surroundings every time circumstances change.

The solutions to these needs will manifest in dramatically different ways over the next 50 years, but the needs themselves are unlikely to disappear.

How will wellness become more integrated?

Julian: Wellness will move deeper into the core decisions that shape everyday performance.

Daylight, window placement and performance, shading, material choices, air filtration, thermal zoning, and access to outdoor space will be considered together, rather than added as isolated features.

We also expect the idea of restorative space to become more distributed. A home does not need one wellness room if daylight, nature, movement, quiet, and thermal comfort are part of the daily path through the house. That makes wellness more relevant across housing types and price points.

The larger shift is from visible elements to a measurable and felt experience: cleaner air, better control, more useful daylight, a stronger relationship to the outdoors, and spaces that support both activity and retreat.

Design is already leaning away from fully open concept. How might this evolve?

Wagner: People want connection without constant exposure. The open plan still serves cooking, gathering, and shared family life extremely well, but a home now has to absorb more simultaneous activities. A call, homework, quiet conversation, and meal preparation may all happen at once.

People do not necessarily want more rooms; they want more control over how rooms relate.

These allow a space to borrow light and belong to the larger home when open, then become visually or acoustically distinct when needed.

Over time, this can make floor plans less defined. A room may shift between office, study, guest space, care space, or retreat because its boundaries and connections were designed to change.

The goal is not maximum openness at every moment. It is to give the homeowner control over when spaces participate in the life of the home and when they recede.

How will the design partnership with AI evolve?

Wagner: AI can already help teams generate and compare more early visual directions, translate abstract language into discussable imagery, and communicate a concept before investing in a complete visualization package. It can also help align a client and design team when they’re using the same word to mean different things.

The important limitation is that human expertise remains vital in framing the challenge, recognizing what is plausible, selecting the direction that serves the client best, and turning an evocative image into architecture that functions.

AI can quickly generate ideas and multiply options, but the designer must still decide which options deserve to move forward and turn them into a workable, real plan.

The near-term model is therefore collaborative. AI broadens the field of possibilities, while human experts frame the question, curate the outputs, and carry the selected idea into a coherent, buildable design.

Homeowners are placing greater importance on opportunities for social connection. How will future site and community planning support this?

Julian: Instead of relying only on a large destination facility such as a clubhouse or pool area, communities can offer a network of smaller lawns, gardens, play and sport areas, outdoor work settings, cafes or neighborhood retail, and places to sit along daily routes.

Smaller scale can also make participation easier and more approachable. It’s easier to join one of a few seats than to become the only person in a room designed for dozens. The same amount of common area can create more opportunities for connection when it’s placed closer to where people live and is shaped for different levels of participation.

When social space is woven into day-to-day patterns, community becomes a series of low-pressure encounters that can grow into familiarity and belonging.

Why will flexibility be the key to longevity in design?

Julian: Flexibility supports longevity when it reduces the cost and disruption of change. A room that has no assigned use may be flexible on paper, but true adaptability comes from practical decisions: useful daylight, appropriate openings, accessible routes, service relationships, and connections to indoor and outdoor space.

Those decisions determine whether a garage bay can credibly become an office or gym, or whether an ADU can serve a renter, a returning child, or an aging parent at different points in time.

The benefit is not that one design and layout lasts forever. It’s designing change into the bones of the home so that the home can adapt for a wide variety of family configurations without becoming obsolete.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.

#5478. More Roofing Choices Without More Complexity

For roofing professionals, the expectations surrounding a roofing project continue to expand. A roof is no longer evaluated solely on its ability to protect homes from the elements. In addition to standing up to increasingly unpredictable weather, roofing products are expected to deliver lasting value while complementing and even elevating the architectural style and character of a home.

With greater regularity, roofing professionals are learning to navigate a market where performance expectations, design preferences, and project requirements have become more challenging.

It’s a combination of factors that has made flexibility increasingly important. A roofing solution that works well for one architectural style or climate may not be the right fit for another. There’s a growing need to access materials that can meet a range of aesthetic preferences and performance demands, while homeowners want the confidence that their choices will provide both the protection they expect and the look they envision.

Against that backdrop, a roofing brand called US Tile is bringing two established roofing materials—concrete and clay—together under a single, made-in-the-U.S. portfolio. The aim is to offer a more comprehensive selection of tile roofing options while simplifying the process of navigating those choices.

Benefits of Concrete and Clay From a Single Source

Rather than looking across multiple sources to find the right combination of styles, profiles, colors, and performance characteristics, roofing contractors and builders can explore a broader portfolio within a unified offering.

Some projects may call for the versatility and design range of concrete, while others may benefit from the distinctive character of clay. With both materials represented within the same portfolio, there’s greater flexibility to match a roof to the look of the home, the preferences of the homeowner, and the durability demands of the local environment.

Beyond aesthetics, having access to concrete and clay roofing from the same manufacturer makes it easier to spec and offer homeowners two energy-efficient, Class A fire-rated materials that hold up to prolonged exposure to the elements and extreme weather.

More Productive Conversations Between Roofing Professionals and Homeowners

A broader range of materials and possibilities can make homeowner discussions more fruitful. Instead of starting with a limited set of materials and working backward from what is available, offering concrete and clay from the same source means each project can be approached with a wider range of potential solutions. There’s more opportunity to balance appearance, performance, budget, and other project considerations without unnecessarily complicating the specification process.

A unified portfolio can result in simplified access to product information and support while reducing some of the hurdles that can arise when coordinating different materials and suppliers. Across multiple busy projects, those efficiencies can matter just as much as the products themselves.

A Broader Portfolio and Greater Design Flexibility

Ultimately, combining concrete and clay roofing under one made-in-the-U.S. brand is about giving professionals more ways to meet the demands of their projects. A broader portfolio allows for greater design flexibility, while the performance characteristics of concrete and clay tile roofing help address homeowners’ growing expectations for resilience and long-term value.

With more options and a more streamlined path to finding them, roofing professionals can approach each project with greater confidence—and homeowners can have more faith in their next roof as a smart long-term choice that adds value and peace of mind.

#5477. More Than a Closing: The Growing Role of Financial Services in Home Building

Historically, financial services have occupied a relatively straightforward role in the home builder business model. Mortgage, title insurance, and related services could generate ancillary revenue while helping buyers move from contract to closing.

Today, that traditional role has shifted amid a challenging affordability environment, mounting pressure on margins, and heightened buyer expectations. Financial services have elevated from an adjacent business opportunity to a more strategic part of the home building platform.

The question is increasingly not simply how much revenue these services can generate, but how they can help builders sell homes, create a more consistent home buyer experience, and operate more efficiently at scale.

Mortgage services may provide the most obvious example. With mortgage rates recently returning to the 7% range, affordability remains a defining challenge for the industry. In September, 66% of builders surveyed by the National Association of Home Builders reported using sales incentives. Zonda similarly reported that more than 80% of new-home communities offered incentives on quick move-in homes in August.

In that environment, financing is no longer simply what happens after a buyer decides to purchase a home; rather, it becomes a core part of what makes the purchase possible in the first place.

It may be with this in mind that large builders have placed such emphasis on their mortgage capabilities. For example, two of the nation’s largest public builders recently reported mortgage capture rates above 80%, underscoring how closely financing has become integrated with the home sale.

The strategic value goes beyond capturing mortgage revenue. An effective financing platform gives builders another lever to address affordability, tailor incentives, and help qualified buyers get across the finish line.

The same strategic thinking increasingly applies to title, settlement, and other services surrounding the transaction.

Consider title and closing. These services sit at a critical point in the home buyer journey: the moment when months of searching, financing, construction, and anticipation culminate in ownership.

For the buyer, those distinctions between companies and functions may matter very little. The mortgage process, communications leading up to closing, signing experience, and delivery of the keys can all become part of a single perception of the builder’s brand. Delivering a consistently superior closing experience becomes an increasingly important element of how buyers remember the home builder.

For builders operating across multiple markets, however, delivering consistency can be difficult. Growth through geographic expansion or acquisition can leave behind fragmented networks of local providers, processes, and systems.

“What works well across a handful of communities can become much harder to manage across dozens of markets and thousands of closings,” says Anne Law, president of First American Title’s Homebuilder Services Division. “That’s why builders are increasingly looking at financial services as a scalable platform with consistent processes, strong underwriting, and an excellent closing experience, rather than a collection of individual transactions.”

Importantly, a more integrated strategy does not necessarily mean bringing every capability in-house. Builders are placing greater emphasis on capital efficiency and asset-light operating models, and those same principles now drive decisions on how they approach financial services.

The objective is not necessarily ownership. It is control over the things that matter most: the customer experience, service standards, data visibility, operating consistency, and economics. Scale adds another consideration. Licensing, regulatory requirements, and operating standards can vary across jurisdictions, adding complexity as builders expand into new markets. Experienced financial services partners like First American Title can provide infrastructure and expertise to help navigate those requirements.

That creates room for a range of models, including wholly owned operations and strategic partnerships. The right structure will vary by builder, service, and market. What matters is whether the model balances control, investment, and operating responsibility while supporting scalable growth, regulatory compliance, and a consistent customer experience.

From Ancillary Revenue to Strategic Infrastructure

The evolution of financial services ultimately reflects a broader change in how builders compete.

When affordability is strained, financing can help sell the home. When buyers expect a seamless process, well-executed and consistent title and closing services can reinforce and enhance the home-buying experience. And when builders operate across expanding footprints, standardized financial-services relationships can create greater consistency, visibility, and efficiency.

Revenue matters. But there are other parts of the equation that are important. For example, builders today are closely examining how mortgage, title, and settlement fit into the broader operating model and whether those capabilities are structured to support the next stage of growth.

In that sense, financial services are becoming less ancillary to the home building business and more integral to how modern builders sell, serve, and scale.

#5476. Joanna Gaines Shares a Sweet Moment at Her Family’s Waco Farmhouse as Her Youngest Helps Celebrate the Holiday Season a ‘Little Early’

Joanna Gaines and her youngest child, Crew, are busy decking the halls of the family’s beautiful Waco, TX, farmhouse.

While some people are staunchly against putting up a Christmas tree before Thanksgiving, the Magnolia co-founder has already brought some seasonal joy into her home.

In a Nov. 15 Instagram Post, Joanna, 48, shared a video of her 8-year-old son excitedly turning on the family’s tree—a stunning display of twinkling lights and metallic-hued baubles.

The "Fixer Upper" star acknowledged the potentially premature timing of the decor with a tongue-in-cheek caption, writing, “For those who like celebrating the season a little early…”

The audio the mom of five selected for the clip really drove the message home, as she selected a song called “Christmas in November,” with lyrics that say, “They say it’s a little early, I say it’s right on time.”

This particular corner of the HGTV family’s dwelling was also featured on the cover of the Winter 2026 issue of “Magnolia,” with Joanna donning a festive red gown as she poses in front of a selection of jars of holiday candy.

The tree makes an appearance on the cover, as well, shining alongside the statement-making picture-frame windows and rustic checkerboard flooring that make the Gaines home so recognizable.

Set on 40 acres, the property has plenty of room for a large family to celebrate together. The family purchased the home back in 2012, and at the time, it was a quaint two-bedroom abode. After countless improvements—which most recently included an extensive kitchen renovation—it's become a home Joanna has come to love, despite being unsure of it initially.

Even though it’s only mid-November, the holiday season has been on Joanna’s mind for quite a while already as she plans ahead for all Magnolia has in store this winter. In fact, she kicked things off with a Sept. 9 post, when she first brought out a variety of wreaths and garlands for a holiday photoshoot.

In a Nov. 10 editor’s note in Magnolia Journal, she wrote about her philosophy as she heads into another merry time of year.

“Every season holds a blend of the big and small, the milestones and the everyday, the photo-worth celebrations and the not-so-picture-perfect moments,” she wrote. “There’s something about the holidays that bridges the gap between these.”

She noted that as the years go by, she’s “come to realize” that the most important memories are the ones that might not be captured with a camera, and exist only in memory.

“Maybe there’s no physical evidence they happened at all, except for the fact that you were there—and you felt it,” Gaines continued. “It’s these softer moments that give us life and ground us in presence. The days that held no agenda, the mornings I took slow, the smiles you won’t see in my camera roll because I was simply bearing witness.”

But that’s not to say she’s not planning make a splash when it comes to home decor.

In a chat with USA Today, Joanna revealed that her approach to holiday decorating has gotten more over-the-top as the years go by.

“The older I get, the more free I feel to deck the halls,” she said. “I do think this is the one time of year where you can really go big if you want to—or keep things timeless and simple.”

Although she’s well on the way to turning her family’s corner of Waco into a winter wonderland, Joanna understands the importance of staying true to one’s own desires.

“There’s no right or wrong because the holidays really are so personal and sentimental,” she said. “It’s just a matter of what you love and how you want your home to feel for your family.”

As excited as Joanna seems to be for the most wonderful time of the year, she doesn’t appear to be blowing past any holidays too quickly. She also has big plans for turkey day, an occasion that she looks forward to for its delicious meals.

“Food really is the center of our holidays,” she told USA Today, remarking that she’s been honing her own traditional recipes since she first married husband Chip Gaines back in 2003. “Thanksgiving especially is the day I can taste all year long because our family really does make the same dishes year after year.”

#5473. Talkdesk’s life sciences play shows why industry depth beats AI cost-cutting

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The customer experience arena, specifically the contact center, has been the low-hanging fruit for artificial intelligence deployments, with much of the focus on cost-cutting. The goals include fewer agents, shorter calls, higher containment and lower cost per interaction.

Those are legitimate goals, but they lead every vendor to the same pitch. When everyone sells the same savings, the market becomes a price war that favors the companies with the deepest pockets.

Talkdesk Inc. is taking a different path, and today’s announcement reinforces that. This week, the company introduced Talkdesk Life Sciences Experience Cloud, a platform designed for biopharmaceutical companies’ patient services operations. The goal is not to make calls cheaper. It is to move patients from a written prescription to therapy faster and keep them there.

That outcome is one a pharma executive will pay for, and one a generic contact-center-as-a-service platform is poorly equipped to deliver. This adds to Talkdesk’s portfolio of industry clouds, including financial services, government, retail, travel and others.

The new offering connects AI agents, human specialists, systems, and workflows across the specialty care journey, which typically includes enrollment, prior authorizations and specialty pharmacy handoffs. Talkdesk cites IQVIA research showing that nearly one in three commercially insured patients cannot access a prescribed therapy within 30 days, and Boston Consulting Group data indicating that 90% of biopharma leaders view fragmented platforms as their primary bottleneck.

The platform analyzes patient service conversations to pinpoint where patients get stuck, assists specialists in real time, and coordinates tasks among hubs, providers, payers, specialty pharmacies and safety teams. It supports the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s 21 CFR Part 11 requirements for electronic records and signatures and integrates with existing customer relationship management, hub, pharmacy and safety systems.

One of the world’s five largest pharmaceutical companies has already deployed it. That customer uses AI to classify and route inbound calls and to monitor live conversations for potential reportable events, or PREs, which are adverse event signals that must be captured and sent to pharmacovigilance systems. When the system detects a PRE, it guides the frontline agent to collect the required details, preserves the source conversation and triggers approved workflows to document and route the information.

“A prescription should mark the start of healing, not the beginning of an administrative maze,” said Patty Hayward, general manager of healthcare and life sciences at Talkdesk. “We are focusing first on Therapy Access because quickly getting patients onto prescribed treatments is one of the most urgent, measurable challenges in healthcare today.”

Hayward’s choice of the word “measurable” is the key point. Time to therapy is a metric that appears on a drug maker’s revenue line and in patient outcomes, not just on a contact center dashboard.

Talkdesk competes in a crowded market against much larger companies. NiCE Ltd. and Genesys Cloud Services Inc. have scale in the contact center, while Microsoft Corp., Salesforce Inc., and Amazon Web Services Inc. can bundle customer service capabilities into platforms that customers already own. A smaller company cannot outspend those rivals on horizontal features, and it should not try.

What it can do is go deeper into specific industries than the giants are willing to go. Talkdesk has been building industry-specific clouds for several years, and life sciences is a logical next step from its healthcare work. Pharmacovigilance workflows, Part 11 compliance, hub services and specialty pharmacy coordination are not features a horizontal vendor casually adds to its roadmap. They require domain expertise, regulatory knowledge and integrations that take time to build, and that time becomes a competitive moat.

The industry approach also changes the sales conversation. A generic platform is evaluated on price per seat and feature checklists, usually by the information technology department and the contact center leader. An industry platform is evaluated on whether it solves a business problem the executive team already worries about.

In pharma, patient abandonment between prescription and first fill represents lost revenue and a failed treatment. That conversation happens with the head of patient services, which is a much better place for a smaller vendor to be.

The industry approach has helped channel partners sell Talkdesk. I asked Joe Rittenhouse, co-CEO of Converged Technology Professionals Inc., one of the premier communications resellers, about it.

“We’re no longer leading with features or price per seat,” he said. “We’re leading with the customer’s workflows, their compliance requirements and the outcomes they’re measured on. That industry approach is a key differentiator for us. It lets us skip the generic AI conversation and get straight to the problems that keep the business up at night, shortening the sales cycle and making the deployment stick.”

The bigger story is how this fits into Talkdesk’s customer experience automation or CXA strategy, which is not a typical contact center-as-a-service sell. The idea is to coordinate AI agents, people, knowledge and enterprise systems to resolve a customer need from start to finish, rather than simply answering or routing an interaction faster. Resolving issues across systems is a far bigger value proposition than call deflection, but it is also much harder to deliver in the abstract.

That is where industry depth becomes critical. End-to-end automation is only possible when the platform understands what “end” means. In a retail return, the end might be a refund. In specialty pharma, the end is a patient who has completed benefits verification, obtained prior authorization, had the drug shipped and is still taking it six months later.

Each step involves different systems, organizations and regulatory obligations. A horizontal AI agent cannot orchestrate that journey without someone first mapping it. Talkdesk is effectively packaging that work into the product.

This is also why the industry approach shifts AI from a cost story to a transformation story. Using AI to reduce handle time on patient service calls might save a few dollars per interaction, and identifying that patients in each program repeatedly stall at prior authorization, then fixing that bottleneck, can change how many patients start therapy. The first is an efficiency gain. The second changes the economics of the business.

The pharmacovigilance use case makes the same point. Missing a reportable adverse event carries regulatory consequences. AI that detects those signals and routes them correctly reduces risk and improves quality, rather than reducing headcount, a value proposition that is far easier to justify to a board.

For life sciences leaders, the lesson is to stop evaluating customer engagement technology based solely on contact center metrics. Start with the patient journey, identify where patients drop off and measure vendors on their ability to shorten time to therapy and improve adherence. Insist on proof of regulatory readiness, particularly for Part 11 and adverse event handling, and validate integration with the hub, CRM and safety systems already in place.

For buyers in other industries, the broader point still holds. AI that only cuts costs will eventually commoditize. AI that understands your business’s specific workflows, regulations and outcomes can transform it. Ask CX vendors how well they understand your industry, not just how good their models are.

For Talkdesk, life sciences is a smart focus area. It will not win every horizontal deal against larger rivals, but it does not need to. By targeting industries with complex, regulated journeys tied to clear outcomes, it can make CXA tangible and give customers a reason to buy that has nothing to do with price.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5470. Beyond Beauty: Kitchens That Work as Well as They Look

A kitchen at Skyline by Toll Brothers in Summit at Orchard Hills in Irvine, California.

Gena Kirk had a couple of non-negotiables when she renovated her Southern California kitchen: a Moroccan door that would open to the pantry and a touchless faucet that she “couldn’t live without.” Turns out, Kirk’s design decisions are in lockstep with many homeowners today who prioritize multifunctional kitchens that are inherently personal.

“Home buyers are less afraid of taking some risk and making their kitchens more curated to feel like it’s their own,” says Kirk, vice president of KB Home Corporate Design Studio.

In fact, today’s more nuanced kitchen is reflected in the 2027 National Kitchen and Bath Association’s Kitchen Trends Report, released in October. Among the findings are expanding kitchen floor plans with more clearly defined zones and a growing preference for personalized gathering spaces over bland, impersonal kitchens designed with resale in mind.

A kitchen at Toll Brothers at Thornebrook in Bulverde, Texas.

“While the kitchen has always been the ‘heart of the home,’ that idea has taken on new meaning,” said Bill Darcy, global president and CEO of NKBA, commenting on the report. “We’ve entered a new era of what the kitchen can do for homeowners—solving real problems … and elevating the way we live.”

We ask more of our kitchens today. Beyond meal preparation, they serve as gathering places for everything from homework and family dinners to entertaining. As their role expands, so does their connection to surrounding spaces. Mudrooms, pantries, and back kitchens are becoming more common, along with dedicated coffee and beverage stations, baking centers, and pet areas.

“[Kitchen] design is becoming more intentional to reflect how people cook, entertain, and connect,” says Lisa McClelland, senior vice president of the Toll Brothers Design Studio. “The emphasis is on creating spaces that feel open and welcoming while providing distinct areas for preparation, dining, and conversation.”

According to the NKBA report, kitchen footprints are expected to continue growing over the next three years. Yet even as kitchens get larger, their layouts are becoming simpler, “with less clutter and a more spacious feel,” the report states. The traditional kitchen work triangle remains important, along with multifunctional features that support a wider range of activities.

“People are thinking about how they operate in their kitchen,” Kirk says. She also predicts continued growth in products designed to simplify everyday tasks, such as motion-activated faucets, workstation sinks that combine a cutting board and built-in strainer, and countertop cabinets and drawers to store small appliances.

“It’s really about form and function,” Kirk says. “People want to be organized so everything is in one place versus spread throughout the kitchen.”

A kitchen at KB Home’s Primrose community in Lancaster, California.

Kitchen islands have evolved beyond their strictly utilitarian roots, too, becoming larger and more central to everyday living. Features such as “thoughtful seating, storage, and room to work” enhance their role as gathering spaces, McClelland says. “The goal is a kitchen that feels effortless, whether you’re making breakfast or hosting a large celebration with family and friends.”

Although kitchens are working harder, homeowners want them to look as good as they cook. Furniture-like cabinetry, layered lighting, and handcrafted, artisanal details help seamlessly bridge kitchens with the rest of the home.

“Faucets, cabinet hardware, and lighting can coordinate without matching exactly, creating a layered, collected look that feels personal rather than overly designed,” McClelland says.

Kirk notes a marketplace shift toward using more natural materials, including quartzite countertops and backsplashes and woods such as walnut that show natural graining. The NKBA report highlights this shift, with quartzite and quartz as the top two countertop materials that will be a key design feature in the coming years.

“Consumers are more interested in natural products, period. Not only in what they’re putting in their mouths, but what they’re putting around them,” Kirk says.

A kitchen at Toll Brothers at Sedona in Sedona, Arizona.

Lighting is emerging as a key design element, as well. “Good kitchen lighting gives you useful choices, and placement is critical, especially at work surfaces,” lighting designer Nathan Orsman notes in the NKBA report. Layered lighting designs include undercabinet, task, and decorative lighting, all part of the recipe that helps “shape a space that feels both practical and inviting throughout the day,” McClelland says.

Layered lighting designs include under-the-counter and built-in cabinet, task, and decorative lighting, all part of the recipe that helps “shape a space that feels both practical and inviting throughout the day,” McClelland adds.

Mixed metal hardware and plumbing fixtures that blend finishes, from brushed brass and gold tones to matte black, nickel, and stainless, are another way homeowners are expressing their individual styles, McClelland says. Likewise, she adds, “blending natural wood tones, creamy neutrals, and rich textures creates spaces that feel both refined and welcoming.”

Beyond the visible design elements, technology and wellness features are playing an increasingly important role in kitchen design. Solutions that enhance natural light, improve ventilation, and filter water are helping create healthier, more comfortable spaces. Multifunctional appliances are also gaining traction as homeowners look for greater convenience and versatility.

“Consumers are looking for convenience, form, and functionality,” Kirk says.

A kitchen at KB Home’s Gateway community in El Cajon, California.

According to the NKBA report, top appliance features include ovens with air-frying and steam-cooking capabilities, dedicated beverage units, and refrigerators with zoned storage that supports healthy habits.

“Manufacturers are getting smarter about the products they are producing that follow the health and wellness trends the consumers are after,” Kirk says.

Kitchens have long commanded a significant share of homeowners’ design budgets. More and more, though, their influence extends well beyond the kitchen itself, shaping design decisions throughout the home.

“We’re building the kitchen first, and then that’s leading to the rest of their home design,” Kirk says.

Although design preferences vary by region, the desire for kitchens tailored to homeowners’ lifestyles remains consistent. “The common thread is a desire for kitchens that feel warm, functional, and highly personalized,” McClelland says. “Buyers want spaces that support everyday living while still delivering the craftsmanship and luxury details that make a home special.”

Kelly Ryan Kegans is a Minneapolis-based writer and editor with more than 25 years of experience covering home design, architecture, and lifestyle topics. As a contributing editor and story producer for several national publications, her work has appeared in Better Homes & Gardens, Country Living, HGTV magazine, The Dallas Morning News, and more.

#5469. Three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of GraphSummit 2026

AI agents need more than enterprise data to be effective; they also need the business context that data lives in. Knowledge graphs could consolidate the enterprise context currently fed to different AI agents into a single knowledge layer.

Developers are already providing AI agents with business context through prompts. But without a central source of truth, they must repeat that work every time they build a new agent, rather than drawing on a shared knowledge layer, according to Jesús Barrasa (pictured), field chief technology officer of gen AI at Neo4j Inc.

“This knowledge layer, this idea of capturing your enterprise knowledge and using it as the context engine for your agents, not only gives you the consistency … it gives you the explainability,” he said during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “That’s the source of my data. These are the elements that I use to produce the answer.”

During interviews at GraphSummit, theCUBE Research’s John Furrier spoke with industry experts from Collibra BV, Blitzy Inc., Raymond James Financial Inc., and Qiagen N.V., among others. They discussed how knowledge graphs can ground AI agents in shared, traceable enterprise knowledge to improve explainability, enable safer coding at scale, support drug discovery and transform business operations. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jesús Barrasa:

Governance is a key question for enterprise AI deployments. How do you ensure AI agents behave appropriately as they become more autonomous? Judgment calls that used to be made by people now need to be made by agents in seconds, requiring a shift toward runtime governance, according to Felix Van de Maele, chief executive officer and co-founder of Collibra BV.

Collibra has introduced several capabilities – Live Map, Maestro, Guardian Agents and Agent Contracts – built on Neo4j’s graph database. Together, they form a control system that helps businesses make sure their AI agents use the right information and follow the rules.

“The challenge is: how do you govern at the speed of AI, which is different than the way we had to govern five years ago?” Van de Maele told theCUBE. “Maestro gives our customers the ability to build these governance steward agents that automate up to 80% of the governance work. You’re able to govern quickly and efficiently enough to keep up with the demands of new AI workloads.”

Other solutions, such as Agent Contracts, focus on enforcing boundaries around AI agents’ behavior. They monitor agents’ actions and block those that violate predefined rules, helping prevent unauthorized actions, according to Van de Maele.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Felix Van de Maele:

Changing one small piece of software can unexpectedly break something somewhere else. For Blitzy Inc., which runs thousands of AI coding agents at once to help businesses make large-scale system changes, a knowledge graph can map dependencies and the risks of change within a system.

A knowledge graph gives agents the context they need to make changes safely without being overwhelmed by millions of lines of code, according to Neeraj Deshmukh, director of engineering at Blitzy. The company also uses human-approved action plans and automated testing to keep the coding process on track.

“On top of that, we have agents who are watching other agents to make sure that they abide by the spec, the plan that we had created and approved by the human in the loop,” Deshmukh told theCUBE. “That ensures that there is no drift or hallucination.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Neeraj Deshmukh:

A knowledge graph helps Raymond James Financial Inc. put AI agents to work on data from established sources, according to Naveen Mahankali, vice president of technology at Raymond James.

We have golden sources; we have systems that we can rely on today, and we’re able to use agents to build and compare what we are building against the golden sources,” he told theCUBE. “With the knowledge graph, even when we pull the data from different sources, it sits in the Neo4j, and we run evals compared to the golden sources and make sure they’re 100% accurate before launching.”

Raymond James is also exploring how AI agents can help financial advisors serve clients more efficiently. The company has already launched Raimond, its proprietary AI assistant, explained Jeff Griffith, vice president of AI engineering and data science at Raymond James, who joined Mahankali during the interview.

“We have an AI assistant … it’s gotten huge adoption, and it’s just going to get smarter,” Griffith said. “That’s part of the core evolution of what we’re doing in terms of engineering. We’re changing how people — how everyone — works with a desktop that gives people the best AI tools to move from doing all the menial tasks to managing agents that are doing those tasks. In terms of skills and what we are looking for, it is shifting just from people who can do tasks to people who have a drive to solve a meaningful problem.”

#5468. U.S. Chamber Backs Capital Gains Tax Exclusion Bill Aimed To Reduce Taxes on Profits From Home Sales

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has announced support for reducing taxes on the profits homeowners make on the sale of their home, saying it could stimulate more home sales.

Raising the capital gains tax exclusion—something hundreds of members of Congress and a number of real estate groups have pushed for this year—is one key lever that Washington, DC hasn't yet pulled. It could have major implications for the housing market, the Chamber said.

"Capital gains taxes tend to distort housing choices by discouraging individuals from selling their homes because of changing family or health circumstances," the group said. "And the taxation of capital gains in excess of exemption caps creates inequities between homeowners with different job circumstances and those living in different parts of the country."

The most visible effort in Congress comes from the More Homes on the Market Act, sponsored by Rep. Jimmy Panetta (R-CA), which would double the current exclusion. Realtor.com® has reached out to his office for comment.

Both the Senate and the House have versions of the bill, which are almost identical. The Chamber said that bill offers a "reasonable, cost-effective solution" to spur more home sales.

The two versions have picked up 186 sponsors and cosponsors in Congress, including large numbers of Democrats and Republicans. Earlier this year, Panetta acknowledged the push faces resistance. A congressional analysis from last year estimated such a change could deprive the government of $46.4 billion in tax revenue. Even a more targeted approach, like raising the exclusion only for people over 55, could still cost $4.9 billion.

The National Association of Realtors® also champions the bill to change the tax scheme, because it could allow more people to sell their homes without incurring a punishing tax bill. Kevin Brown, president of NAR, lobbied for the law as he spoke to a panel in Congress in June.

Congress set the current capital gains scheme in 1997. Sellers can exclude up to $250,000 in profit if single, or $500,000 if married and filing jointly, when they sell a primary home, with few strings attached.

But the law didn't include adjustments for inflation. As home prices have appreciated in the years since, homeowners see a mounting impact. The longer the value of their home appreciates, the larger the cut the federal government can take as a capital gains tax when they do sell.

Oftentimes, these might be older Americans whose lifestyle might support downsizing. But they're "locked in" to their homes thanks to high mortgage rates.

That causes large tax bills, especially for those who have stayed in their homes the longest. Or, those who live in areas where home prices have grown the fastest. NAR has estimated that nearly 13 million homeowners would face a tax penalty if they sold their homes today. Brown argued that raising the exclusion limits would help free up housing inventory at a time when the country is facing a major supply crunch.

"Capital gains indexing has huge bipartisan support," Colin Allen, executive director of the American Property Owners Alliance told Realtor.com. He brought up the possibility that it might appear in the next Congress in the form of a reintroduced bill or as a part of a reconciliation package.

"It would certainly unlock a number of homes immediately and free up their owners to do something else once they retire, and help families looking to make that next move," Allen said.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5467. Job Growth Slows Nationally, but Some Local Markets Tell a Different Story

Job growth is one of the most important signals for home builders, as employment security helps shape consumer confidence, household formation, and the willingness to make a major purchase. And right now, the latest employment picture is a mixed one for the housing industry.

While employment growth remained positive, the U.S. added just 29,000 positions in September 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Meanwhile, unemployment edged up to 4.2%. The slowdown fits a broader pattern of relatively modest hiring rather than a sharp deterioration in the labor market.

The composition of growth is equally important. Education and health services remained the strongest employment engine, expanding 1.7% from a year earlier. Information employment, by contrast, fell 4% year over year, while financial activities declined 1.1% over the same period.

These differences matter for builders. Two markets can add a similar number of jobs but generate different levels of housing demand depending on the industries driving growth and the incomes associated with those positions.

The national slowdown also masks significant geographic variation.

Salt Lake City led the major markets tracked by Zonda with 2.8% year-over-year employment growth in September, followed by Raleigh at 2.1% and Las Vegas at 1.9%.

The picture changes when looking at the number of jobs created since last year. Dallas added 36,200 positions despite employment growing a more modest 0.8%. New York City added 29,800, Los Angeles 28,600, Houston 25,100, and Phoenix 24,400.

That distinction is also important: percentage growth can identify accelerating economies, while absolute job creation provides another measure of the potential scale of household demand.

At the other end of the spectrum, Washington, D.C., lost 66,800 jobs and employment declined 2% since September 2025. Indianapolis fell 1.1%, Portland 0.9%, and Atlanta 0.3%. Still, several markets with declining employment have not experienced unusually high unemployment rates, suggesting builders should avoid treating negative job growth as a standalone demand signal.

For builders making multiyear land decisions, the outlook through 2031 may be even more important. The strongest projected employment gains cluster in Texas, the Mountain and Desert region, and the Carolinas, per Moody’s. Raleigh is forecast for 9.9% total employment growth from December 2026 through December 2031, followed by Austin at 9.7%, Orlando at 8.4%, and Las Vegas at 7.9%.

#5466. Shoppable Model Homes Bring New Convenience to Buyers

Homeowners are becoming more practical in nearly every aspect of homeownership. This pragmatic mindset is also influencing the model home experience. For today’s home shopper, inspiration has greater value when buyers can actually put it to use.

Although buyers are drawn to the blank-canvas opportunity of a new build, decision fatigue is real, and tools that build confidence and save time are a welcome relief.

“We are seeing a lot of interest in making models actionable through features like the shoppable model home,” says Ali Richert, enterprise sales, head of home builder at Wayfair Professional.

In addition to shoppable models, furnished homes are popular too. A Zonda survey showed that 73% of buyers would be open to buying a furnished or partially furnished home.

With affordability still a challenge, buyers are looking closely at the overall value of a new-home purchase, including what builders can offer beyond the home itself.

“Regardless of why someone is buying a house, most home buyers will have one thing in common after getting the keys. They will need to furnish the home,” says Richert.

“Historically, the relationship between a builder and buyer ended at closing. Now builders are asking how they can help make the full journey easier.”

“This is one of the ideas that drive innovations like our shoppable model homes or even alternative closing incentives, like home buyer Wayfair gift cards. Instead of furnishing a model to inspire buyers, builders are beginning to view furnishing as an extension of the home buying experience itself,” she says.

In shoppable models, features like scannable QR codes, product links, online storefronts, or other purchasing arrangements simplify the process and bridge the gap between inspiration and real-life functionality, a pragmatic benefit that saves time and builds confidence when envisioning what life will look and feel like at home.

Various buyer groups see benefit in these features, explains Richert.

Investors may need to furnish a whole home quickly to go to market. A second-home buyer might want their home furnished immediately, so that vacations can be taken. First-time and move-up buyers may not have enough existing furniture to fill a space.

But regardless of why you are buying a home, “having a turnkey option for furnishing solutions can remove time, stress, and uncertainty from a process that can seem overwhelming,” she says.

“For a lot of buyers, especially after the long process of choosing a builder, a lender, a community, finishes, cabinets, flooring, and countless other decisions, the appeal of having to skip another major project full of decisions can be incredibly appealing.”

Love the look and the vibe of the model? Model home merchandisers make it look easy, but the aesthetic and the experience are the result of a highly curated, researched process that requires training, talent, and access to products.

Model homes not only display the latest trends and demonstrate how to make the best use of various spaces, but their design details are also selected to appeal to the target market. It’s no wonder that buyers find the aesthetic compelling.

“We focus heavily on purposeful merchandising and thoughtful space planning, showing buyers how each room can function, including multifunctional spaces and ideas they can realistically incorporate into their own home,” says Megan Calmes, director of sales and marketing with Creative Design.

“Additionally, we think about the buyer’s journey beyond the purchase. We want the model to feel aspirational, but also attainable.”

Models aren’t like generic furniture showrooms. The specifics of the floor plan guide the selection of furnishings, which means buyers are seeing pieces chosen for the very spaces they may soon call home.

For example, a buyer might choose a sofa on their own for the new living room, but that’s only a small part of the overall design. Accents like tables, rugs, and artwork matter too. The model demonstrates how these pieces work together, both aesthetically and within the room’s dimensions.

The model shows you how to assemble a look, not just admire it.

A flex room has a ton of potential, but will various uses work comfortably in real life? A model can demonstrate the size and placement of furniture and accents to support a particular purpose, or even multiple functions, within the available space.

Having shoppable tools, or the option to purchase the home furnished as demonstrated, can make those possibilities easier to recreate.

The vast majority of house hunters aren’t designers, so having access to professionally selected furnishings and decor gives buyers a practical head start.

Personalization is always possible, of course. Buyers might purchase the larger anchor pieces, such as a sofa, rug, and dining table, then bring in their own artwork, textiles, or accessories to make the space their own.
