#5465. Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max with training, attention optimizations

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. today introduced Qwen4-Max, its newest and most capable large language model.

The algorithm not only generates higher-quality output than its predecessor but also costs less. Those improvements are the result of a new architecture, Qwen4, that made the LLM’s training run more efficient. Additionally, Alibaba has equipped the model with an upgraded attention mechanism.

Qwen4-Max’s backbone, the part of an LLM that functions as its main processing engine, comprises 2.4 trillion parameters. The model activates only 71 billion at any given time. The backbone is supported by 328 billion so-called N-gram parameters, which function as a kind of cache. They save the results of oft-repeated calculations and thereby remove the need to compute them from scratch every time.

An LLM’s artificial neurons are organized into sets known as layers. When the model learns something new during training, a piece of data called a gradient travels through the layers and refines their output. The gradient moves through them one by one starting from the last layer, which finalizes and displays prompt responses.

Qwen4-Max includes a feature that enables the gradient to skip some layers. That feature, or residual, is effectively a shortcut inside the LLM. Its purpose is to reduce errors during the training workflow, which in turn lowers costs and improves output quality.

Residuals can also be found in many other LLMs. Historically, the mechanism was implemented as a single gradient transportation channel. Qwen4-Max’s implementation of the technology features four channels. Moreover, those channels have a “gate” that can adjust the movement of gradients to further improve the training process.

Qwen4-Max’s attention mechanism, a module that helps it understand user prompts, features two key customizations. The first is a technology called Gated DeltaNet that lowers the amount of hardware needed to process large prompts. The second optimization, QSA, skips pieces of data that the LLM doesn’t need to answer a prompt. That arrangement further lowers infrastructure costs.

Alibaba compared Qwen4-Max with its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, using an internal benchmark that includes knowledge work tasks. The former model achieved a higher score and used up to 35% fewer tokens to complete tasks. Those savings grew to 49% when the models were tested using the Terminal-Bench 4.0 suite of coding challenges.

Qwen4-Max is available through Alibaba’s cloud platform. The company plans to open-source a collection of smaller models based on the same technologies further down the line. It’s also open-sourcing Qwen-Live-Delivery-Plugin, an extension that makes Qwen4-Max better at performing time-consuming tasks.

When an LLM is assigned a long-horizon project, users often have to wait until the model completes its work before they can review the results. Alibaba’s plugin shortens the wait. It enables Qwen4-Max to quickly deliver an initial draft and then iteratively add improvements. Users can give the model feedback along the way to refine its work.

#5464. Builder Sentiment Falls to 14-Year Low in November

Builder confidence fell sharply in November as higher mortgage rates, persistent affordability challenges, and rising construction costs continued to weigh on the new-home market, according to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB).

The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell four points to 25 in November, its lowest reading since April 2012. The index stood at 29 in October. Any reading below 50 indicates more builders view market conditions as poor than good.

“Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” says Bill Owens, chairman of the NAHB. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.”

All three components of the HMI declined during the month. The index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, while the component measuring sales expectations over the next six months declined two points to 30. Prospective buyer traffic dropped two points to 16, its lowest level in 15 years excluding the onset of the pandemic in 2020.

In response to weaker demand, builders continued to rely heavily on incentives and price reductions to attract buyers. The share of builders cutting home prices increased to 46% in November, the highest level of the post-Covid period. The average price reduction remained at 6% for the eighth consecutive month.

Meanwhile, 68% of builders offered sales incentives, also a post-Covid high. November marked the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders reported using incentives. That represents a further deterioration from October, when 43% of builders reported cutting prices and 65% used incentives.

“The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” says Robert Dietz, NAHB chief economist. “Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence, and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.”

On a three-month moving-average basis, builder confidence declined in every region. The Northeast fell four points to 34, the Midwest declined five points to 35, the South dropped three points to 27, and the West fell three points to 23.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5463. Alex Trebek’s Former 578-Acre California Ranch and Winery Heads to Auction for $6.45 Million

A sprawling California ranch where Alex Trebek helped run a winery is heading to auction, giving buyers a chance to purchase nearly 578 acres of the Central Coast once owned by the longtime “Jeopardy!” host.

Known as Creston Manor, the property in San Luis Obispo County near Paso Robles is listed for $6.45 million.

In a press release shared with Realtor.com®, Concierge Auctions revealed bidding is scheduled to open on Dec. 4 and conclude live on Dec. 16 at The Dominick in New York City, where the ranch will be offered as part of the company’s year-end sale.

Lindsey Harn of Christie’s International Real Estate and Mike Goldfarb of Coldwell Banker Residential Brokerage Company are working with the auction house on the sale.

Creston Manor is the second former Trebek property in the area to come up for auction through the company this year.

Earlier in 2026, Concierge Auctions sold Windfall Farms, a nearly 724-acre property in nearby Paso Robles, for $16.9 million. The auction house said it marketed that property for 39 days before the sale.

Creston Manor was established in 1900, decades before Trebek became a partner in Creston Manor Vineyards and Winery in 1987.

According to the auction house, the game show host used the property primarily for ranching and wine production.

One vintage detail from the auction announcement ties the ranch to Washington, DC. Concierge Auctions says wine from the estate was served at President George H.W. Bush’s inauguration.

The vineyard and winery are still operational, according to the sale announcement.

The estate also retains parts of its ranching history, including a preserved blacksmith shop and the original Highway 58 bridge.

Those structures sit on the same property as the barns, stables, and livestock facilities that support its current agricultural use.

The ranch covers approximately 577.65 acres, with rolling pastureland and mountain views. Livestock pens are set up to accommodate cattle, horses, sheep, and pigs, and the stables provide dedicated space for horses.

The existing agricultural facilities are a central part of the offering, particularly for buyers who want to continue ranching or producing wine on the property.

Beyond the agricultural buildings, the property has five residences and a separate private suite. Together, the living quarters span approximately 7,550 square feet and contain 14 bedrooms and 14 full bathrooms.

According to Concierge Auctions, the estate can accommodate more than 30 guests.

Harn pointed to the combination of housing, winemaking facilities, and equestrian infrastructure as a distinguishing feature of the property.

The ranch is in Creston, a community in northern San Luis Obispo County with agricultural ties of its own. Goldfarb highlighted the estate’s seclusion and its proximity to Paso Robles, where the surrounding wine region is home to more than 200 wineries.

Paso Robles also has a downtown dining scene and the Tin City tasting district. Nearby Santa Margarita Lake offers kayaking, fishing, and hiking.

Concierge Auctions is handling the sale through its division focused on wineries, vineyards, and other wine country real estate.

Creston Manor brings those uses together on a single property, with the working winery and vineyard sharing the acreage with livestock facilities and multiple homes.

Chad Roffers, the auction house’s CEO and co-founder, said the company hopes to draw international bidders to Creston Manor, just as it did when it brought Windfall Farms to auction earlier this year.

The auction house also says a closing will trigger a contribution toward building homes for families in need through its Key for Key program, a partnership with Giveback Homes.

The company says the recognition adds to a growing list of honors earned by WREA and reinforces the company’s reputation as a franchise organization dedicated to helping entrepreneurs achieve their goals while maintaining the independence of local ownership.

#5461. Noeri raises $110M to help companies build living AI systems that self-improve over time

Noeri Inc., a startup developing artificial intelligence systems that continuously improve their outputs as they learn from an organization’s data and work, is launching with $110 million in funding.

Today’s round was led by Menlo Ventures and saw participation from Seattle-based Madrona Ventures, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Snowflake and Cisco Ventures also took part in the round.

Noeri is the brainchild of Yejin Choi (pictured, left) and Carlos Guestrin (right), two prominent AI researchers from Stanford University, who spent years developing self-improving systems at the University of Washington prior to moving. The startup’s software is designed to study a company’s data, workflows and business processes.

Then as it learns about them, it will begin to propose changes regarding specific tasks, in order to make them more efficient. The co-founders refer to it as a “living” AI system that gets better at what it does over time.

For instance, it might offer different instructions, suggest different tools or switch out the model that handles each step of a workflow for another. Each of these suggestions comes with an explanation and is sent to a human for review before it’s accepted, similar to how AI-generated code changes are implemented.

Noeri is compatible with both open-weight and proprietary AI models and ensures that customers retain full ownership of their workflows and the AI systems they develop. Choi told Bloomberg in an interview that Noeri is trying to appeal to organizations that find themselves having to choose between either paying fees they can’t afford for the most capable AI models, or else accepting results from a less effective one.

The idea for the company stemmed from an effort to help a microbiology and immunology team at Stanford use OpenAI Group PBC’s models in a more cost effective way. According to Choi, she and Guestrin developed a small AI model that learned how to use OpenAI’s older models, and to their surprise, managed to fine-tune it to perform better than the more advanced GPT-5 on that research team’s projects.

The startup’s name was carefully chosen. Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” and it’s meant to reflect Choi’s and Guestrin’s belief that the future of AI won’t be dominated by just one or a handful of extremely powerful AI models.

Guestrin especially is a big proponent of choice in the AI industry. In a speech at Madrona Ventures’ IA40 Summit in September, he notably argued that the future of intelligence cannot be controlled by just one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in a blog post outlining the startup’s mission. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t the only proponent of such a multimodel future. Similar arguments have been made by Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Labs Inc., which last year debuted Tinker, a cloud-based service that anyone can use to fine-tune AI models and enhance their performance. Similarly, Applied Compute Inc. embeds engineers with its customers to help them fine-tune AI systems.

Guestrin previously helped develop a popular machine learning tool called XGBoost, which is used by researchers to boost the performance of AI models. He also co-founded an early machine learning startup GraphLab Inc., later known as Turi Inc., which was acquired by Apple Inc. in 2016.  After that, he joined Apple too and went on to lead that company’s machine learning and AI research organization.

Choi previously led the Allen Institute for AI’s common-sense reasoning research team before joining Nvidia Corp. in 2024 as a distinguished scientist. She quit about a year later to join Stanford in early 2025, from where she helped Guestrin start Noeri in May.

Noeri represents the culmination of two separate research projects. Guestrin pioneered a new self-distillation technique that allows AI models to become their own teachers, turning mistakes into lessons that allow them to improve their responses over time. Meanwhile, Choi’s work on agentic orchestration has shown that smaller models that conduct teams of AI agents and tools can outperform much larger frontier models at lower costs.

Those two projects are the foundation of Noeri’s systems. The startup says it’s now working with partners across multiple industries, including some of its investors, which were deliberately chosen to ensure its systems could be exposed to a wide variety of work.

“Most new AI labs ask the market to wait years for a breakthrough,” said Menlo Ventures Partner Venky Ganesan. “Carlos and Yejin are doing world-class research and putting it to work inside companies at the same time. That combination is rare, and it’s why we moved quickly to lead this round.”

#5460. Abandoned Property for Sale: How To Buy an Abandoned Home

Buying an abandoned property can be a bargain for homebuyers—if you can actually find such a property.

Properties that are unclaimed by their owners are potential low-cost purchases that might be attractive to prospective homebuyers. They certainly have become all the rage on TikTok, with influencers snatching up properties left and right and sharing their renovation journeys.

Still, "abandoned house for sale" isn't a sign you're likely to see on the roadside. (There might actually be laws against that!)

An abandoned property is usually a property whose original owner is no longer in possession of the home. Due to the owner's financial difficulties, the house is typically run-down and in desperate need of repair. If the law in your area allows you to claim this type of home and you're handy, it might be worth investigating.

However, some abandoned homes for sale can turn out to be in good condition, with the owner hoping to unload the property before foreclosure. This could provide the right buyer with an opportunity to purchase the abandoned property or unclaimed home at a discount—and possibly a significant return on investment if you later flip it.

Purchasing an abandoned or unclaimed property involves following the same procedures as buying any other piece of real estate. Before setting out on your journey to find an abandoned home, review your financial situation.

Remember, there will be additional expenses over and above the original sale price of the property. A pre-qualification from your bank or lender will help you estimate what mortgage amount you qualify for. Many banks also require pre-approval letters, so you can make quick decisions on the property you wish to purchase.

Most abandoned homes for sale are on their way to foreclosure, but the bank has not yet initiated the process. Various lists of abandoned properties or unclaimed properties are available, or you can search for abandoned foreclosures or pre-foreclosures online.

Check for listings of homes for sale with certain phrases that might indicate an abandoned property, such as "immediate possession," "must sell," "below market value," or "under appraisal." Don't forget to add "near me."

Real estate agents will usually have valuable knowledge of abandoned properties in the area and the law relating to claiming them, and can provide you with a selection of homes about to be foreclosed on by the bank.

Some properties might look abandoned but are not listed for sale. You might also check into the laws regarding unclaimed property and whether there is a statute of limitations on its return.

If you find an interesting unclaimed property like this, visit your county clerk’s office. It will have information about the homeowners, the home's current appraised value, liens, or tax problems.

You could then try tracking down the owners and asking them to sell their property. If the property has had liens or tax problems, the owners might be more willing to sell.

Abandoned homes will almost always have issues. Due to months (or years) of neglect, a lack of maintenance, and overall aging, vacant homes are far from pristine. They are often sold as is, which means what you see is what you get.

One major risk? Abandoned homes usually have had their utilities turned off. With no way to check the water, electricity, gas, heating and cooling systems, or appliances, even a professional home inspector will be unable to thoroughly evaluate the house. There could be wiring problems, water leaks, or gas leaks—any of which would be extremely costly to repair.

It might be possible to have utilities turned on temporarily, but that requires paying a deposit and putting the utilities in your name. Even if utilities are turned on, you'll likely have to accept some elements of the abandoned home as is. But remember, forgoing major system inspections is a huge gamble.

A second major risk factor is the deferred maintenance involved with the purchase of a property that's been left to the elements. If previous owners abandoned the home or lost it to foreclosure, they probably didn't pay attention to routine maintenance tasks. Costly repairs will crop up sooner than expected, and you'll have to budget for future repairs.

And to top it off, obtaining home insurance on an abandoned home is difficult. Most insurance agencies won't insure a vacated house without an inspection from one of their agents. And that agent might require you to make costly repairs before issuing a policy.

If the insurer issues a policy, premiums for an unoccupied structure will likely be significantly higher. Because no one has watched over the home, it's more likely to have suffered vandalism or fire damage. Vacant homes often have broken pipes or leaking roofs with resulting water damage, stolen copper wiring, mold, pest issues, and damaged appliances.

Assuming you have found a potential abandoned property for sale and been pre-approved, you will want to factor in costs that will be needed to get the home into solid condition. Get a thorough maintenance inspection performed on the property, and note what needs to be fixed and how much it will cost.

Claiming a property like this also involves adding in the cost of the appraisal fee, pest and lead inspection fees, title insurance, closing costs, and other legal fees.

Crunch the numbers before you consider a bid. A real estate agent can also accompany you to the abandoned property for sale and point out the extra expenses you will incur after the purchase of this property. The agent can also help you figure out how high your bid should be. Look for the right opportunities, and you might find a home that is just right for your budget.

Angela Colley writes about real estate and all things renting and moving for Realtor.com. Her work has appeared in outlets including TheStreet, MSN, and Yahoo.

#5459. Corma raises $125M to train cybersecurity-optimized foundation models

Corma.ai Ltd., a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for cybersecurity teams, has raised $125 million in funding.

NEA led the Series A round. Corma stated today that returning backers Khosla Ventures, Coatue and Sequoia Capital chipped in as well. The company is now valued at $1 billion.

Corma, which has offices in San Francisco and Tel Aviv, says competing AI models are often better at launching cyberattacks than fixing them. The company recently conducted a test in which it asked several large language models to hack a simulated corporate network. They succeeded at installing a malicious file across 85% of the test runs. In contrast, the models found only 12% of the malicious files that they themselves installed.

According to Corma, the gap between LLMs’ offensive and defensive capabilities can give hackers an edge over cybersecurity teams. That’s the issue the company is tackling with its cybersecurity-optimized AI models. Corma says that the algorithms can speed up some breach response workflows by a factor of 100 while reducing the associated costs.

The company benchmarked one of its models against the competition using an evaluation called DefenseBench V5. The test measures two metrics: how reliably a model performs defensive cybersecurity tasks and how fast it completes them. Corma says that its model outperformed GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and several other cutting-edge LLMs.

The company’s algorithms find breaches by analyzing data from other cybersecurity tools. Corma can ingest telemetry generated by firewalls, network monitoring software and a range of other applications. The company says that its models not only find threats but also generate remediation guidance for each one.

Automating breach response tasks is difficult because it requires LLMs to filter numerous false positives and duplicate alerts. Moreover, models often have access to only partial information about breaches. Many companies discard cybersecurity logs after a relatively short amount of time to reduce data storage costs.

Corma says that its algorithms can perform breach investigations on a fully autonomous basis. If human input is needed, they alert a relevant member of the cybersecurity team. It’s also possible to manually steer Corma’s models via a Slack chatbot. An administrator could, for example, ask Corma to double-check whether a recent effort to remove malware from a compromised server was successful.

“Since we came out of stealth, demand from the world’s largest organizations has been overwhelming, and one of our hardest problems has been securing capacity fast enough to keep up with the demand,” said Corma co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Alon Pluda.

Corma will use its newly raised funds to buy more infrastructure and enhance its AI models.

#5458. At SC26, Nvidia debuts new Rubin HPC chip, scientific research libraries

Nvidia Corp. today introduced a set of offerings designed to speed up scientific research across a range of fields.

The lineup is headlined by Rubin HPC, an upcoming graphics card with significantly more cores than the company’s current flagship chip. It’s joined by more than a half-dozen software tools geared toward scientists and engineers. The technologies made their debut at the SC26 high-performance and supercomputing conference in Chicago.

Nvidia’s flagship Rubin graphics processing unit features 898 Tensor cores, transistor clusters specifically optimized for large language models. It also includes over 28,000 CUDA cores. Those circuits can run not only LLMs but also other workloads such as scientific simulations.

The Rubin HPC (pictured), the upcoming chip that Nvidia previewed today, will feature more than 50,000 CUDA cores. It will also ship with a new iteration of NVLink, the interconnect that Nvidia’s GPUs use to exchange data with central processing units. The current version of the technology can move 3.6 terabits per second per graphics card.

Nvidia stated that Rubin HPC will also include a “sparse data acceleration” feature. Sparse data is the technical term for datasets that contain a large number of zeros. Many scientific projects generate such data, particularly in fields such as biology and astrophysics. A telescope, for example, might use zeros to represent sections of space without any visible stars.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”

Nvidia plans to ship Rubin HPC in 2028. In the meantime, customers can speed up their scientific workloads using the software tools that debuted alongside the chip today.

Nvidia ships its GPUs  with a collection of libraries called CUDA-X that is designed to ease scientific research projects. The company’s SC26 announcement introduced several new additions to the suite.

Astrophysicists are gaining access to cuPhoton.xBeam, a library that makes it easier to analyze data from the Event Horizon Telescope network. It’s a collection of observatories used study black holes. According to Nvidia, cuPhoton.xBeam can perform data analysis tasks that historically took a month in eight minutes. It’s rolling out alongside cuPhoton.xLens, a library for simulating the plasma that fusion reactors use to generate electricity.

On the biology research side, Nvidia is open-sourcing cuSpa. It speeds up cell polygon calculations, which are used to study the structure of cells and the manner in which they interact with one another. Plus, an existing cellular analysis tool called rapids-singlecell is now available to Nvidia users in a containerized format.

Nvidia’s new biology research tools are joined by an AI bundle called Nemotron for Science. It’s built on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open-source LLM the company introduced last month. The model features 124 billion parameters and activates about a 10th of them at any given time. It’s partly based on Mamba-2, a more hardware-efficient alternative to the ubiquitous Transformer model architecture.

Nemotron for Science pairs the LLM with a set of pre-packaged post-training workflows. Researchers can use them to optimize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for specific scientific tasks. Additionally, Nvidia has added in nearly 50,000 chemistry-related questions. They can be used to post-train AI models and evaluate the capabilities of models that have already gone through the process.

“Nemotron for Science gives researchers open models, scientific data and post-training recipes to build specialized agents that reason through scientific problems and use CUDA-X accelerated tools to turn ideas into discoveries,” Buck said.

Quantum computers rely on a conventional processor to manage their qubits. Nvidia provides a set of software tools called CUDA-Q that makes it easier to link quantum hardware to its GPUs and CPUs. The company today expanded the suite with new building blocks for developing quantum software and an algorithm that can mitigate qubit errors.

Nvidia is teaming up with IBM Corp. and the U.S. Energy Department’s Fermilab to create a “modular quantum codesign platform.” It will combine the chip giant’s DGX B200 systems with quantum hardware from IBM. According to the companies, the goal is to create an environment that researchers can use to develop new qubit error correction algorithms and other quantum software.

#5457. EXCLUSIVE: Google Co-Founder Sergey Brin and Ex-Wife Nicole Shanahan List Malibu Home for $33 Million

The elegant Malibu estate that Google co-founder Sergey Brin purchased with his ex-wife, Nicole Shanahan, has hit the selling block for $33.5 million—months after it was listed as a rental.

Brin, 53, and Shanahan—who went on to join Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s short-lived presidential campaign—bought the "dreamy" Point Dume dwelling for $13.5 million in September 2020, just over a year before it was revealed that they had split after three years of marriage.

The details of their divorce settlement, which was finalized in 2023, were never fully revealed. However, reports suggest that Shanahan walked away with around $1 billion in assets, including shares in Alphabet, Google's parent company.

It has never been revealed how the former couple split their shared properties. Brin purchased another Malibu residence for $35 million just a few months after their separation, a move that many saw as a sign that Shanahan, 41, had kept their former marital home.

Property records viewed by Realtor.com® show that the five-bedroom, 7.5-bathroom dwelling is currently registered to a limited liability company in Nevada that is managed by Shanahan's family office. That LLC lists the same mailing address as her charitable organization, the Bia-Echo Foundation, which is named for the former couple's daughter, Echo.

While it's unclear whether Shanahan ever used the property as her primary residence, she revealed in an October 2025 interview with Frontier Magazine that she was living in a different California property: a mountaintop ranch where she was residing with her partner, Jacob Strumwasser.

Although the home was listed for rent for $175,000 a month in May, the property has now vanished from the rental market and is now available for purchase.

The listing, which is held by Michael Cunningham of Pinnacle Estate Properties, notes that it has undergone an extensive series of overhauls in recent months, describing it as a "newly completed estate."

"A long, private driveway leads to a secluded sanctuary surrounded by mature trees, lush landscaping, and beautiful ocean views, with the rare privilege of keyed access to Little Dume Beach. Meticulously designed with every detail reflects an uncompromising commitment to quality and sophistication," the listing notes.

The property comes with an array of upscale features and amenities, including "keyed access to Little Dume beach," a stunning stretch of sand that is known as one of Malibu's best areas for surfing.

The dwelling itself has plenty to offer, both inside and out. The 1.2-acre lot includes a dazzling swimming pool with a large spa and a pagoda-style area for shade.

The parcel is incredibly private, featuring a gated entrance, a long driveway, and tall trees surrounding the home.

The listing describes the home as the "epitome of 'quiet luxury,'" constructed with top-of-the-line materials and quality craftsmanship.

Upon entering the home, visitors are greeted with a spacious, airy foyer that opens to an elegant dining space and living room, where walls of windows flood the space with natural light. A curved ceiling elevates the room, while a fireplace keeps it cozy.

The dining area separates the living space from the enormous open-plan kitchen, which features a curved island and huge French doors that open to a private deck overlooking the grounds.

For those with a fondness for entertaining, a second meal prep area with its own stove and additional appliances will no doubt prove to be one of the most-used spaces in the dwelling.

Elsewhere on the main floor are a media room—which the listing notes could be turned into an office or library—as well as a generous gym and wellness suite.

"Designed with wellness and longevity in mind, the residence incorporates advanced clean-building technologies and carefully selected materials, including a state-of-the-art VRF climate system, copper and cast-iron plumbing, rigid metal HVAC ducting, sustainable denim insulation, and specialized wiring and shielding intended to reduce EMF exposure," the description adds.

Two more bedrooms can be found on this upper level, each with its own bathroom. Another bedroom is located in a separate apartment space with a private entrance, as well as an additional kitchen and living room.

In addition to Brin, the property has a history of A-list residents, having previously been owned by pop star Pink, who purchased it for $11.9 million in 2010 and used it as her primary residence until 2016, when she sold it for $12.5 million.

The property is located just a mile away from the Malibu home Brin bought for $35 million in April 2022, just a few months after it was revealed that he and Shanahan had split.

He has since expanded his Malibu holdings with another pricier property that he picked up for $49.7 million in July 2025.

However, Brin has recently joined the growing list of billionaires pulling their fortunes out of California amid the threat of Proposition 40, a one-time, 5% wealth tax on residents worth over $1 billion—a proposal that has since been rejected.

The Google co-founder has been an outspoken critic of the tax, likening California to the Soviet Union when asked why he left the state.

"I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same place," he told The New York Times in April.

California voters rejected Proposition 40, which would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth, with most proceeds earmarked for healthcare. Opponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argued that the measure could drive wealthy residents out of the state and reduce future tax revenue.

Brin has, quite literally, put his money where his mouth is, snapping up several properties outside of California in anticipation of the tax, including a $42 million mansion on the Nevada shore of Lake Tahoe and a $51 million Miami Beach dwelling that he bought from LVMH CEO Michael Burke at the start of the year.

The Miami property is located on the exclusive Allison Island, a 35-acre stretch of land that sits in the Biscayne Bay, between La Gorce and Miami Beach. The 24/7 guard-gated island is home to fewer than 50 single-family homes.

It was custom-built for Burke and his wife, Brigitte Burke, in 2019, five years after they purchased the 1-acre plot of land on which the home now sits for $11.7 million.

The spectacular property spans 10,000 square feet and has seven bedrooms, 8.5 bathrooms, a waterfront pool, and a private dock. The modernist design includes two separate wings of the home connected by a central walk-through area.

It's unclear whether Brin has any plans to offload either of his Malibu homes in the wake of his move from California. Neither dwelling is currently listed on the multiple listing service.

#5454. Open AI hit with lawsuit in California over Hugging Face rogue agent incident

California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced the state has launched a lawsuit against OpenAI Group PBC after the company’s AI agents earlier this year went rogue and hacked the open-source AI platform Hugging Face Inc.

The 31-page lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, claims Open AI has engendered the public and put institutions at risk by developing products without suitable safeguards. Bonta likened Open AI’s behavior to being a “public nuisance,” asking the judge to order the company to change its practices while imposing financial penalties for any money the company made from the high-risk areas of its business.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta said in a statement at a press conference. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”

Bonta believes that without external pressure, the scope and frequency of such attacks will increase in the future. “In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company,” he added.

The “unprecedented” rogue attack in question occurred on July 21 this year when one of Open AI’s agents escaped what was supposed to be an isolated testing environment — a sandbox. To break out of their restricted environment and access the internet, the AI models exploited a previously unknown security flaw in OpenAI’s systems. From there, they gained access to other parts of the company’s network, stole login credentials, and exploited further security weaknesses to break into Hugging Face’s servers.

In response to the lawsuit, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said he believes the company has been singled out when similar challenges have been faced at other major AI firms. “Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” he told media, adding that the company will continue to work with the state and share information to ensure public and institutional safety.

Nonetheless, Bonta has expressed skepticism about Open AI’s willingness to conform to safety practices, writing that through a “lack of transparency and misrepresentations” the company has continued to develop dangerous models with the ability to deceive and engage in malicious behavior.

Open AI is already facing lawsuits in eight states over a number of incidents. The company stands accused of developing technologies that have harmed the public by providing dangerous medical advice or steering people to make bad, sometimes harmful, decisions that threaten their safety.

#5453. Zillow Launches Four Tools to Narrow Down Homes, Agents and Affordability

To help renters and homebuyers answer questions, Zillow has announced the release of four new tools to help users rent or buy with more confidence.

According to a release, Zillow’s Home Loans’ BuyAbility℠ tool allows users to answer the question: How much can I afford? The Home Loans’ BuyAbility tool can help keep a buyer’s home budget more current and accurate.

Buyers can link to Experian—the credit reporting company—once to verify their credit and debt, and their target home price will update automatically each month based on any changes. BuyAbility is also refreshed daily with updated interest rates from Zillow Home Loans, Zillow notes.

Because the Experian integration is built on a verified credit score, the release notes that Zillow Home Loans can estimate what buyers can afford more accurately, so they can search with more confidence from the start.

Buyers can also plan for and track their progress toward homeownership as they pay down debt and improve their credit. The BuyAbility tool is free, has no impact on credit scores and doesn’t obligate buyers to use Zillow Home Loans.

“Moving is a series of important decisions, and each one gets easier when you have clear information in front of you,” said Cynthia Taylor, Zillow’s senior vice president of product. “These tools give both buyers and renters clarity at every step, and connect homeowners with local experts if they’re ready to sell.”

Zillow’s Regional Insights page addresses the questions of: Where should I live? The release says that it can also describe what it’s like to live in cities and neighborhoods across the U.S., so renters and buyers can weigh neighborhood tradeoffs and compare prices early in their search.

The “compare homes” module further narrows down lists of homes for buyers. Now, buyers and renters can view their top homes side by side, with photos, financial information and key details in one place. They can start a comparison from search results, listing or their “favorites,” and stop toggling between multiple tabs.

For the final new tool available, the release states that for off-market homes, Zillow now displays a curated list of Zillow Preferred℠ agent partners who recently sold similar homes nearby, allowing homeowners to compare and contact local listing agents who may be a good match.

All four tools are live on Zillow, with availability that varies according to the tool and the user’s platform, such as the web, iOS or Android.

For more information, visit https://www.zillow.com/product-releases/fall-2026/.

#5452. With $5M in funding, Pretxt launches runtime oversight layer to supervise AI agents in real time

Artificial intelligence supervision pioneer Pretxt AI is launching with $5 million in seed funding today as it tries to contain the very real risk of unleashing autonomous agents in production environments.

It has created a new kind of “AI Supervision” tool that applies oversight at runtime to ensure those agents follow a company’s rules at all times. Today’s round was led by Deciens Capital and saw participation from Howdy Partners, Service Provider Capital and NSV Wolf Capital.

The startup is pitching the idea of a continuous runtime supervision layer that monitors AI agents as they’re getting work done, contrasting their behavior with the parent organization’s rules and policies. If it spots an agent is starting to drift off-course, it will immediately intervene to put it back on the right track, before it can make a critical mistake that hurts the business.

Real-time guardrails like Pretxt has designed are likely going to become a priority for enterprises as they begin to trust AI agents with more consequential work than simply drafting emails or creating images. For instance, if agents are to be trusted with handling customer refunds and accessing mission-critical databases and modifying records within them, companies will need the strongest reassurance that they’re not going to mess up those tasks.

But those assurances are few and far between. AI is notorious for “hallucinating” responses when it doesn’t know the answer to a question, and autonomous agents have shown erratic behavior time and again. They don’t need a malicious prompt injection to start missing critical required steps in a workflow or invent policy exceptions to simplify a task they’re trying to complete. They’ve shown they can do this in both labs and in the real world.

In response, most security tools take a heavy-handed approach, blocking agents outright, but this means that work slows down. The other approach is to flag errors after the fact, but by the time that happens they could have already caused massive damage.

Pretxt’s co-founders Brian Soby (pictured, left) and Aaron Costello (right) realized that companies need a more balanced approach to agentic security and oversight. Soby, who serves as the startup’s chief executive, previously held senior security roles at Salesforce Inc. and Mitre Inc. before founding the software-as-a-service security startup AppOmni Inc.

It was there that he met Costello, who now serves as Pretxt’s chief technology officer. During their time at AppOmni, they uncovered several major vulnerabilities in AI agents developed by Salesforce and ServiceNow Inc. and began to understand what’s required to ensure those agents can still work safely.

Many traditional agent monitoring tools use a second large language model as a “judge” to monitor the behavior of the main LLM that’s doing the work. But Pretxt’s co-founders shunned this idea because it creates latency, increases compute costs and involves too much guesswork.

Instead, their AI Supervision platform is powered by a near-deterministic engine that evaluates agent’s actions in milliseconds in order to spot those that break the rules and intercept them in progress. The company reckons it can do this up to 60 times faster than LLM-as-a-Judge-based security tools.

The approach is effective. In tests on Zapier’s AutomationBench, Pretext was able to reduce agent policy violations from around one in five to zero. The tool is designed to be easy to implement, so teams don’t need a thorough understanding of the models or agents they’re trying to supervise.

Instead, they simply choose which policies, standards and guardrails should apply to an agent, and then they can keep track of them in real time. The platform allows users to track approvals, roll back plan versions and escalate any tricky edge cases to human decision-makers.

That last capability is especially useful, because many organizations’ security plans have gaps when agents encounter situations that were not previously envisaged. In such cases, Pretxt halts the agent and asks a human to decide what the rules should be.

“Supervising an AI agent shouldn’t mean becoming an expert in everything it touches or in how it’s built,” Costello said. “Teams tell us in plain language how it should behave and where the boundaries are, and we supervise and steer the agent to stay within them. So there’s no untangling permissions or digging into the agent’s internals.”

Pretxt’s AI Supervision tool is available in early access now. It’s primarily targeting high-stakes regulated industries where mistakes and hallucinations simply cannot be tolerated.

For financial services and insurance companies, it can enforce borrower verification rules and route complex claims to humans, while in healthcare and life sciences it ensures that agents don’t step outside of strict boundaries. In customer support applications, it can prevent agents from offering unapproved discounts or refunds to customers.

AI Supervision can provide a lot of different benefits to a lot of different people. Chief information officers and other senior executives will be able to scale higher-value AI projects safely, while security teams, compliance officers and platform engineers can address gaps in risk management and ensure low-latency policy enforcement without needing to stack additional models.

Enterprise Management Associates analyst Chris Steffen said the thing that really sets Pretxt apart is its focus on the basics. Not only does it check that agents are behaving themselves, but it also makes sure they’re doing the work they’ve been assigned without breaking any rules or cutting any corners, creating what is effectively a new category of AI supervision tool.

“Most tools ask if an agent is secure, compliant or observable, but far fewer can show if the agent is correctly doing the job it was given,” Steffen said. “Most tools can only report what went wrong after the fact, when it’s too late. Pretxt intervenes while the outcome can still change to get agents back on track.”

#5451. Buyers Need Cheaper Homes. Airbnb Is Putting $1 Million Toward Finding New Solutions.

For many Americans these days, affordable housing is still out of reach.

Airbnb is stepping up to the plate to try to change that.

The company announced a $1 million annual Housing Innovation Prize to support innovators and entrepreneurs who are striving to make it faster, easier, and cheaper to buy homes. It plans to distribute one award per year over a five-year period.

The $1 million prizes are intended for U.S.-based companies and nonprofits with ideas that are already in the works but need funding to succeed. These may include factory-built homes, faster construction sides, expedited permitting, or easier financing for new homes.

“Airbnb started as a way to help my co-founders pay their rent. Today millions of people do the same. Now we are helping to finance the building of housing in communities nationwide. We want to encourage others, through this prize, to think more creatively and ambitiously about home building and delivering affordability. Necessity is the mother of invention,” said Nathan Blecharczyk, Airbnb’s co-founder and chief strategy officer, in a recent press release.

While Airbnb’s efforts are a step in the right direction, experts agree that addressing the affordability crisis as a whole requires more funding, innovation, and collaboration across the industry.

Airbnb's initiative brings renewed attention to the need for more housing in the U.S., and finding ways to build it more efficiently and affordably is becoming increasingly important.

Realtor.com® data shows how serious the housing supply gap has become.

In 2025, new-home construction fell short of household formations, pushing the U.S. housing supply gap to an estimated 4.03 million homes. This demonstrates the need for new solutions that can make it easier and more efficient to build homes.

Addressing the shortage will also require evaluating and changing policies and regulations that may slow down construction and raise costs. That’s where the Realtor.com Let America Build initiative comes in.

It strives to encourage discussions and solutions on the U.S. home inventory and affordability crisis.

Several factors are slowing down homebuilding and driving up construction costs in the U.S., and initiatives like Airbnb’s could help.

“Builders cite slow permit processes, increased material expenses, and lack of skilled labor as the main factors raising construction costs,” says Michael Pearson, senior vice president of business development at A&D Mortgage LLC in Ft. Lauderdale, FL.

Additionally, with expenses on the rise and the pressure to keep homes marketable and affordable, margins for contractors and developers are very low.

Innovations for factory-built or modular homes, for example, could improve the situation. These homes are traditionally built homes assembled off site and delivered to a plot of land.

“While modular homes are more economical, as you don’t have to ship supplies and workers to a site build and you can better control costs and material overages, they come with logistical concerns, primarily getting the modular home on site. Innovation may find a solution that so far has not shown itself,” adds Pearson.

Gay Cororaton, chief economist at MIAMI Realtors + RWorld in Miami, points out that modular homes are simply more attainable for more households.

“The average price of a new manufactured home is less than $150,000, which could go up to, say, $300,000 for a double-wide home. At today's mortgage rates, for a household with $100,000 in income, that’s more affordable than a traditional home,” Cororaton explains.

Still, while the Airbnb Housing Innovation Prize could turn promising ideas into realities, Pearson believes $1 million prizes won’t be enough and innovations must be part of a greater strategy where we highlight issues, communicate ideas, and have demonstrable progress. It’s also important for other organizations to jump on board.

“I’d like to see more companies, nonprofits, and government agencies get involved with this kind of action. Housing safety and affordability is this issue of this generation, and together we can find solutions,” says Pearson.

Robert Trent, CEO and principal at Builders Capital in Puyallup, WA, agrees with Pearson and believes the success of Airbnb’s initiative will depend on what gets built after the award.

“The best-case scenario is quality homes people can afford, delivered at a lower total cost, with results that can be replicated across different communities,” Trent adds.

#5450. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

#5449. Wisconsin Couple Seek To Enforce $1,350 Judgment Against Each of Their Neighbors in HOA Dispute

A neighborhood outside Green Bay, WI, is locked in a yearslong legal battle, as one couple is now taking legal action against their neighbors to collect a $200,000 settlement.

What began as a dispute over a backyard fence has turned into an ongoing series of lawsuits, with neighbors being forced to pay $1,350 each in a settlement—and those who haven’t are now being taken to court.

The case is centered around Michael and Lisa Newman and their five children, who reside in the Nazcr Trac neighborhood in De Pere, WI. After some of their children were diagnosed with autism, the Newmans wanted to build a fence around their backyard, as they wanted the children to be able to play outside safely.

Citing the children’s diagnoses and that two of their children “demonstrated significant risk of elopement,” according to a press release from the Metropolitan Milwaukee Fair Housing Council, the Newmans wrote to the Nazcr Trac Property Owners Association (NTPOA) to request an accommodation to the subdivision’s “no fence” rule.

Neither the initial request, sent in July 2019, nor a subsequent request in December 2020, which included information about the association’s legal obligation to consider an accommodation due to the children’s disabilities, were answered by the association.

In August 2021, the Newmans filed a lawsuit against the association in federal court, alleging that it had discriminated based on disability, a violation of the Fair Housing Amendments Act. A judge granted a preliminary injunction in May 2022 that prohibits the NTPOA from enforcing the rule, and the family built their fence in time for summer, three years after the initial request.

While the family got their wish, the battle was just beginning for other residents of Nazcr Trac.

In August 2024, a settlement was reached, requiring the NTPOA to pay the Newmans $200,000—a payment that would be passed on directly to each household in the association.

Following the settlement, each property in the neighborhood was looking at a $1,350 bill. Residents told WGBA that they were frustrated by the situation and many had been unaware of the dispute until they received the charge.

One anonymous resident told the local station that most residents would have had no issue with the fence, and a poll of members could have saved a lot of time and money.

“If the board had polled us as members, a large amount of the members would have said, 'Absolutely, let the family do what they need to do to take care of their family,’” the resident said during WGBA’s initial coverage in 2025.

At the time, Lisa Newman told the station that she felt “not great” about her neighbors being on the hook for the settlement payment.

“It's just a really unfortunate situation, I think, for everybody involved, and the board kind of made that decision for everybody,” she told WGBA.

However, in September, the Newmans filed a new lawsuit against the NTPOA and a number of homeowners who still owe on the settlement.

Sixty-nine homeowners settled following the initial lawsuit, the Newmans’ attorney, Victoria Davis Dávila, told WGBA. The rest are now facing legal troubles of their own.

“There’s an outstanding judgment," Davis Dávila told WGBA. "You had the opportunity to pay. You chose not to pay it."

In addition to the association, 33 residents are named in the new filing.

“The Newmans want just as bad as anybody else to put this behind them,” Davis Dávila said, adding that the NTPOA membership as a whole could potentially be held liable if the outstanding amount isn’t paid.

The new lawsuit is frustrating and stressful for many homeowners who thought the issue would be behind them by now.

“Why is this coming back to us? It’s so unfair,” an anonymous homeowners told WGBA.

An answer and affirmative defense was filed by the Property Owner’s Association on Nov. 16, but the contents of the document were not publicly available at the time of publication.

Realtor.com® reached out to the legal counsel of both the association and the Newmans, but received no response.

#5448. SuperDial revamps its healthcare voice agent platform to stop AI bots wasting time calling each other

SuperDial Inc., the creator of voice-first artificial intelligence agents for automating healthcare workflows, is overhauling its platform with a new Agent-to-Agent RCM architecture.

The goal is to eliminate the compute inefficiencies that have arisen as autonomous workers become more prevalent in the industry.

The startup, which raised $15 million in a Series A funding round last year, is best known for its voice agents that automate payer operations, revenue cycle management and administrative outreach. It aims to alleviate the time-consuming burden of having to call health insurance providers, waste time on hold, navigate phone trees and check online portals for information. Traditionally, SuperDial has seen itself as a voice-first platform that’s focused on call automation, but the shift to its Agent-to-Agent RCM architecture suggests it wants to deemphasize phone calls as much as possible.

The company is addressing the friction that has emerged from the slightly dystopian reality that both healthcare providers and insurance payers have largely replaced humans with AI agents in order to automate routine calls. But the fact that agents are handling the calls on both sides creates huge inefficiencies, resulting in those bots wasting time and compute resources as they engage in unnecessary robotic conversations. Rather than streamline insurance eligibility checks, claim follow-ups and prior authorizations, those agents find themselves stuck in multi-minute phone exchanges to relay structured data verbally that both sides already possess.

SuperDial founder and Chief Executive Sam Schwager refers to these scenarios as the “bot wars,” and says they’re increasingly engaging in relentless and destructive battles with one another that cost both healthcare providers and insurance companies money.

“One side deploys AI to secure approvals and payment for care,” he said. “The other deploys AI to review those requests and, at times, deny them. Neither has a reason to stop. Every extra round costs more in AI spend, pulls in staff on both sides to handle what the bots can’t settle, and can delay payment and care. The result is more friction, not less.”

With Agent-to-Agent RCM, SuperDial is trying to sidestep the bot wars by no longer defaulting to outbound calls. Instead, it acts as a kind of omnichannel orchestration layer, where success is determined by the number of requests resolved, rather than completed phone calls. When a revenue cycle team initiates a request, SuperDial’s agents will first check the relevant electronic data interchange feeds and application programming interfaces to find the information they need.

If they find it, great, but if not, they will then try the payer’s web portals. If they’re still out of luck after exhausting all options for digital retrieval, only then will they proceed to place a voice call. Those calls are more efficient too, since SuperDial’s agents will retain all of the context from their initial search, so they only need to query the agent on the other side of the line for the information that’s missing.

Schwager said Agent-to-Agent RCM puts more emphasis on resolution, allowing a provider’s agent and a payer’s system to connect and work together to resolve administrative requests with less work on both sides.

“The difference between this and the bot wars is the definition of done,” he said. “Two agents were optimizing for their own side of the exchange, but now those two agents are optimizing for a usable answer — that is, the information the provider needs to move the account forward, delivered in response to a request the payer can actually answer.”

For customers, life becomes much simpler. All they have to do is tell SuperDial what it needs to know, and its agents will work to get the answers in the fastest time and most efficient manner possible. “How we get the answer is our problem, not theirs,” Schwager said.

Schwager said the industry needs to move away from the idea that healthcare administration can be improved by having two bots argue with each other faster. “If an agent already has the information, that context should travel with the request,” he explained. “If a digital channel can answer it, there should be no call. The goal is fewer exchanges, not faster ones.”

The company’s long-term goal is to create an AI-native network that facilitates seamless, automated payer-provider communications. The goal is to eliminate repetitive inquiries and cut down on the administrative delays that can negatively impact patient outcomes, Schwager added.

SuperDial says it’s already having a big impact. Since it founded its platform in 2021, it has handled more than 10 million automated calls between healthcare providers and insurance firms – interactions that would once have been made by humans. Had humans made those calls, it would have been much slower, because SuperDial says its agents average about four minutes per call when dealing with insurers’ automated voice systems, compared with 17 minutes or more when reaching a human representative.

With its architectural overhaul, SuperDial is now targeting insurers, in addition to the healthcare providers it already serves. Earlier this year, it announced it had signed a key deal with Guardian Life Insurance Co. of America to modernize its dental provider data attestation workflows.

#5447. Five Signs a Seller Has Genuine Negotiating Flexibility

Redfin’s September analysis estimated that sellers outnumbered buyers by 57.9% nationally in August, the largest gap in its records dating to 2013. Nashville, Miami and Houston had more than twice as many sellers as buyers.

“Buyers hear that sellers are negotiating again and understandably want to know how much they can take off the price,” says Nick Nastos, real estate broker and founder of Chicago’s Property Shop. “Before we talk about a discount, I want to know what else they could buy. If there are only two suitable homes in their budget, they may have less leverage than the headline suggests.”

Nastos recommends checking five signs before deciding how aggressively to negotiate.

Similar homes are selling below their asking prices. Recent closed sales reveal what buyers actually paid. Compare properties with similar condition, size and location, and check whether sellers provided credits.

“A seller asking $500,000 is giving you their opening position,” Nastos says. “If comparable homes are closing at $470,000, you have something concrete to discuss.”

The listing is taking longer than its competitors. A home sitting beyond the typical selling time for comparable properties may offer an opening. However, buyers should investigate why it remains available, including repairs, unusual layouts or financing complications. Check the original listing date and any previous withdrawals or relistings, rather than relying only on the current days-on-market count.

Buyers have several realistic alternatives. More national inventory means little if the additional homes fall outside a buyer’s budget or requirements. Count suitable alternatives in the same neighborhood and price range.

“If you can genuinely walk away and choose another home, that changes the conversation,” Nastos notes. “Ten listings you would never buy do not give you the same leverage.”

The seller is already adjusting the offer. Repeated price reductions or advertised closing-cost assistance can signal flexibility. A reduction alone does not establish a bargain, particularly if the original price was inflated. Buyers should assess the revised price against recent sales and expected repair costs.

Price is not the seller’s only priority. A seller may value a dependable closing date, flexible possession or fewer logistical complications. Buyers can also ask about repair credits or closing-cost contributions, subject to lender rules.

“Ask what the seller needs before assuming every negotiation has to end with a lower price,” Nastos says. “Sometimes you can solve a timing problem for them and preserve cash for yourself.”

His final advice is to set a firm spending limit before negotiating. A competitive neighborhood may justify a stronger offer, but it does not make an unaffordable payment safer.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5446. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.
