#5445. Three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Dell’s “AI Leadership Symposium”

Moving enterprise AI workloads into production introduces practical challenges for chief information officers. Those challenges include managing costs, scaling enterprise AI infrastructure and establishing governance models to keep agents in check and data secure.

Cost and control were major themes of discussion at Dell Technologies Inc.’s “AI Leadership Symposium.” Expanding AI workloads can drive up infrastructure and model costs, while deploying autonomous agents introduces new questions about security, oversight and data access.

At the same time, organizations are exploring different ways to run AI, from private cloud environments to models operating directly on devices. That is creating demand for enterprise AI infrastructure and partnerships that can accommodate a wider range of deployment needs.

“No one is asking whether to adopt AI; that’s pretty much a done deal,” said John Furrier, executive analyst at theCUBE Research. “They’re asking who controls it, where it runs and whose law it operates.”

Furrier spoke with industry experts from Dell, Deepgram Inc., Singulr AI Inc., MisaLabs Inc. and Intel Corp., among others, during the AI Leadership Symposium. The interviews covered the infrastructure, partnerships and computing power needed to scale AI. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete keynote analysis from John Furrier:

Cloud token bills remain a major pressure point on enterprise AI budgets. That’s leading some businesses to look for ways to relieve that pressure, according to Helen O’Sullivan, AI business development manager and solutions specialist at Dell.

“A lot of our customers I support in the Bay Area, they’re dealing with this real immediate struggle of running through their token budget in a matter of weeks that they had allotted for months,” she told theCUBE. “You still use those frontier models, but you use the open source and infrastructure on-prem to at least eliminate some of the token stress and token maxing going on right now.”

Organizations can also make better use of existing data center capacity when evaluating enterprise AI infrastructure investments. Dell and Intel are helping customers evaluate those options, according to Tim Wood, sales director for the Northwest region at Intel, who joined O’Sullivan during the discussion.

“A lot of enterprises already have [central processing units] in their data center,” he said. “There may be existing resources and headroom in the infrastructure they already have that’s capable of doing some of these next-generation apps and workloads.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Helen O’Sullivan and Tim Wood:

As companies deploy more AI agents, they need better ways to monitor what those agents actually do and ensure their actions align with company policies and intentions. That means introducing runtime governance that can assess AI agent behavior during execution, according to Shiv Agarwal, co-founder and chief executive officer of Singulr AI Inc., who spoke alongside Sri Viswanath, founder and chief executive officer of Sycamore Labs Inc., and Victor Jakubiuk, co-founder of MisaLabs Inc.

“[It’s] as simple as an action where it reaches out to the internet to get some data or sends out an email to a private account or something,” Agarwal told theCUBE. “That could be deeply hidden inside an agentic action.”

Good AI governance also means setting boundaries around where models can access data and how they process it. CIOs often prefer virtual private clouds to keep sensitive information within a controlled environment, according to Viswanath.

“They’re also trying to architect in a way that all of the data stays there,” he said. “They don’t trust sending it outside because then we don’t know where it goes.”

The pace of AI development complicates those governance efforts. Companies need to ensure their systems behave as intended even as AI capabilities evolve, according to Jakubiuk.

“AI has no limit to the speed of development, speed of progress,” he said. “As an enterprise, as that AI lead, you want to be able to take the latest and greatest and stay on top.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Victor Jakubiuk, Shiv Agarwal and Sri Viswanath:

Deepgram is working with Dell and Fortanix Inc. to bring its voice AI models beyond the cloud and onto customer devices. Potential applications range from interactive voice response systems for small businesses to AI-enabled laptops for students, according to Nick Mann, staff technical program manager at Deepgram.

“I want our models on those, on the hardware, to run natively,” he told theCUBE. “Air-gapped. That’s where we want to get to. That’s where AI as a whole needs to start meeting people where they are and how they’re going to use it.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Nick Mann:

Deepgram’s plans reflect a broader push to develop AI solutions tailored to how customers want to build and deploy the technology. In Silicon Valley, where technically sophisticated buyers often prefer building their own solutions over buying packaged products, Dell is expanding its partner ecosystem to help meet that demand, according to Sean O’Connor (pictured), regional manager of ENT West, large enterprise and acquisition, at Dell.

“For us, that notion of ecosystem is starting to change,” he told theCUBE. “Today we’re here with Intel [Corp.], we’re here with SHI [International Corp.], we’re here with Microsoft [Corp.]. But that ecosystem also now is starting to bleed into private equity and venture capital.”

#5444. Billy Joel–Linked Palm Beach Retreat Seeks $17.9 Million—With a Private Pool and Lavish Primary Suite

A recently renovated Palm Beach, FL, townhouse associated with Billy Joel has been listed for $17.9 million. It features a private pool, an elevator, and a primary suite complete with separate bathrooms and walk-in closets.

The four-bedroom property is being listed with Christian Angle of Christian Angle Real Estate. Its Mediterranean architecture and courtyard entrance set the scene for a residence that pairs formal entertaining rooms with outdoor spaces for dining and lounging.

The asking price puts the home well above its previous purchase price. According to Mansion Global, which cited PropertyShark records, the limited liability company that owns the townhouse paid $9.05 million in 2021.

A sale at the current asking price would represent an $8.85 million increase over that purchase, before accounting for renovation expenses, transaction costs, and other ownership expenses.

It would also put the closing price within striking distance of twice the amount paid five years ago. Joel’s association with the property has been reported through the company that holds its title. In 2022, Palm Beach Daily News reported the ownership connection.

Upon entering the residence, guests are greeted with a soaring foyer, where a staircase with iron detailing rises beneath a coffered ceiling.

The layout provides distinct spaces for hosting, working, and everyday meals, with a formal living room, a dining room, an office, and a breakfast nook adjoining the kitchen. A pecky cypress ceiling adds a wood accent to the cooking space.

The primary suite includes a Juliet balcony, along with its two bathrooms and two walk-in closets. Across the home, there are five full bathrooms and one half-bathroom.

The property, which was built in 2022, spans 4,956 square feet. A two-car garage and paved driveway round out the practical amenities.

Beyond the interiors, the pool is accompanied by an open patio, a built-in barbecue, and a sheltered area for outdoor meals. Worth Avenue, Mid-Town beach, and the Australian Docks are all within blocks, according to the listing.

The property adds another chapter to the musician’s extensive history of buying and selling homes in Florida.

The townhouse’s arrival on the market comes as Joel prepares for a public appearance in Boca Raton next month.

On Dec. 14, the songwriter is scheduled to take part in an event at Florida Atlantic University, where students will have the opportunity to ask him about his career and creative process, according to the Palm Beach Post.

Although the event’s title includes a reference to music, Joel’s representative clarified to the newspaper that the evening is intended as a conversation. Any playing would consist of short musical demonstrations to help explain his answers, with no band or prepared setlist.

The appearance follows a period in which Joel stepped away from his scheduled concerts after being diagnosed with normal pressure hydrocephalus.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5442. SiMa.ai’s Palette 3.0 runs many AI models on one chip and lifts throughput up to 3.5 times

Physical artificial intelligence chip startup SiMa Technologies Inc. today released Palette 3.0, a new version of its Palette software suite intended to allow many AI models to run concurrently on one chip.

According to the company, the release, which builds on the Palette Neat agentic development environment launched in June, can raise model throughput by as much as 3.5 times.

Developers building drones, robots and other autonomous machines, which need to run AI models on the device rather than in a data center, are a primary focus of the release. SiMa.ai argues that while industry incumbents rely on adapting legacy data center technology, it builds its software and silicon exclusively for physical AI.

Leading the new capabilities in Palette 3.0 is improved concurrent model execution on SiMa.ai’s Modalix MLSoC. Maintaining what the company describes as a low-power profile, a single chip can handle complex reasoning and multimodel workloads at the same time. The platform can also run separate Docker containers on the chip. Supported workloads include large language models and vision-language models.

Perception, depth and reasoning models used by drones and robots are also said to run faster on the new version. Working with ecosystem partners, SiMa.ai has added unified sensor fusion, dense neural depth fields and closed-loop digital twin simulation to the platform. The goal of the additions, SiMa.ai says, is to remove the integration and validation bottlenecks that slow down autonomous development.

Performance figures for those models are published in a new Model Registry, which SiMa.ai says measures every result within real-world power constraints. The company is offering competitive benchmarking details on request.

Also new in the release is a set of open-source capabilities for generative AI application development. Behind the 3.5-times throughput figure is speculative decoding, using the EAGLE3, DFlash and Gemma 4 MTP algorithms. Support has also been added for large mixture-of-experts models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s GPT-OSS-20B, which can now run on the Modalix MLSoC 16GB system-on-module.

Developers are free to adapt the open-source code, which is available on GitHub. Documentation for Palette 3.0 is provided through SiMa.ai’s Developer Center.

Founded in 2018 by Chief Executive Krishna Rangasayee, SiMa.ai offers a platform that combines purpose-built silicon with software for AI on physical devices. Notable customers and partners include Robert Bosch GmbH, Emerson Electric Co. and Synopsys Inc.

SiMa.ai raised $150 million in a Series C round at a $1.45 billion valuation in September. Fidelity Management & Research Co. and Amplify Partners co-led the round. The company has raised $500 million to date.

#5441. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.
